A filthy composition, sufficient to provoke vomiting

questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Articles*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Breeches; coat, waistcoat, and articles.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Avoir Du Pois Lay*?
questions.answer: Stealing brass weights off the counters of shops
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Stealing brass weights off the counters of shops. CANT.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Babes in the Wood*?
questions.answer: Criminals in the stocks, or pillory

questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Criminals in the stocks, or pillory.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Badge-Coves*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Bam*?
questions.answer: A jocular imposition, the same as a humbug

questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A jocular imposition, the same as a humbug. See HUMBUG.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Bandog*?
wrong: The act of hooking goods out of windows
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A bailiff or his follower; also a very fierce mastiff: likewise, a bandbox. CANT.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Bang Straw*?
questions.answer: A nick name for a thresher, but applied to all the servants of a farmer
wrong: Wearing apparel and bedding used by seamen
That part where the loaves have touched the oven
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A nick name for a thresher, but applied to all the servants of a farmer.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Barnaby*?
questions.answer: An old dance to a quick movement
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: An old dance to a quick movement. See Cotton, in his Virgil Travesti; where, speaking of Eolus he has these lines, Bounce cry the port-holes, out they fly, And make the world dance Barnaby.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Bear Leader*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A travelling tutor.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Beau-Nasty*?
wrong: A smart fillip on the nose
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A slovenly fop; one finely dressed, but dirty.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Beck*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A beadle. See HERMANBECK.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Bedizened*?
questions.answer: Dressed out, over-dressed, or awkwardly ornamented
wrong: A discovery, or the confusion occasioned by one
A clever cheat, a clean trick
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Dressed out, over-dressed, or awkwardly ornamented.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Beetle-Headed*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Dull, stupid.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Beggar Maker*?
wrong: A rogue, a hector, a bully, or sharper
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A publican, or ale-house keeper.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Belch*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: All sorts of beer; that liquor being apt to cause eructation.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Bellows*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: The lungs.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Bellower*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: The town crier.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Bellowser*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Transportation for life: i.e. as long.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Belly Cheat*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: An apron.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Belly Timber*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Food of all sorts.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Bellwether*?
questions.answer: The chief or leader of a mob
wrong: Beggars plying in a body at funerals

questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: The chief or leader of a mob; an idea taken from a flock of sheep, where the wether has a bell about his neck.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Bene Bowse*?
questions.answer: Good beer, or other strong liquor
wrong: A piece of lead of any shape, to be fired from a blunderbuss
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Good beer, or other strong liquor. Cant.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Bene Cove*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Bene Darkmans*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Goodnight. Cant.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Bene Fearers*?
wrong: A jeering name for a militiaman
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Counterfeiters of bills. Cant.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Bene Feakers of Gybes*?
wrong: A tumbler, juggler, or shewer of tricks
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Counterfeiters of passes. Cant.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Beneshiply*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Worshipfully. Cant.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Betwattled*?
questions.answer: Surprised, confounded, out of one's senses
wrong: A swindler, a sharper, a cheat
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Surprised, confounded, out of one's senses; also bewrayed.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Bever*?
wrong: Said of a person lying on his face
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: An afternoon's luncheon; also a fine hat; beaver's fur making the best hats,

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Bingo*?
wrong: A tumbler, juggler, or shewer of tricks
To shake, towzle, or tumble about
Level with the surface, every thing cut away
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Brandy or other spirituous liquor. Cant.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Bingo Boy*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A dram drinker. Cant.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Bird-Witted*?

Taking bounties from several regiments and immediately deserting
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Inconsiderate, thoughtless, easily imposed on.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *To Blast*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)

questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)

questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Blood*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)

questions.note: A jeering appellation for a soldier, alluding to his scarlet coat.

questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Blow-Up*?
questions.answer: A discovery, or the confusion occasioned by one
wrong: A person who lives by passing base coin

questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Blue Devils*?

questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Bluffer*?

questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)

questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Bolus*?

questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)

questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Borachio*?
questions.answer: A skin for holding wine, commonly a goat's

questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Borde*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Botch*?
questions.answer: A nick name for a taylor
wrong: Quips, taunts, severe or biting reflections
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A nick name for a taylor.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Botherams*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Bottle-Headed*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)

questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Bread*?

questions.note: Said of one absent, in a reverie, or thoughtful.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Brusher*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A bumper, a full glass. See BUMPER.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Bub*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Strong beer.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Bubber*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Bufe Nabber*?

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Buffle-Headed*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Bull*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Bull Calf*?

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Bull's Eye*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Bumkin*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Bummed*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Bung Upwards*?

questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Bunt*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Bus-Napper's Kenchin*?

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Caddee*?

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Cag Magg*?

Linen hung out to dry or bleach
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: An hypocrite, a double-tongue palavering fellow. See PALAVER.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Canticle*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A parish clerk.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Canterbury Story*?
wrong: A nick name for a shoemaker
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A long roundabout tale.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *To Cap*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: To take one's oath. I will cap downright; I will swear home. CANT.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Captain Copperthorne's Crew*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: All officers; a saying of a company where everyone strives to rule.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Captain Lieutenant*?
questions.answer: Meat between veal and beef, the flesh of an old calf
wrong: Those, who fabricate counterfeit passes, licences, and certificates for beggars
A college runner or errand-boy at Cambridge, called at Oxford a scout
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Meat between veal and beef, the flesh of an old calf; a military simile, drawn from the officer of that denomination, who has only the pay of a lieutenant, with the rank of captain; and so is not entirely one or the other, but between both.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Captain Tom*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: The leader of a mob; also the mob itself.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Caravan*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A large sum of money; also, a person cheated of such sum. CANT.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Cardinal*?
questions.answer: A cloak in fashion about the year 1760
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A cloak in fashion about the year 1760.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Carrion Hunter*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: An undertaker; called also a cold cook, and death hunter. See COLD COOK and DEATH HUNTER.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Carry Witchet*?
questions.answer: A sort of conundrum, puzzlewit, or riddle
wrong: Linen hung out to dry or bleach
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A sort of conundrum, puzzlewit, or riddle.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Casting Up One's Accounts*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Vomiting.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Cat Lap*?
wrong: An address to a supposed simple fellow, or nysey
To be a match for one who attempts to cheat or deceive
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Tea, called also scandal broth. See SCANDAL BROTH.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Cat Match*?
questions.answer: When a rook or cully is engaged amongst bad bowlers
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: When a rook or cully is engaged amongst bad bowlers.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Catch Penny*?
questions.answer: Any temporary contrivance to raise a contribution on the public
wrong: A lock in wrestling, by which he who uses it throws his adversary over his head
To reproach a person, or remind him of favours conferred
Grinning or laughing in a man's face
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Any temporary contrivance to raise a contribution on the public.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Catch Pole*?
questions.answer: A bum bailiff, or sheriff's officer
wrong: A taylor with a long bill
Easy to be imposed on, or taken in
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A bum bailiff, or sheriff's officer.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Cater Cousins*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Good friends. He and I are not cater cousins, i.e. we are not even cousins in the fourth degree, or four times removed; that is, we have not the least friendly connexion.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Caterpillar*?
questions.answer: A nick name for a soldier
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A nick name for a soldier. In the year 1745, a soldier quartered at a house near Derby, was desired by his landlord to call upon him, whenever he came that way; for, added he, soldiers are the pillars of the nation. The rebellion being finished, it happened the same regiment was quartered in Derbyshire, when the soldier resolved to accept of his landlord's invitation, and accordingly obtained leave to go to him: but, on his arrival, he was greatly surprised to find a very cold reception; whereupon expostulating with his landlord, he reminded him of his invitation, and the circumstance of his having said, soldiers were the pillars of the nation. If I did, answered the host, I meant CATERpiliars.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Cathedral*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Old-fashioned. An old cathedral-bedstead, chair, &c.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Caudge-Pawed*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Left-handed.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Cent Per Cent*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: An usurer.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Chapt*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Dry or thirsty.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Charm*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A picklock. CANT.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Chaw Bacon*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A countryman. A stupid fellow.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Cheats*?
questions.answer: Sham sleeves to put over a dirty shift or shirt
wrong: A slap on the face, and a kick on the breech
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Sham sleeves to put over a dirty shift or shirt. See SHAMS.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Cheese It*?
questions.answer: Be silent, be quiet, don't do it
wrong: Wine, or any other good liquor
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Be silent, be quiet, don't do it. Cheese it, the coves are fly; be silent, the people understand our discourse.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Cheeser*?
wrong: Criminals in the stocks, or pillory
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A strong smelling fart.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Chicken Butcher*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A poulterer.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Chips*?
questions.answer: A nick name for a carpenter
wrong: When a rook or cully is engaged amongst bad bowlers
A foul feeder, one that eats much greasy food
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A nick name for a carpenter.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Chirping Merry*?
wrong: To confess, or impeach a confederate
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Exhilarated with liquor. Chirping glass, a cheerful glass, that makes the company chirp like birds in spring.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Chitterlins*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: The bowels. There is a rumpus among my bowels, i.e. I have the colic. The frill of a shirt.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Choice Spirit*?
questions.answer: A thoughtless, laughing, singing, drunken fellow
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A thoughtless, laughing, singing, drunken fellow.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *To Chouse*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: To cheat or trick: he choused me out of it. Chouse is also the term for a game like chuck-farthing.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Chuck Farthing*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A parish clerk.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Chunk*?
questions.answer: Among printers, a journeyman who refuses to work for legal wages
wrong: An inferior in any office, or department
A meeting of apprentices and mechanics to rehearse different characters in plays
Usurers who attend the gaming-tables, and lend money at great premiums
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Among printers, a journeyman who refuses to work for legal wages; the same as the flint among taylors. See FLINT.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Circumbendibus*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A roundabout way, or story. He took such a circumbendibus; he took such a circuit.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Clack-Loft*?
questions.answer: A pulpit, so called by orator Henley
wrong: Usurers who lend money to the gamesters
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A pulpit, so called by orator Henley.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Clank*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A silver tankard. CANT.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Clank Napper*?
wrong: Linen hung out to dry or bleach
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A silver tankard stealer. See RUM BUBBER.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Clanker*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A great lie.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Clear*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Very drunk. The cull is clear, let's bite him; the fellow is very drunk, let's cheat him. CANT.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Clerked*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Soothed, funned, imposed on. The cull will not be clerked; i.e. the fellow will not be imposed on by fair words.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *To Click*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: To snatch. To click a nab; to snatch a hat. CANT.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Clicker*?
wrong: A stitch fallen in a stocking
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A salesman's servant; also, one who proportions out the different shares of the booty among thieves.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Clink*?
questions.answer: A place in the Borough of Southwark, formerly privileged from arrests
wrong: Usurers who attend the gaming-tables, and lend money at great premiums
An expression meaning an assemblage of low people, the mobility of all sorts
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A place in the Borough of Southwark, formerly privileged from arrests; and inhabited by lawless vagabonds of every denomination, called, from the place of their residence, clinkers. Also a gaol, from the clinking of the prisoners' chains or fetters: he is gone to clink.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *To Clip*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: To hug or embrace: to clip and cling. To clip the coin; to diminish the current coin. To clip the king's English; to be unable to speak plain through drunkenness.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Clod Hopper*?
wrong: A cowardly fellow, who gives himself airs of great bravery
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A country farmer, or ploughman.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Clod Pate*?
wrong: The old title for a country parson
The chief or leader of a mob
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A dull, heavy booby.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Cloy*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: To steal. To cloy the clout; to steal the handkerchief. To cloy the lour; to steal money. CANT.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Cloves*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Thieves, robbers, &c.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Clunch*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: An awkward clownish fellow.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Clyster Pipe*?
questions.answer: A nick name for an apothecary
wrong: The top side the other way
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A nick name for an apothecary.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Cobble*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A kind of boat.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Cobble Colter*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A turkey.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Cobblers Punch*?
wrong: A deposit in part of payment, to bind a bargain
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Treacle, vinegar, gin, and water.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Codders*?
questions.answer: Persons employed by the gardeners to gather peas
wrong: An expression meaning an assemblage of low people, the mobility of all sorts
The gaol at Kingston in Jamaica
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Persons employed by the gardeners to gather peas.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Cod's Head*?
wrong: King or chief of the link-boys
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A stupid fellow.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *To Cog*?
wrong: A gentle hand gallop, or canter
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: To cheat with dice; also to coax or wheedle, To cog a die; to conceal or secure a die. To cog a dinner; to wheedle one out of a dinner.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Cogue*?
questions.answer: A dram of any spirituous liquor
wrong: Stupid, melancholy for want of society
Soft paper for the necessary house or torchecul
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A dram of any spirituous liquor.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Cold Cook*?
questions.answer: An undertaker of funerals, or carrion hunter
wrong: One reeling, and ready to fall at the least touch
Tea, water-gruel, or any innocent beverage taken medicinally
Ballad-singers and hawkers of penny histories
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: An undertaker of funerals, or carrion hunter. See CARRION HUNTER.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *To Collogue*?
wrong: A quart pot, or a pint
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: To wheedle or coax.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Cool Crape*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A shroud.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Cool Tankard*?
questions.answer: Wine and water, with lemon, sugar, and burrage
wrong: A disposition liable to be cheated, an unsuspecting nature, open to imposition
Whispering on one side to borrow money
To use an unfair motion of the hand in plumping at taw
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Wine and water, with lemon, sugar, and burrage.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Colt*?
questions.answer: One who lets horses to highwaymen
wrong: To vomit from excess of liquor
A nick name for a taylor
Drawing in unwary persons to play or game
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: One who lets horses to highwaymen; also a boy newly initiated into roguery; a grand or petty juryman on his first assize. CANT.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Confect*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Counterfeited.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Conscience Keeper*?
questions.answer: A superior, who by his influence makes his dependants act as he pleases
wrong: Broken petty-fogging attornies, or Newgate solicitors
A slap on the face, and a kick on the breech
A cowardly fellow, who gives himself airs of great bravery
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A superior, who by his influence makes his dependants act as he pleases.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Content*?
questions.answer: A thick liquor, in imitation of chocolate, made of milk and gingerbread
wrong: A plant, once in great estimation as a medicine
To speak through the nose, to snuffle
An illiterate unbeneficed curate, a patrico
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A thick liquor, in imitation of chocolate, made of milk and gingerbread.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Cork-Brained*?
wrong: A stealer of cows and calves
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Light-headed, foolish.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Corporation*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: The magistrates, &c. of a corporate town. Corpus sine ratione. Freemen of a corporation's work; neither strong nor handsome.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Cosset*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A foundling. Cosset colt or lamb; a colt or lamb brought up by hand.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Costard*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: The head. I'll smite your costard; I'll give you a knock on the head.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *To Couch a Hogshead*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: To lie down to sleep. CANT.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Crab Lanthorn*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A peevish fellow.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Crabs*?
questions.answer: A losing throw to the main at hazard
wrong: A thief who hides himself under a bed, in Order to rob the house
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A losing throw to the main at hazard.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *To Crack*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: To boast or brag; also to break. I cracked his napper; I broke his head.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Cracker*?
questions.answer: Crust, sea biscuit, or ammunition loaf
wrong: To vomit from excess of liquor
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Crust, sea biscuit, or ammunition loaf; also the backside. Farting crackers; breeches.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Cracksman*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A house-breaker. The kiddy is a clever cracksman; the young fellow is a very expert house-breaker.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Crag*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: The neck.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Cramp Rings*?
wrong: The highway, or a robber thereon
Meat between veal and beef, the flesh of an old calf
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Bolts, shackles, or fetters. CANT.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Crank*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Gin and water; also, brisk, pert.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *To Creeme*?
questions.answer: To slip or slide any thing into the hands of another
wrong: To speak through the nose, to snuffle
Those, who fabricate counterfeit passes, licences, and certificates for beggars
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: To slip or slide any thing into the hands of another. CANT.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Creepers*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Gentlemen's companions, lice.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Croaker*?
questions.answer: One who is always foretelling some accident or misfortune
wrong: The point at which schoolboys stand to shoot their marbles at taw
A man imprisoned for any offence
An illiterate unbeneficed curate, a patrico
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: One who is always foretelling some accident or misfortune: an allusion to the croaking of a raven, supposed ominous.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Croakers*?
questions.answer: Forestallers, called also Kidders and Tranters
wrong: A place in the Borough of Southwark, formerly privileged from arrests
A rogue, a hector, a bully, or sharper
A modern card meeting at a private house
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Forestallers, called also Kidders and Tranters.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Croker*?
wrong: A person who lives by passing base coin
A gentle hand gallop, or canter
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A groat, or four pence.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Crook*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Sixpence.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Cropsick*?
questions.answer: Sickness in the stomach, arising from drunkenness
wrong: A horse that shrinks from the collar and will not draw
King or chief of the link-boys
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Sickness in the stomach, arising from drunkenness.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Crowd*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A fiddle: probably from CROOTH, the Welch name for that instrument.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Crowdero*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A fiddler.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Crowdy*?
wrong: A spruce, trim, or smart fellow
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Oatmeal and water, or milk; a mess much eaten in the north.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Cull*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A man, honest or otherwise. A bob cull; a good-natured, quiet fellow. CANT.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Cunningham*?
questions.answer: A punning appellation for a simple fellow
wrong: Half a quarter of a sheet
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A punning appellation for a simple fellow.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Curbing Law*?
questions.answer: The act of hooking goods out of windows
wrong: To snatch, or tear any thing forcibly from the person
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: The act of hooking goods out of windows: the curber is the thief, the curb the hook. CANT.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Cursitors*?
questions.answer: Broken petty-fogging attornies, or Newgate solicitors
wrong: A two-wheeled chaise, buggy, or noddy, drawn by two horses, one before the other
To game by tossing up halfpence
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Broken petty-fogging attornies, or Newgate solicitors. CANT.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *To Cut Bene*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: To speak gently. To cut bene whiddes; to give good words. To cut queer whiddes; to give foul language. To cut a bosh, or a flash; to make a figure. CANT.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Dace*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Two pence. Tip me a dace; lend me two pence. CANT.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Daisy Kickers*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Ostlers at great inns.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Damber*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A rascal. See DIMBER.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Damper*?
questions.answer: A luncheon, or snap before dinner
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Dandy Grey Russet*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Dandy Prat*?
wrong: Sickness in the stomach, arising from drunkenness
A false evidence, one that is ready to swear any thing for hire
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: An insignificant or trifling fellow.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Dapper Fellow*?
wrong: A cloak in fashion about the year 1760
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A smart, well-made, little man.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Darby*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Ready money. CANT.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Darkmans*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: The night. CANT.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Dash*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A tavern drawer. To cut a dash: to make a figure.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Dead Cargo*?
questions.answer: A term used by thieves, when they are disappointed in the value of their booty
wrong: An undertaker of funerals, or carrion hunter
The department of stealing portmanteaus, trunks, &c
To pawn or sell to a receiver of stolen goods
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)

A mixture of half tea and half coffee

questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)

questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A neat little man.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Devil Drawer*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A miserable painter.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Devil's Dung*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Assafoetida.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Devil's Guts*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A surveyor's chain: so called by farmers, who do not like their land should be measured by their landlords.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Deusea Ville*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: The country. Cant.

wrong: A man imprisoned for any offence
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)

questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)

questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A sham shirt.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *To Diddle*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: To cheat. To defraud. The cull diddled me out of my dearee; the fellow robbed me of my sweetheart. See Jeremy Diddler In Raising The Wind.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Dimber Damber*?
questions.answer: A top man, or prince, among the canting crew
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A top man, or prince, among the canting crew: also the chief rogue of the gang, or the completest cheat. CANT.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Ding*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: To knock down. To ding it in one's ears; to reproach or tell one something one is not desirous of hearing. Also to throw away or hide: thus a highwayman who throws away or hides any thing with which he robbed, to prevent being known or detected, is, in the canting lingo, styled a Dinger.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Ding Boy*?
questions.answer: A rogue, a hector, a bully, or sharper
wrong: Grinning or laughing in a man's face

Taking bounties from several regiments and immediately deserting
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A mittimus, or justice of the peace's warrant, for the commitment of a rogue.

questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Loaded or false dice.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Diver*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A pickpocket; also one who lives in a cellar.

wrong: Quips, taunts, severe or biting reflections
An inferior in any office, or department
A modern card meeting at a private house
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Milk and water, with a little rum, and some nutmeg; also the name of a composition used by distillers, to make spirits appear stronger than they really are, or, in their phrase, better proof.

questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Loaded dice, that will run but two or three chances. They put the doctors upon him; they cheated him with loaded dice.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Dog's Soup*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Dowse On the Chops*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Drop in the Eye*?

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Dub the Jigger*?

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Eves*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)

questions.answer: One that lurks about to rob hen-roosts
wrong: A coach drawn by three horses
A foul feeder, one that eats much greasy food
Proper, as it ought to be
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Feak*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: The fundament.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Fellow Commoner*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: An empty bottle: so called at the university of Cambridge, where fellow commoners are not in general considered as over full of learning. At Oxford an empty bottle is called a gentleman commoner for the same reason. They pay at Cambridge 250 l. a year for the privilege of wearing a gold or silver tassel to their caps. The younger branches of the nobility have the privilege of wearing a hat, and from thence are denominated HAT FELLOW COMMONERS.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *To Fence*?

wrong: Usurers who lend money to the gamesters

A camp game with three dice

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Fencing Ken*?
questions.answer: The magazine, or warehouse, where stolen goods are secreted
wrong: To slip or slide any thing into the hands of another

questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: The magazine, or warehouse, where stolen goods are secreted.

questions.note: A trick, wheedle, or invention to deceive.

questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)

questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: All sixpences: sixpence being the usual sum paid by each couple, for music at country wakes and hops. Fiddler's fare; meat, drink, and money. Fiddler's pay; thanks and wine.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Field Lane Duck*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A baked sheep's head.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Fine*?
questions.answer: A man imprisoned for any offence
wrong: A house of office, a cacatorium
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A man imprisoned for any offence. A fine of eighty-four months; a transportation for seven years.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Finger Post*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A parson: so called, because he points out a way to others which he never goes himself. Like the finger post, he points out a way he has never been, and probably will never go, i.e. the way to heaven.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *To Fire a Slug*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Floating Hell*?

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Fun*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A cheat, or trick. Do you think to fun me out of it? Do you think to cheat me?--Also the breech, perhaps from being the abbreviation of fundament. I'll kick your fun. CANT.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *To Funk*?
questions.answer: To use an unfair motion of the hand in plumping at taw
wrong: To pawn or sell to a receiver of stolen goods
A coach drawn by three horses
Oatmeal and water boiled to a jelly
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: To use an unfair motion of the hand in plumping at taw. SCHOOLBOY'S TERM.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Funk*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: To smoke; figuratively, to smoke or stink through fear. I was in a cursed funk. To funk the cobler; a schoolboy's trick, performed with assafoettida and cotton, which are stuffed into a pipe: the cotton being lighted, and the bowl of the pipe covered with a coarse handkerchief, the smoke is blown out at the small end, through the crannies of a cobler's stall.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Furmen*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Aldermen.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Fustian*?
wrong: To vomit from excess of liquor
A quirk or quibble in the law
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Bombast language. Red fustian; port wine.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *To Fuzz*?
wrong: A nick name for a taylor
An hypocrite, a double-tongue palavering fellow
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: To shuffle cards minutely: also, to change the pack.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Gabby*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A foolish fellow.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *To Gaff*?
questions.answer: To game by tossing up halfpence
wrong: Ballad-singers and hawkers of penny histories
When a rook or cully is engaged amongst bad bowlers
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: To game by tossing up halfpence.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Gage*?
questions.answer: A quart pot, or a pint
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A quart pot, or a pint; also a pipe. CANT.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Galimaufrey*?
questions.answer: A hodgepodge made up of the remnants and scraps of the larder
wrong: A pace between a walk and a run, a dog-trot
A deposit in part of payment, to bind a bargain
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A hodgepodge made up of the remnants and scraps of the larder.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Galligaskins*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Breeches.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Gamon*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: To humbug. To deceive, To tell lies. What rum gamon the old file pitched to the flat; how finely the knowing old fellow humbugged the fool.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Gamon and Patter*?
questions.answer: Common place talk of any profession
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Common place talk of any profession; as the gamon and patter of a horse-dealer, sailor, &c.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Gan*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: The mouth or lips. Cant.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Gentle Craft*?
wrong: A coach, cart, or other wheeled carriage
The vulgar word for a skeleton
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: The art of shoemaking. One of the gentle craft: a shoemaker: so called because once practised by St. Crispin.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Gentleman Commoner*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: An empty bottle; an university joke, gentlemen commoners not being deemed over full of learning.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Gibbe*?
questions.answer: A horse that shrinks from the collar and will not draw
wrong: A camp game with three dice
A jeering name for a militiaman
Mead and ale sweetened with honey
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A horse that shrinks from the collar and will not draw.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Gin Spinner*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A distiller.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Gingerbread Work*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Gilding and carving: these terms are particularly applied by seamen on board Newcastle colliers, to the decorations of the sterns and quarters of West-Indiamen, which they have the greatest joy in defacing.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Girds*?
questions.answer: Quips, taunts, severe or biting reflections
wrong: Linen hung out to dry or bleach
One whose employment is to empty necessary houses
A term used by sailors, to signify all landsmen on board their ships
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Quips, taunts, severe or biting reflections.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Glaze*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A window.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Glimfenders*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Andirons. CANT.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Glimflashy*?
wrong: A club or society of citizens of London
A nick name for a taylor
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Angry, or in a passion. CANT.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Glim Jack*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A link-boy. CANT.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Glimmerers*?
questions.answer: Persons begging with sham licences, pretending losses by fire
wrong: A college runner or errand-boy at Cambridge, called at Oxford a scout
A bumper, a glass filled so full as to leave no room for the lip
A mittimus, or justice of the peace's warrant, for the commitment of a rogue
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Persons begging with sham licences, pretending losses by fire.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Glimstick*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A candlestick. CANT.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Glybe*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A writing. CANT.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Goads*?
questions.answer: Those who wheedle in chapmen for horse-dealers
wrong: A thief or receiver of stolen goods
A top man, or prince, among the canting crew
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Those who wheedle in chapmen for horse-dealers.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Gob String*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A bridle.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Godfather*?
questions.answer: He who pays the reckoning, or answers for the rest of the company
wrong: A cloak in fashion about the year 1760
A gamester, one who rattles Saint Hugh's bones, i.e. the dice
A deposit in part of payment, to bind a bargain
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: He who pays the reckoning, or answers for the rest of the company: as, Will you stand godfather, and we will take care of the brat; i.e. repay you another time. Jurymen are also called godfathers, because they name the crime the prisoner before them has been guilty of, whether felony, petit larceny, &c.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Gog and Magog*?
questions.answer: Two giants, whose effigies stand on each side of the clock in Guildhall, London
wrong: Goods taken up at thrice their value, by young spendthrifts, upon trust
A kind of fiddle, originally made perhaps out of a gourd
A two-wheeled chaise, buggy, or noddy, drawn by two horses, one before the other
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Two giants, whose effigies stand on each side of the clock in Guildhall, London; of whom there is a tradition, that, when they hear the clock strike one, on the first of April, they will walk down from their places.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Gold Finder*?
questions.answer: One whose employment is to empty necessary houses
wrong: A broker's shop, or that of a receiver of stolen goods
A man in the civil line, a townsman, or tradesman
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: One whose employment is to empty necessary houses; called also a tom-turd-man, and night-man: the latter, from that business being always performed in the night.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Gollumpus*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A large, clumsy fellow.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Goree*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Money, chiefly gold: perhaps from the traffic carried on at that place, which is chiefly for gold dust. CANT.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Grannum's Gold*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Hoarded money: supposed to have belonged to the grandmother of the possessor.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Grappling Irons*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Handcuffs.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Great Joseph*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A surtout. CANT.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Green Bag*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: An attorney: those gentlemen carry their clients' deeds in a green bag; and, it is said, when they have no deeds to carry, frequently fill them with an old pair of breeches, or any other trumpery, to give themselves the appearance of business.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Grey Parson*?
questions.answer: A farmer who rents the tithes of the rector or vicar
wrong: A drone, one that cannot rise in the morning
A two-wheeled chaise, buggy, or noddy, drawn by two horses, one before the other
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A farmer who rents the tithes of the rector or vicar.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Grig*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A farthing. A merry grig; a fellow as merry as a grig: an allusion to the apparent liveliness of a grig, or young eel.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Ground Squirrel*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A hog, or pig. SEA TERM.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Grunter's Gig*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A smoaked hog's face.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Grunting Peck*?
questions.answer: Pork, bacon, or any kind of hog's flesh
wrong: A violent, pettish, or passionate person
Beggars plying in a body at funerals
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Pork, bacon, or any kind of hog's flesh.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Gudgeon*?
wrong: A lawyer who has a confused understanding
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: One easily imposed on. To gudgeon; to swallow the bait, or fall into a trap: from the fish of that name, which is easily taken.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Gullgropers*?
questions.answer: Usurers who lend money to the gamesters
wrong: When a rook or cully is engaged amongst bad bowlers
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Usurers who lend money to the gamesters.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Gum*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Abusive language. Come, let us have no more of your gum.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Gutfoundered*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Exceeding hungry.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Guy*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A dark lanthorn: an allusion to Guy Faux, the principal actor in the gunpowder plot. Stow the guy: conceal the lanthorn.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Gyp*?
questions.answer: A college runner or errand-boy at Cambridge, called at Oxford a scout
wrong: A drone, one that cannot rise in the morning
Any temporary contrivance to raise a contribution on the public
Beggars plying in a body at funerals
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A college runner or errand-boy at Cambridge, called at Oxford a scout. See SCOUT.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Haberdasher of Pronouns*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A schoolmaster, or usher.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Half Seas Over*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Almost drunk.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Hark-Ye-Ing*?
questions.answer: Whispering on one side to borrow money
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Whispering on one side to borrow money.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Harman Beck*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A beadle. CANT.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Harmans*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: The stocks. CANT.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Harry*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A country fellow. CANT.--Old Harry; the Devil.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Hasty Pudding*?
questions.answer: Oatmeal and milk boiled to a moderate thickness, and eaten with sugar and butter
wrong: One who moistens his clay freely, in order to make it stick together
To use an unfair motion of the hand in plumping at taw
A nick name for a thresher, but applied to all the servants of a farmer
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Oatmeal and milk boiled to a moderate thickness, and eaten with sugar and butter. Figuratively, a wet, muddy road: as, The way through Wandsworth is quite a hasty pudding. To eat hot hasty pudding for a laced hat, or some other prize, is a common feat at wakes and fairs.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Havy Cavy*?
wrong: A deposit in part of payment, to bind a bargain
Very old and strong beer, called also stingo
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Wavering, doubtful, shilly shally.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Heavers*?
questions.answer: Thieves who make it their business to steal tradesmen's shop-books
wrong: One whose employment is to empty necessary houses
A head of a house, or master of a college, at the universities
Regular drinking over the left thumb
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Thieves who make it their business to steal tradesmen's shop-books. CANT.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Hedge Priest*?
questions.answer: An illiterate unbeneficed curate, a patrico
wrong: A lawyer who has a confused understanding
That part where the loaves have touched the oven
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: An illiterate unbeneficed curate, a patrico.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Hell*?
questions.answer: A taylor's repository for his stolen goods, called cabbage
wrong: Food, good meat roasted or boiled
Misnaming and misapplying any hard word
A great hulkey or clumsy fellow
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A taylor's repository for his stolen goods, called cabbage: see CABBAGE. Little hell; a small dark covered passage, leading from London-wall to Bell-alley.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Hell Fire Dick*?
questions.answer: The Cambridge driver of the Telegraph
wrong: A swindler, a sharper, a cheat
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: The Cambridge driver of the Telegraph. The favorite companion of the University fashionables, and the only tutor to whose precepts they attend.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Here and Thereian*?
questions.answer: One who has no settled place of residence
wrong: A nick name for the purser of a ship
A term used by sailors, to signify all landsmen on board their ships
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: One who has no settled place of residence.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Hertfordshire Kindness*?
questions.answer: Drinking twice to the same person
wrong: Those who wheedle in chapmen for horse-dealers
Paint for the face, or cosmetic water
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Drinking twice to the same person.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Hidebound*?
wrong: A tumbler, juggler, or shewer of tricks
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Stingy, hard of delivery; a poet poor in invention, is said to have a hidebound muse.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *High Flyers*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Tories, Jacobites.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Hobbled*?
wrong: One who lets horses to highwaymen
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Impeded, interrupted, puzzled. To hobble; to walk lamely.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Hobbledygee*?
questions.answer: A pace between a walk and a run, a dog-trot
wrong: Wine and water, with lemon, sugar, and burrage
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A pace between a walk and a run, a dog-trot.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Hobson's Choice*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: That or none; from old Hobson, a famous carrier of Cambridge, who used to let horses to the students; but never permitted them to chuse, always allotting each man the horse he thought properest for his manner of riding and treatment.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Hocks*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: vulgar appellation for the feet. You have left the marks of your dirty hocks on my clean stairs; a frequent complaint from a mop squeezer to a footman.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Hodmandods*?
wrong: Common place talk of any profession
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Snails in their shells.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Hog Grubber*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A mean stingy fellow.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Hogo*?
questions.answer: Corruption of haut goust, high taste, or flavour
wrong: A cowardly fellow, who gives himself airs of great bravery
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Corruption of haut goust, high taste, or flavour; commonly said of flesh somewhat tainted. It has a confounded hogo; it stinks confoundedly.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *To Hop the Twig*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: To run away. CANT.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Hop Merchant*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A dancing master. See CAPER MERCHANT.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Horse Buss*?
questions.answer: A kiss with a loud smack
wrong: Coarse lace once much in fashion
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A kiss with a loud smack; also a bite.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Hubble De Shuff*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Confusedly. To fire hubble de shuff, to fire quick and irregularly. OLD MILITARY TERM.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Huckle My Buff*?
questions.answer: Beer, egg, and brandy, made hot
wrong: Mead and ale sweetened with honey
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Beer, egg, and brandy, made hot.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Hugger Mugger*?
questions.answer: By stealth, privately, without making an appearance
wrong: A foul feeder, one that eats much greasy food
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: By stealth, privately, without making an appearance. They spent their money in a hugger mugger way.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Hugotontheonbiquiffinarians*?
wrong: A foul feeder, one that eats much greasy food
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A society existing in 1748.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Hum Box*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A pulpit.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Hum Cap*?
questions.answer: Very old and strong beer, called also stingo
wrong: Thrown from a horse, or overturned in a carriage
An illiterate unbeneficed curate, a patrico
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Very old and strong beer, called also stingo. See STINGO.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Hummer*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A great lye, a rapper. See RAPPER.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Humming Liquor*?
wrong: Wearing apparel and bedding used by seamen
A fine silk, cambric, or holland handkerchief
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Double ale, stout pharaoh. See PHARAOH.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Hunting*?
questions.answer: Drawing in unwary persons to play or game
wrong: A piece of lead of any shape, to be fired from a blunderbuss
A lock in wrestling, by which he who uses it throws his adversary over his head
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Drawing in unwary persons to play or game. CANT.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Hurdy Gurdy*?
questions.answer: A kind of fiddle, originally made perhaps out of a gourd
wrong: Goods taken up at thrice their value, by young spendthrifts, upon trust
Cutting out the backs of coaches, and robbing the seats
A cup, or beggar's wooden dish
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A kind of fiddle, originally made perhaps out of a gourd. See HUMSTRUM.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Jack*?
questions.answer: A farthing, a small bowl serving as the mark for bowlers
wrong: Said of one absent, in a reverie, or thoughtful
One that robs ships in the river Thames
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A farthing, a small bowl serving as the mark for bowlers. An instrument for pulling off boots.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Jack At a Pinch*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A poor hackney parson.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Jack in an Office*?
wrong: A horse that shrinks from the collar and will not draw
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: An insolent fellow in authority.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Jack Nasty Face*?
questions.answer: A sea term, signifying a common sailor
wrong: To pawn or sell to a receiver of stolen goods
To snatch, or tear any thing forcibly from the person
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A sea term, signifying a common sailor.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Jack Pudding*?
questions.answer: The merry andrew, zany, or jester to a mountebank
wrong: A cold in the head, attended with a running at the nose
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: The merry andrew, zany, or jester to a mountebank.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Jacob*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A soft fellow. A fool.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Jakes*?
questions.answer: A house of office, a cacatorium
wrong: The department of stealing portmanteaus, trunks, &c
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A house of office, a cacatorium.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Jarkmen*?
