questions.note: A sheep's heart and pluck.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Milch Cow*?
questions.answer: One who is easily tricked out of his property
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: One who is easily tricked out of his property; a term used by gaolers, for prisoners who have money and bleed freely.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *To Milk the Pigeon*?
wrong: Easy to be imposed on, or taken in
Proper, as it ought to be
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: To endeavour at impossibilities.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Mill*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A chisel.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Mill Lay*?
questions.answer: To force open the doors of houses in order to rob them
wrong: Ale in which wormwood has been infused, or ale and bitters drunk warm
A sheriff's officer, who arrests debtors
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: To force open the doors of houses in order to rob them.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Minor Clergy*?
wrong: A taylor with a long bill
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Young chimney sweepers.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Mite*?
questions.answer: A nick name for a cheesemonger
wrong: The old title for a country parson
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A nick name for a cheesemonger: from the small insect of that name found in cheese.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Mix Metal*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A silversmith.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Mohair*?
questions.answer: A man in the civil line, a townsman, or tradesman
wrong: A coach, cart, or other wheeled carriage
Robbing houses by picking the locks
A sea term, signifying a common sailor
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A man in the civil line, a townsman, or tradesman: a military term, from the mohair buttons worn by persons of those descriptions, or any others not in the army, the buttons of military men being always of metal: this is generally used as a term of contempt, meaning a bourgeois, tradesman, or mechanic.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Mooncurser*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A link-boy: link-boys are said to curse the moon, because it renders their assistance unnecessary; these gentry frequently, under colour of lighting passengers over kennels, or through dark passages, assist in robbing them. Cant.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Moped*?
questions.answer: Stupid, melancholy for want of society
wrong: To stand engaged or bound for any one
Throwing, or rather trundling, the dice the whole length of the board
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Stupid, melancholy for want of society.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Morglag*?
questions.answer: A brown bill, or kind of halbert, formerly carried by watchmen
wrong: A head of a house, or master of a college, at the universities
Grinning or laughing in a man's face
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A brown bill, or kind of halbert, formerly carried by watchmen; corruption of MORE, great or broad, and GLAVE, blade.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Mouth*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A silly fellow. A dupe. To stand mouth; i.e. to be duped.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Mow Heater*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A drover: from their frequent sleeping on hay mows. CANT.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Mud*?
wrong: Breaking shop-windows, and stealing some article thereout
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A fool, or thick-sculled fellow; also, among printers the same as dung among journeymen taylors. See DUNG.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Muffling Cheat*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A napkin.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Mummer*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: The mouth.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Mumpers*?
questions.answer: Originally beggars of the genteel kind, but since used for beggars in general
wrong: To make use of false pretences, or unfair shifts
A cunning fellow, under the mask of simplicity
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Originally beggars of the genteel kind, but since used for beggars in general.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Mumpers Hall*?
questions.answer: An alehouse where beggars are harboured
wrong: A hodgepodge made up of the remnants and scraps of the larder
Criminals in the stocks, or pillory
Forestallers, called also Kidders and Tranters
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: An alehouse where beggars are harboured.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Mushroom*?
questions.answer: A person or family suddenly raised to riches and eminence
wrong: Regular drinking over the left thumb
A jocular method of hobbling or bothering a troublesome teller of long stories
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A person or family suddenly raised to riches and eminence: an allusion to that fungus, which starts up in a night.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Muzzler*?
questions.answer: A violent blow on the mouth
wrong: Wine, or any other good liquor
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A violent blow on the mouth. The milling cove tipped the cull a muzzler; the boxer gave the fellow a blow on the mouth.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Napper*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: The head; also a cheat or thief.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Napper of Naps*?
wrong: Wine, or any other good liquor
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A sheep stealer. CANT.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Natty Lads*?
wrong: A nick name for a taylor
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Young thieves or pickpockets. CANT.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Navy Office*?
wrong: A house of office, a cacatorium
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: The Fleet prison. Commander of the Fleet; the warden of the Fleet prison.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Needle Point*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A sharper.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Nick Ninny*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A simpleton.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Niffynaffy Fellow*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A trifler.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Nip Cheese*?
questions.answer: A nick name for the purser of a ship
wrong: Breaking shop-windows, and stealing some article thereout
Dressed out, over-dressed, or awkwardly ornamented
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A nick name for the purser of a ship: from those gentlemen being supposed sometimes to nip, or diminish, the allowance of the seamen, in that and every other article. It is also applied to stingy persons in general.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Nipperkin*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A small measure.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Nob*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: The head.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Nobthatcher*?
wrong: A violent blow on the head
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A peruke-maker.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Nocky Boy*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A dull simple fellow.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Noddle*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: The head.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Nokes*?
wrong: The sign of the Cheshire cheese
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A ninny, or fool. John-a-Nokes and Tom-a-Stiles; two honest peaceable gentlemen, repeatedly set together by the ears by lawyers of different denominations: two fictitious names formerly used in law proceedings, but now very seldom, having for several years past been supplanted by two other honest peaceable gentlemen, namely, John Doe and Richard Roe.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *None-Such*?
wrong: A dram of any spirituous liquor
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: One that is unequalled: frequently applied ironically.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Nonsense*?
wrong: A losing throw to the main at hazard
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Melting butter in a wig.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Nose*?
questions.answer: A man who informs or turns king's evidence
wrong: A gamester, one who rattles Saint Hugh's bones, i.e. the dice
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A man who informs or turns king's evidence.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *To Nose*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: To bully.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Nous-Box*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: The head.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Nug*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: An endearing word: as, My dear nug; my dear love.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Numms*?
questions.answer: A sham collar, to be worn over a dirty shirt
wrong: One who moistens his clay freely, in order to make it stick together
A hodgepodge made up of the remnants and scraps of the larder
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A sham collar, to be worn over a dirty shirt.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *To Nurse*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: To cheat: as, they nursed him out of it. An estate in the hands of trustees, for the payment of bdebts, is said to be at nurse.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Nutcrackers*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: The pillory: as, The cull peeped through the nutcrackers.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Old Dog At It*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Expert, accustomed.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Old One*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: The Devil. Likewise an expression of quizzical familiarity, as "how d'ye do, OLD ONE?"

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Old Poger*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: The Devil.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Old Doss*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Bridewell.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *One in Ten*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A parson: an allusion to his tithes.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Ottomy*?
questions.answer: The vulgar word for a skeleton
wrong: Half common ale, mixed with stale and double beer
To game by tossing up halfpence
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: The vulgar word for a skeleton.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Packet*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A false report.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Pad*?
questions.answer: The highway, or a robber thereon
wrong: A thief who hides himself under a bed, in Order to rob the house
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: The highway, or a robber thereon; also a bed. Footpads; foot robbers. To go out upon the pad; to go out in order to commit a robbery.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Pad Borrowers*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Horse stealers.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Pam*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: The knave of clubs.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Pantler*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A butler.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Papler*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Milk pottage.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Parings*?
wrong: Common place talk of any profession
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: The chippings of money. CANT.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Parish Soldier*?
questions.answer: A jeering name for a militiaman
wrong: A filthy composition, sufficient to provoke vomiting
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A jeering name for a militiaman: from substitutes being frequently hired by the parish from which one of its inhabitants is drawn.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Parson's Journeyman*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A curate.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Passage*?
questions.answer: A camp game with three dice
wrong: A nick name for an apothecary
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A camp game with three dice: doublets, making up ten or more, to pass or win; any other chances lose.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Pattering*?
questions.answer: The maundering or pert replies of servants
wrong: Sellers of old mended shoes and boots, between coblers and shoemakers
A smart fillip on the nose
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: The maundering or pert replies of servants; also talk or palaver in order to amuse one intended to be cheated. Pattering of prayers; the confused sound of a number of persons praying together.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Paviour's Workshop*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: The street.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *To Paum*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: To conceal in the hand. To paum a die: to hide a die in the palm of the hand. He paums; he cheats. Don't pretend to paum that upon me.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Peak*?
wrong: The top side the other way
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Any kind of lace.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Pear Making*?
questions.answer: Taking bounties from several regiments and immediately deserting
wrong: A heavy, bungling thief or rogue
Half common ale, mixed with stale and double beer
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Taking bounties from several regiments and immediately deserting. The cove was fined in the steel for pear making; the fellow was imprisoned in the house of correction for taking bounties from different regiments.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Peck*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Victuals. Peck and booze; victuals and drink.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Ped*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A basket. CANT.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Peery*?
wrong: One that robs ships in the river Thames
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Inquisitive, suspicious. The cull's peery; that fellow suspects something. There's a peery, tis snitch we are observed, there's nothing to be done.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Pelt*?
wrong: Beggars plying in a body at funerals
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A heat, chafe, or passion; as, What a pelt he was in! Pelt is also the skin of several beasts.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Penance Board*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: The pillory.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Penthouse Nab*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A broad brimmed hat.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Perkin*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Water cyder.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Peter*?
wrong: A tumbler, juggler, or shewer of tricks
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A portmanteau or cloke-bag. Biter of peters; one that makes it a trade to steal boxes and trunks from behind stage coaches or out of waggons. To rob Peter to pay Paul; to borrow of one man to pay another: styled also manoeuvring the apostles.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Peter Lay*?
questions.answer: The department of stealing portmanteaus, trunks, &c
wrong: To be a match for one who attempts to cheat or deceive
A bumper, a glass filled so full as to leave no room for the lip
A college runner or errand-boy at Cambridge, called at Oxford a scout
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: The department of stealing portmanteaus, trunks, &c.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Pharaoh*?
wrong: An old dance to a quick movement
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Strong malt liquor.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Phrase of Paper*?
questions.answer: Half a quarter of a sheet
wrong: A clerk, scribe, or hackney writer
A man imprisoned for any offence
Pork, bacon, or any kind of hog's flesh
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Half a quarter of a sheet. See VESSEL, PHYSOG.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Picaroon*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A pirate; also a sharper.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Pickthank*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A tale-bearer or mischief maker.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *To Pike*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: To run away. Pike off; run away.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Piper*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A broken winded horse.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Pit*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A watch fob. He drew a rare thimble from the swell's pit. He took a handsome watch from the gentleman's fob.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Pitch-Kettled*?
wrong: Whispering on one side to borrow money
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Stuck fast, confounded.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Plumb*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: An hundred thousand pounds.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Plyer*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A crutch; also a trader.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Poll*?
questions.answer: The head, jolly nob, napper, or knowledge box
wrong: A nick name for an apothecary
To punish by course of law
A sheriff's officer, who arrests debtors
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: The head, jolly nob, napper, or knowledge box; also a wig.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Postilion of the Gospel*?
questions.answer: A parson who hurries over the service
wrong: A head of a house, or master of a college, at the universities
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A parson who hurries over the service.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Pound*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A prison. See LOB'S POUND. Pounded; imprisoned. Shut up in the parson's pound; married. POWDER

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Prate Roast*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A talkative boy.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Prating Cheat*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: The tongue.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Pratts*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Buttocks; also a tinder box. CANT.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Prattling Box*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: The pulpit.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Prig*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A thief, a cheat: also a conceited coxcomical fellow.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Prig Napper*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A thief taker.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Priggers*?
wrong: King or chief of the link-boys
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Thieves in general. Priggers of prancers; horse stealers. Priggers of cacklers: robbers of hen-roosts.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Prigstar*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A rival in love.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Princox*?
wrong: Waiting in the streets to rob carts or waggons
Cutting out the backs of coaches, and robbing the seats
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A pert, lively, forward fellow.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Provender*?
questions.answer: He from whom any money is taken on the highway
wrong: A trick, wheedle, or invention to deceive
When a rook or cully is engaged amongst bad bowlers
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: He from whom any money is taken on the highway: perhaps provider, or provider. CANT.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Public Man*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A bankrupt.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Puddings*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: The guts: I'll let out your puddings.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Pudding Sleeves*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A parson.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Pug Drink*?
wrong: Proper, as it ought to be
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Watered cyder.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Purl*?
questions.answer: Ale in which wormwood has been infused, or ale and bitters drunk warm
wrong: A nick name for a thresher, but applied to all the servants of a farmer
A low mean fellow, employed in all sorts of dirty work
Throwing, or rather trundling, the dice the whole length of the board
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Ale in which wormwood has been infused, or ale and bitters drunk warm.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Pursenets*?
questions.answer: Goods taken up at thrice their value, by young spendthrifts, upon trust
wrong: A slap on the face, and a kick on the breech
To fling dust or snuff in the eyes of the person intended to be robbed
A piece of lead of any shape, to be fired from a blunderbuss
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Goods taken up at thrice their value, by young spendthrifts, upon trust.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Purser's Pump*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A bassoon: from its likeness to a syphon, called a purser's pump.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Puzzle-Cause*?

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *To Simper*?

questions.note: Honest, not roguish. A square cove, i.e. a man who does not steal, or get his living by dishonest means.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Square Toes*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: An old man: square toed shoes were anciently worn in common, and long retained by old men.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Squeak*?
wrong: A sea term, signifying a common sailor
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A narrow escape, a chance: he had a squeak for his life. To squeak; to confess, peach, or turn stag. They squeak beef upon us; they cry out thieves after us. CANT.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *To Stag*?
wrong: To stand engaged or bound for any one
The act of hooking goods out of windows
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: To find, discover, or observe.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Stalling*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Making or ordaining. Stalling to the rogue; an ancient ceremony of instituting a candidate into the society of rogues, somewhat similar to the creation of a herald at arms. It is thus described by Harman: the upright man taking a gage of bowse, i.e. a pot of strong drink, pours it on the head of the rogue to be admitted; saying,--I, A.B. do stall thee B.C. to the rogue; and from henceforth it shall be lawful for thee to cant for thy living in all places.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Stalling Ken*?
questions.answer: A broker's shop, or that of a receiver of stolen goods
wrong: An old dance to a quick movement
An inferior in any office, or department
A set of subterraneous rooms in the Fleet Prison
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A broker's shop, or that of a receiver of stolen goods.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Starched*?
wrong: To pawn or sell to a receiver of stolen goods
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Stiff, prim, formal, affected.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Staring Quarter*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: An ox cheek.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Starter*?
questions.answer: One who leaves a jolly company, a milksop
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: One who leaves a jolly company, a milksop; he is no starter, he will sit longer than a hen.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Star Lag*?
questions.answer: Breaking shop-windows, and stealing some article thereout
wrong: A meeting of apprentices and mechanics to rehearse different characters in plays
The old title for a country parson
A thorough-paced rogue, a sly designing fellow
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Breaking shop-windows, and stealing some article thereout.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Staytape*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A taylor; from that article, and its coadjutor buckram, which make no small figure in the bills of those knights of the needle.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Steel*?
wrong: Beggars plying in a body at funerals
The act of hooking goods out of windows
Regular drinking over the left thumb
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: The house of correction.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Steel Bar*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A needle. A steel bar flinger; a taylor, stay-maker, or any other person using a needle.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Sticks*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Household furniture.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Sticks*?
wrong: A cup, or beggar's wooden dish
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Pops or pistols. Stow your sticks; hide your pistols. CANT. See POPS.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Stick Flams*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A pair of gloves.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Stiff-Rumped*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Proud, stately.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Stingo*?
wrong: Dressed out, over-dressed, or awkwardly ornamented
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Strong beer, or other liquor.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Stitchback*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Strong ale.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Stone Jug*?
wrong: Beer, egg, and brandy, made hot
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Newgate, or any other prison.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Stoter*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A great blow. Tip him a stoter in the haltering place; give him a blow under the left ear.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Stoup*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A vessel to hold liquor: a vessel containing a size or half a pint, is so called at Cambridge.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Strait-Laced*?
wrong: The maundering or pert replies of servants
A kiss with a loud smack
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Precise, over nice, puritanical.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Strike*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Twenty shillings. CANT.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Stubble It*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Hold your tongue. CANT.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Suck*?
wrong: Men employed to load and unload the coal vessels
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Strong liquor of any sort. To suck the monkey; see MONKEY. Sucky; drunk.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Sunny Bank*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A good fire in winter.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Sunshine*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Prosperity.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Supernacolum*?
questions.answer: Good liquor, of which there is not even a drop left sufficient to wet one's nail
wrong: A roasted turkey garnished with sausages
The maundering or pert replies of servants
To reproach a person, or remind him of favours conferred
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Good liquor, of which there is not even a drop left sufficient to wet one's nail.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Surveyor of the Pavement*?
wrong: A man void of every principle of honour
Stupid, melancholy for want of society
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: One standing in the pillory.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Sutrer*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A camp publican: also one that pilfers gloves, tobacco boxes, and such small moveables.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Swabbers*?
questions.answer: The ace of hearts, knave of clubs, ace and duce of trumps, at whist
wrong: One reeling, and ready to fall at the least touch
A thick liquor, in imitation of chocolate, made of milk and gingerbread
A broker's shop, or that of a receiver of stolen goods
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: The ace of hearts, knave of clubs, ace and duce of trumps, at whist: also the lubberly seamen, put to swab, and clean the ship.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Sweet*?
questions.answer: Easy to be imposed on, or taken in
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Easy to be imposed on, or taken in; also expert, dexterous clever. Sweet's your hand; said of one dexterous at stealing.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Swig*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A hearty draught of liquor.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Swill Tub*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A drunkard, a sot.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Swimmer*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A counterfeit old coin.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Swop*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: An exchange.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Syebuck*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Sixpence.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Syntax*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A schoolmaster.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Tace*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Silence, hold your tongue. TACE is Latin for a candle; a jocular admonition to be silent on any subject.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Tag-Rag and Bobtail*?
questions.answer: An expression meaning an assemblage of low people, the mobility of all sorts
wrong: To pawn or sell to a receiver of stolen goods
Stealing brass weights off the counters of shops
A punning appellation for a simple fellow
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: An expression meaning an assemblage of low people, the mobility of all sorts. To tag after one like a tantony pig: to follow one wherever one goes, just as St. Anthony is followed by his pig.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Tall Boy*?
wrong: Mead and ale sweetened with honey
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A bottle, or two-quart pot.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Tandem*?
questions.answer: A two-wheeled chaise, buggy, or noddy, drawn by two horses, one before the other
wrong: A modern card meeting at a private house
A false evidence, one that is ready to swear any thing for hire
By stealth, privately, without making an appearance
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A two-wheeled chaise, buggy, or noddy, drawn by two horses, one before the other: that is, AT LENGTH.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Tanner*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A sixpence. The kiddey tipped the rattling cove a tanner for luck; the lad gave the coachman sixpence for drink.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Tantadlin Tart*?
wrong: A stealer of cows and calves
A man who informs or turns king's evidence
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A sirreverence, human excrement.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Taplash*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Thick and bad beer.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Taradiddle*?
wrong: A house of office, a cacatorium
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A fib, or falsity.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Tart*?
wrong: The head, jolly nob, napper, or knowledge box
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Sour, sharp, quick, pert.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Tats*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: False dice.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Tat Monger*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: One that uses false dice.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Tayle Drawers*?
questions.answer: Thieves who snatch gentlemens swords from their sides
wrong: Persons employed by the gardeners to gather peas
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Thieves who snatch gentlemens swords from their sides. He drew the cull's tayle rumly; he snatched away the gentleman's sword cleverly.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Taylors Goose*?
questions.answer: An iron with which, when heated, press down the seams of clothes
wrong: Bridewell, Newgate, or any other prison, or house of correction
The act of hooking goods out of windows
Thieves who snatch gentlemens swords from their sides
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: An iron with which, when heated, press down the seams of clothes.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Tea Voider*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A chamber pot.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Teddy My Godson*?
questions.answer: An address to a supposed simple fellow, or nysey
wrong: Paint for the face, or cosmetic water
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: An address to a supposed simple fellow, or nysey,

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Temple Pickling*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Pumping a bailiff; a punishment formerly administered to any of that fraternity caught exercising their functions within the limits of Temple.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Ten in the Hundred*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: An usurer; more than five in the hundred being deemed usurious interest.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Terra Firma*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: An estate in land.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Tester*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A sixpence: from TESTON, a coin with a head on it.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Thick*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Intimate. They are as thick as two inkle-weavers.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Thorough Go Nimble*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A looseness, a violent purging.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Three Threads*?
questions.answer: Half common ale, mixed with stale and double beer
wrong: A person who lives by passing base coin
Wine, or any other good liquor
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Half common ale, mixed with stale and double beer.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *To Thrum*?
questions.answer: To play on any instrument stringed with wire
wrong: Thrown from a horse, or overturned in a carriage
To slip or slide any thing into the hands of another
A parson who hurries over the service
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: To play on any instrument stringed with wire. A thrummer of wire; a player on the spinet, harpsichord, of guitar.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Thwack*?
questions.answer: A great blow with a stick across the shoulders
wrong: A pace between a walk and a run, a dog-trot
One reeling, and ready to fall at the least touch
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A great blow with a stick across the shoulders.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Tib*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Tickrum*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A licence.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Tilbuky*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Sixpence; so called from its formerly being the fare for Crossing over from Gravesend to Tilbury Fort.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Tim Whisky*?
questions.answer: A light one--horse chaise without a head
wrong: One on whom there can be no dependance, a shuffling fellow
Half common ale, mixed with stale and double beer
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A light one--horse chaise without a head.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Tip-Top*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: The best: perhaps from fruit, that growing at the top of the tree being generally the best, as partaking most of the sun. A tip-top workman; the best, or most excellent Workman.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Tipplers*?
wrong: A low mean fellow, employed in all sorts of dirty work
A person or family suddenly raised to riches and eminence
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Sots who are continually sipping.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Tipsey*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Almost drunk.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Tit For Tat*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: An equivalent.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *To Titter*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: To suppress a laugh.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Titter Tatter*?
questions.answer: One reeling, and ready to fall at the least touch
wrong: Men employed to load and unload the coal vessels
A coach drawn by three horses
One who is easily tricked out of his property
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: One reeling, and ready to fall at the least touch; also the childish amusement of riding upon the two ends of a plank, poised upon the prop underneath its centre, called also see-saw. Perhaps tatter is a rustic pronunciation of totter.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Tittup*?
questions.answer: A gentle hand gallop, or canter
wrong: Mending the foot by capping it
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A gentle hand gallop, or canter.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Tizzy*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Sixpence.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Toby Lay*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: The highway. High toby man; a highway-man. Low toby man; a footpad.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Tobacco*?
questions.answer: A plant, once in great estimation as a medicine
wrong: A two-wheeled chaise, buggy, or noddy, drawn by two horses, one before the other
Soft paper for the necessary house or torchecul
Regular drinking over the left thumb
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A plant, once in great estimation as a medicine: Tobacco hic Will make you well if you be sick. Tobacco hic If you be well will make you sick.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Toddle*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: To walk away. The cove was touting, but stagging the traps he toddled; be was looking out, and feeing the officers he walked away.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Tom Cony*?
wrong: A nick name for a blacksmith
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A simple fellow.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Tom Long*?
wrong: Pork, bacon, or any kind of hog's flesh
Helter skelter, in a hasty disorderly manner
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A tiresome story teller. It is coming by Tom Long, the carrier; said of any thing that has been long expected.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Tony*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A silly fellow, or ninny. A mere tony: a simpleton.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Tool*?
questions.answer: The instrument of any person or faction, a cat's paw
wrong: A drone, one that cannot rise in the morning
Paint for the face, or cosmetic water
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: The instrument of any person or faction, a cat's paw. See CATS PAW. TOOTH Music. Chewing.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Tooth-Pick*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A large stick. An ironical expression.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Topper*?
questions.answer: A violent blow on the head
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A violent blow on the head.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Top Lights*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: The eyes. Blast your top lights. See CURSE. Top SAIL. He paid his debts at Portsmouth with the topsail; i.e. he went to sea and left them unpaid. SCT soldiers are said to pay off their scores with the drum; that is, by marching away.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Tofsy-Turvy*?
questions.answer: The top side the other way
wrong: A jocular name for a baker
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: The top side the other way; i.e. the wrong side upwards; some explain it, the top side turf ways, turf being always laid the wrong side upwards.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Torchecul*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Bumfodder.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Tormenter of Sheep Skin*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A drummer.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Tormenter of Catgut*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A fiddler.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Toss Pot*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A drunkard.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Totty-Headed*?
wrong: A stitch fallen in a stocking
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Giddy, hare-brained.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Tovt*?
wrong: The department of stealing portmanteaus, trunks, &c
A great hulkey or clumsy fellow
A broker's shop, or that of a receiver of stolen goods
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A look-out house, or eminence.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Tow Row*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A grenadier. The tow row club; a club or society of the grenadier officers of the line.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Tower*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Clipped money: they have been round the tower with it. CANT.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Tower Hill Play*?
questions.answer: A slap on the face, and a kick on the breech
wrong: Sellers of old mended shoes and boots, between coblers and shoemakers
A pulpit, so called by orator Henley
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A slap on the face, and a kick on the breech.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Translators*?
questions.answer: Sellers of old mended shoes and boots, between coblers and shoemakers
wrong: An expression meaning an assemblage of low people, the mobility of all sorts
Very old and strong beer, called also stingo
A trick, wheedle, or invention to deceive
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Sellers of old mended shoes and boots, between coblers and shoemakers.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *To Transnear*?
questions.answer: To come up with any body
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: To come up with any body.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *To Trapan*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: To inveigle, or ensnare.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Treswins*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: Threepence.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Trib*?
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A prison: perhaps from tribulation.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Trickum Legis*?
questions.answer: A quirk or quibble in the law
wrong: Wine and water, with lemon, sugar, and burrage
questions.source: Grose's Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue (1811 edition)
questions.note: A quirk or quibble in the law.

questions.question: In 1811 slang, what was meant by *Trig*?
questions.answer: The point at which schoolboys stand to shoot their marbles at taw
wrong: An alehouse where beggars are harboured
Oatmeal and water boiled to a jelly

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *All and Sundry*?

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Alter ego*?

questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To angle with a silver hook*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *At arm’s length*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)

wrong: To be buried in one’s native place

questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: A coward who hectors, a fool that apes the wise man. The allusion is to the fable of an ass that put on a lion’s hide, but was betrayed when he began to bray.

The Athenians were noted for their wit and elegant turns of thought, and hence Attic salt means wit as pointed and delicately expressed as by the Athenians. “Attic point,” wit.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Ill furnished in the attic storey*?

questions.note: Some selfish motive in the background; some personal interest to answer. Franklin tells of a man who wanted to grind his axe, but had no one to turn the grindstone. The 13th was the “vantage loaf.” Mr. Riley (Liber Albus) tells us that the 13th loaf was “the extent of the profit allowed to retail dealers,” and therefore the vantage loaf means the loaf allowed for profit. To give one a baker’s dozen, in slang phraseology, is to give him a sound drubbing—i.e. all he deserves and one stroke more.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To take the ball before the bound*?

“It runs in the blood of our family.”—Sheridan: The Rivals, iv. 2.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To blow a cloud*?
questions.answer: To smoke a cigar or pipe
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To smoke a cigar or pipe. This term was in use in Elizabeth’s reign.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *A Blow Out*?
questions.answer: A “tuck-in,” or feast which swells out the paunch
wrong: To lend a helping hand to one in distress
To acknowledge oneself in the wrong
To look askant with shyness or diffidence
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: A “tuck-in,” or feast which swells out the paunch.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Blown upon*?
questions.answer: Made the subject of a scandal
wrong: From this sample you can judge of the whole
An achievement to be proud of
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Made the subject of a scandal. His reputation has been blown upon, means has been the subject of talk wherein something derogatory was hinted at or even asserted. Blown upon by the breath of slander.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Once in a blue moon*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Very rarely indeed. On December 10th, 1883, we had a “blue moon.” The winter was unusually mild.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To blurt out*?
questions.answer: To tell something from impulse which should not have been told
wrong: Perspiration excited by hard manual labour
To suffer some disadvantage while off one's guard
To attack or encounter a threatened danger fearlessly
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To tell something from impulse which should not have been told. To speak incautiously, or without due reflection. Florio makes the distinction, to “flurt with one’s fingers, and blurt with one’s mouth.”

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To keep body and soul together*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To sustain life; from the notion that the soul gives life. The Latin anima, and the Greek psyché, mean both soul and life; and, according to Homeric mythology, the departed soul retains the shape and semblance of the body, hence the notion of ghosts. Indeed, if the soul is the “principle of life,” it must of necessity be the facsimile of every living atom of the body.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Bon Mot*?
wrong: A dispute to be settled by a duel
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: A good or witty saying; a pun; a clever repartee.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Bon Ton*?
questions.answer: Good manners, or manners accredited by good society
wrong: A self-willed fellow who will neither lead nor drive, neither be led nor driven
To go beyond the prescribed limits
Prepare for action by removing everything not required
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Good manners, or manners accredited by good society.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *A Bone of Contention*?
wrong: To be "not at home" to visitors
To barter by the rule of thumb
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: A disputed point; a point not yet settled. The metaphor is taken from the proverb about “Two dogs fighting for a bone,” etc.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Beware of a man of one book*?
questions.answer: Never attempt to controvert the statement of any one in his own special subject
wrong: Of the same size as the object represented
Having a sapient, vacant look, as some persons have when in their cups
Perspiration excited by hard manual labour
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Never attempt to controvert the statement of any one in his own special subject. A shepherd who cannot read will know more about sheep than the wisest bookworm. This caution is given by St. Thomas Aquinas.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Out of my books*?
wrong: He is a soft, a noodle
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Not in favour; no longer in my list of friends.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *A Bootless Errand*?
wrong: An announcement of some coming calamity
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: An unprofitable or futile message. The Saxon bot means “reparation”—“overplus to profit”; as “I will give you that to boot”; “what boots it me?” (what does it profit me?).

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Head Bottle-washer*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Chief agent; the principal man employed by another; a factotum.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *At bottom*?
wrong: An achievement to be proud of
Made the subject of a scandal
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Radically, fundamentally: as, the young prodigal lived a riotous life, but was good at bottom, or below the surface.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *He has a famous bow up at the castle*?
questions.answer: Said of a braggart or pretender
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Said of a braggart or pretender.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *He has two strings to his bow*?
questions.answer: Two means of accomplishing his object
wrong: At the very verge of death
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Two means of accomplishing his object; if one fails, he can try the other. The allusion is to the custom of the British bowmen carrying a reserve string in case of accident.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *In a brace of shakes*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Very soon. Similar phrases are: “In the twinkling of an eye.” “In the twinkling of a bed-post.”

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To take the bread out of one’s mouth*?
wrong: To assume the guidance or direction
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To forestall another; to say something which another was on the point of saying; to take away another’s livelihood.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To break one’s fast*?
questions.answer: To take food after long abstinence
wrong: An actor who appears, speaks, or acts only once
To keep strict watch on the person or thing referred to
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To take food after long abstinence; to eat one’s breakfast after the night’s fast.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To break out of bounds*?
questions.answer: To go beyond the prescribed limits
wrong: To suffer the disgrace of a vanquished army
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To go beyond the prescribed limits.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To break ground*?
questions.answer: To be the first to commence a project, etc.
wrong: I am out of my element
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To be the first to commence a project, etc.; to take the first step in an undertaking.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To break with one*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
To cease from intercourse.

“What cause have I given him to break with me?”—Florence Marryat.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Breakers Ahead*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Hidden danger. Breakers in the open sea always announce sunken rocks, sandbanks, etc.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To broach a new subject*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
To start one in conversation. The allusion is to beer tubs. If one is flat, another must be tapped. A broach is a spit or pin, and to broach a cask is to bore a hole in the top for the vent-peg.

“I did broach this business to your highness.”—Shakespeare: Henry VIII., ii. 4.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *A new broom*?
wrong: Don’t throw good money after bad
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: One fresh in office. New brooms sweep clean. Those newly appointed to an office find fault and want to sweep away old customs.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *He brushed by me*?
questions.answer: He just touched me as he went past
wrong: Worn out, tired out, utterly fatigued, or exhausted
To do something to obviate or prevent exposure or embarrassment
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: He just touched me as he went past. Hence also brush, a slight skirmish. All these are metaphors from brushing with a brush.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Bubble and squeak*?
questions.answer: Cold boiled meat and greens fried
wrong: To disturb the equanimity of a society
The inner disc of a target
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Cold boiled meat and greens fried. They first bubbled in water when boiled, and afterwards hissed or squeaked in the frying-pan. Something pretentious, but of no real value, such as “rank and title,” or a bit of ribbon in one's button-hole.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *A bull in a china shop*?
questions.answer: A maladroit hand interfering with a delicate business
wrong: One who listens stealthily to conversation
My nerves are shaken, my equilibrium of mind is disturbed
A dull, unprogressive person, somewhat fossilised
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: A maladroit hand interfering with a delicate business; one who produces reckless destruction.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To take the bull by the horns*?
questions.answer: To attack or encounter a threatened danger fearlessly
wrong: I am very busy, and cannot attend to anything else
First-rate, thumping, as a thumping legacy
To prevent another from being too familiar
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To attack or encounter a threatened danger fearlessly; to go forth boldly to meet a difficulty. The figure is taken from bull-fights, in which a strong and skilful matadore will grasp the horns of a bull about to toss him and hold it prisoner.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Bull's eye*?
questions.answer: The inner disc of a target
wrong: He is a shrewd fellow not to be imposed on
To be in a state of nervous terror
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
The inner disc of a target.

“A little way from the centre there is a spot where the shots are thickly gathered; some few have hit the bull's-eye.”—Fiske: Excursions, etc., chap. vi. p. 178.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To make a bull's eye*?
wrong: To be doing a brisk business
To acknowledge oneself in the wrong
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To gain some signal advantage; a successful coup. To fire or shoot an arrow right into the centre disc of the target.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Buridan's ass*?
wrong: He exposed himself to needless danger
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: A man of indecision; like one “on double business bound, who stands in pause where he should first begin, and both neglects.” Buridan the scholastic said: “If a hungry ass were placed exactly between two hay-stacks in every respect equal, it would starve to death, because there would be no motive why it should go to one rather than to the other.”

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To burn one's boats*?
questions.answer: To cut oneself off from all means or hope of retreat
wrong: One too heavy to be carried
Fair speeches, which look like promises of favour, but end in nothing
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To cut oneself off from all means or hope of retreat. The allusion is to Julius Cæsar and other generals, who burned their boats or ships when they invaded a foreign country, in order that their soldiers might feel that they must either conquer the country or die, as retreat would be impossible.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Soft words butter no parsnips*?
questions.answer: Saying “Be thou fed,” will not feed a hungry man
wrong: A species of sale by auction
To smoke a cigar or pipe
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
Saying “Be thou fed,” will not feed a hungry man. Mere words will not find salt to our porridge, or butter to our parsnips.

“Fine words, says our homely old proverb, butter no parsnips.”—Lowell.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To have a soul above buttons*?
questions.answer: To be worthy of better things
wrong: To earn a little money by working for it
To doubt the truth of a statement
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To be worthy of better things; to have abilities too good for one's present employment. This is explained by George Colman in Sylvester Daggerwood: “My father was an eminent button-maker... but I had a soul above buttons... and panted for a liberal profession.”

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To take by the button*?
wrong: A maladroit hand interfering with a delicate business
To barter by the rule of thumb
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To detain one in conversation; to apprehend, as, “to take fortune by the button.” The allusion is to a custom, now discontinued, of holding a person by the button or button-hole in conversation.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To buy over a person's head*?
wrong: To get or keep the upper hand
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To outbid another.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To call in question*?
questions.answer: To doubt the truth of a statement
wrong: An achievement to be proud of
To escape accidents in a marvellous manner
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To doubt the truth of a statement; to challenge the truth of a statement. “In dubium vocare.”

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To call to account*?
wrong: He is a soft, a noodle
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To demand an explanation; to reprove.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To sell by the candle*?
questions.answer: A species of sale by auction
wrong: First-rate, thumping, as a thumping legacy
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: A species of sale by auction. A pin is thrust through a candle about an inch from the top, and bidding goes on till the candle is burnt down to the pin, when the pin drops into the candlestick, and the last bidder is declared the purchaser. This sort of auction was employed in 1893, according to the Reading Mercury (Dec. 16), at Aldermaston, near Reading.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *A feather in one's cap*?
questions.answer: An achievement to be proud of
wrong: My prime of life is over
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: An achievement to be proud of; something creditable.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *A capital fellow*?
questions.answer: A good-tempered, jovial, and generous person
wrong: A coward who hectors, a fool that apes the wise man
To exert oneself to the utmost
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: A good-tempered, jovial, and generous person.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *That's the card*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
The right thing; the ticket. The reference is to tickets of admission, cards of the races, and programmes.

“10s. is about the card.”—Mayhew: London Labour, etc.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *A sure card*?
questions.answer: A person one can fully depend on
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: A person one can fully depend on; a person sure to command success. A project to be certainly depended on. As a winning card in one's hand.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *On the cards*?
questions.answer: Projected, and talked about as likely to occur
wrong: He is a shrewd fellow not to be imposed on
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Projected, and talked about as likely to occur. On the programme or card of the races; on the “agenda.”

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To throw up the cards*?
questions.answer: To give up as a bad job
wrong: The contour or expression of his face
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To give up as a bad job; to acknowledge you have no hope of success. In some games of cards, as loo, a player has the liberty of saying whether he will play or not, and if one's hand is hopelessly bad he throws up his cards and sits out till the next deal.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Carpe diem*?
questions.answer: Enjoy yourself while you have the opportunity
wrong: Rebutting a charge by bringing forth a counter-charge
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Enjoy yourself while you have the opportunity. Seize the present day. (Horace: 1 Odes, xi. 8.) “Dum vivimus, vivamus.”

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To carry everything before one*?
wrong: Not yet out of nursery government
Projected, and talked about as likely to occur
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To be beyond competition; to carry off all the prizes. A military phrase. Similarly, a high wind carries everything before it.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To carry one's point*?
wrong: One in which the batsman has made several runs
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To succeed in one's aim. Candidates in Rome were balloted for, and the votes were marked on a tablet by points. Hence, omne punctum ferre meant “to be carried nem. con.,” or to gain every vote; and “to carry one's point” is to carry off the points at which one aimed.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To cast beyond the moon*?
wrong: The land of the leal or “Dixie Land” of sailors
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
To form wild conjectures. One of Heywood's proverbs. At one time the moon was supposed to influence the weather, to affect the ingathering of fruits, to rule the time of sowing, reaping, and slaying cattle, etc.

“I talke of things impossible, and cast beyond the moon.”—Heywood.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To cast into one's teeth*?
questions.answer: To throw a reproof at one
wrong: A “tuck-in,” or feast which swells out the paunch
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
To throw a reproof at one. The allusion is to knocking one's teeth out by stones.

“All my faults observed, Set in a note-book, learned and conned by rote, To cast into my teeth.”—Shakespeare: Julius Cæsar.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Casus belli*?
wrong: Don’t let your enemies hear it
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: A ground for war; an occurrence warranting international hostilities.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To let the cat out of the bag*?
wrong: Some selfish motive in the background
Don’t let your enemies hear it
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
To disclose a secret. It was formerly a trick among country folk to substitute a cat for a sucking-pig, and bring it in a bag to market. If any greenhorn chose to buy a “pig in a poke” without examination, all very well; but if he opened the sack, “he let the cat out of the bag,” and the trick was disclosed.

“She let the cat out of her bag of verse... she almost proposed to her hero in rhyme.”—George Meredith: The Egoist, ii.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To be made a cat's paw of*?
questions.answer: To be the tool of another, the medium of doing another's dirty work
wrong: A small defect which mars the general result
To tell something from impulse which should not have been told
Prepare for action by removing everything not required
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
To be the tool of another, the medium of doing another's dirty work. The allusion is to the fable of the monkey who wanted to get from the fire some roasted chestnuts, and took the paw of the cat to get them from the hot ashes.

“I had no intention of becoming a cat's paw to draw European chestnuts out of the fire.”—Com. Rodgers.

At sea, light air during a calm causing a ripple on the water, and indicating a storm, is called by sailors a cat's paw, and seamen affirm that the frolics of a cat indicate a gale. These are relics of a superstition that cats are witches or demons in disguise.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Catch me at it!*?
questions.answer: Most certainly I shall never do what you say
wrong: To suffer some disadvantage while off one's guard
I am out of my element
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
Most certainly I shall never do what you say.

“‘Catch me going to London!’ exclaimed Vixen.”—Miss Braddon: Vixen.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To be caught napping*?
questions.answer: To suffer some disadvantage while off one's guard
wrong: To forsake a losing side for the stronger party
"No more" can be said on the subject
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To suffer some disadvantage while off one's guard. Pheasants, hares, and other animals are sometimes surprised “napping.” I have myself caught a cock-pheasant napping.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Caveat emptor*?
questions.answer: The buyer must be responsible for his own free act
wrong: To make a casual call, not invited
