questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: The buyer must be responsible for his own free act. Let the buyer keep his eyes open, for the bargain he agrees to is binding. In English law, Chief Justice Tindal modified this rule. He said if the buyer gives notice that he relies on the vendor's judgment, and the vendor warrants the article, then the vendor is bound to furnish an article “reasonable and fit for the purpose required.”

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Chalk it up*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Put it to his credit. As good-humoured sarcasm, Chalk it up! is tantamount to saying, “What you have done so astonishes me that I must make some more or less permanent record of it.”

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *The chapter of accidents*?
wrong: To doubt the truth of a statement
A mighty to-do about a trifle
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Unforeseen events. To trust to the chapter of accidents is to trust that something unforeseen may turn up in your favour. The Roman laws were divided into books, and each book into chapters. The chapter of accidents is that under the head of accidents, and metaphorically, the sequence of unforeseen events.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To give cheek*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To be insolent. “Give me none of your cheek.”

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *It is not the cheese*?
wrong: I am out of my element
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Not the right thing; not what I should choose. He is quite the cheese or just the cheese—i.e. quite the thing. By a double refinement we get the slang varieties, That's prime Stilton, or double Glo'ster—i.e. slap bang up.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To make two bites of a cherry*?
questions.answer: To divide something too small to be worth dividing
wrong: The inner disc of a target
First-rate, thumping, as a thumping legacy
Chief or most important of a person’s works
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To divide something too small to be worth dividing.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To chop and change*?
questions.answer: To barter by the rule of thumb
wrong: Was sold for a mere trifle, for a nominal sum or price
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To barter by the rule of thumb. Boys “chop” one article for another (Anglo-Saxon, cip-an, or ceáp-ian, to sell or barter).

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To keep the hands clean*?
questions.answer: Not to be involved in wrong-doing
wrong: To look askant with shyness or diffidence
A species of sale by auction
A maladroit hand interfering with a delicate business
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Not to be involved in wrong-doing.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To clear the decks*?
questions.answer: Prepare for action by removing everything not required
wrong: To be disagreeable or quarrelsome about anything
You disparage it because it is beyond your reach
To run with the hare and hold with the hounds
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Prepare for action by removing everything not required.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *I am quite cleared out*?
questions.answer: I have spent all my money
wrong: A dispute to be settled by a duel
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: I have spent all my money; I have not a farthing left. Cleared out means, my purse or pocket is cleared out of money.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *A slow coach*?
questions.answer: A dull, unprogressive person, somewhat fossilised
wrong: Some selfish motive in the background
The land of the leal or “Dixie Land” of sailors
It is inherited or exists in the family race
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
A dull, unprogressive person, somewhat fossilised.

“What a dull, old-fashioned chap thou be'st... but thou wert always a slow-coach.”—Mrs. Gaskell: Libbie Marsh (Era 2).

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Cock of the walk*?
questions.answer: The dominant bully or master spirit
wrong: In a difficulty, in a mess
A maladroit hand interfering with a delicate business
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: The dominant bully or master spirit. The place where barn-door fowls are fed is called the walk, and if there is more than one cock they will fight for the supremacy of this domain.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To warm the cockles of one's heart*?
wrong: One too heavy to be carried
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Said of good wine. (Latin, cochleæ cordis, the ventricles of the heart.)

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Against the collar*?
wrong: An expletive, or mild kind of oath
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Somewhat fatiguing. When a horse travels up-hill the collar distresses his neck, so foot-travellers often find the last mile or so “against the collar,” or distressing. Authors of long books often find the last few pages wearisome and against the grain.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Out of collar*?
questions.answer: Out of work, out of place
wrong: To be late or too late for dinner
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Out of work, out of place.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Cool as a cucumber*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Perfectly composed; neither angry nor agitated in the least.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Court holy water*?
questions.answer: Fair speeches, which look like promises of favour, but end in nothing
wrong: He exposed himself to needless danger
To dictate peremptorily and profess superiority of knowledge and experience
The land of the leal or “Dixie Land” of sailors
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Fair speeches, which look like promises of favour, but end in nothing.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To crack up a person*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To praise him highly.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *A drop of the creature*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: A little whisky.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *A crooked stick*?
questions.answer: A self-willed fellow who will neither lead nor drive, neither be led nor driven
wrong: An actor who appears, speaks, or acts only once
Most certainly I shall never do what you say
To attack or encounter a threatened danger fearlessly
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: A self-willed fellow who will neither lead nor drive, neither be led nor driven.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To crop up (or out)*?
questions.answer: To rise out of, to appear at the surface
wrong: To be the tool of another, the medium of doing another's dirty work
Not yet out of nursery government
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To rise out of, to appear at the surface. A mining term. Strata which rise to the surface are said to crop out. We also say, such and such a subject crops up from time to time—i.e. rises to the surface; such and such a thing crops out of what you were saying—i.e. is apropos thereof.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To cry over spilt milk*?
questions.answer: To fret about some loss which can never be repaired
wrong: To put too much water into grog or tea
Perspiration excited by hard manual labour
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To fret about some loss which can never be repaired.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Cui bono?*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
Who is benefited thereby? To whom is it a gain? The more usual meaning attached to the words is, What good will it do? For what good purpose? It was the question of Judge Cassius.

“Cato, that great and grave philosopher, did commonly demand, when any new project was propounded unto him, cui bono, what good will ensue in case the same is effected?”—Fuller: Worthies (The Design, i.).

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To cut the knot*?
wrong: To run with the hare and hold with the hounds
A dispute to be settled by a duel
To suspect something about to happen
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Break through an obstacle. The reference is to the Gordian knot (q.v.) shown to Alexander with the assurance that whoever loosed it would be made ruler of all Asia, whereupon the Macedonian cut it in two with his sword, and claimed to have fulfilled the prophecy.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Cut and dry*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
Already prepared. “He had a speech all cut and dry.” The allusion is to timber cut, dry, and fit for use.

“Sets of phrases, cut and dry, Evermore thy tongue supply.”—Swift.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Cut and run*?
questions.answer: Be off as quickly as possible
wrong: To ridicule a person not openly but in secret
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Be off as quickly as possible. A sea phrase, meaning cut your cable and run before the wind.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *The cut of his jib*?
questions.answer: The contour or expression of his face
wrong: One too heavy to be carried
To be doing a brisk business
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: The contour or expression of his face. This is a sailor's phrase. The cut of a jib or foresail of a ship indicates her character. Thus, a sailor says of a suspicious vessel, he “does not like the cut of her jib.”

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To cut up rough*?
questions.answer: To be disagreeable or quarrelsome about anything
wrong: “Good-bye for the present.” Literally, till seeing you again
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To be disagreeable or quarrelsome about anything.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *The darkest hour is that before the dawn*?
questions.answer: When Fortune's wheel is lowest, it must turn up again
wrong: From this sample you can judge of the whole
To acknowledge oneself in the wrong
Don’t throw good money after bad
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: When Fortune's wheel is lowest, it must turn up again. When things have come to their worst, they must mend. In Latin, Post nubila, Phœbus.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *A day after the fair*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Too late; the fair you came to see is over.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *I have had my day*?
questions.answer: My prime of life is over
wrong: He is a shrewd fellow not to be imposed on
To throw a reproof at one
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
My prime of life is over; I have been a man of light and leading, but am now “out of the swim.”

“Old Joe, sir... was a bit of a favourite... once; but he has had his day.”—Dickens.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Dead drunk*?
questions.answer: So intoxicated as to be wholly powerless
wrong: An expletive, or mild kind of oath
It is in hand, but not yet finished
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
So intoxicated as to be wholly powerless.

“Pythagoras has finely observed that a man is not to be considered dead drunk till he lies on the floor and stretches out his arms and legs to prevent his going lower.”—S. Warren.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *A dead letter*?
questions.answer: A written document of no value
wrong: "No more" can be said on the subject
The buyer must be responsible for his own free act
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: A written document of no value; a law no longer acted upon. Also a letter which lies buried in the post-office because the address is incorrect, or the person addressed cannot be found.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Dead men*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Empty bottles. Down among the dead men let me lie. Let me get so intoxicated as to slip from my chair, and lie under the table with the empty bottles. The expression is a witticism on the word spirit. Spirit means life, and also alcohol (the spirit of full bottles); when the spirit is out the man is dead, and when the bottle is empty its spirit is departed.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Waiting for dead men's shoes*?
wrong: To find a person off his guard
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Looking out for legacies; looking to stand in the place of some moneyed man when he is dead and buried.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *A decoy duck*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: A bait or lure; a duck taught to allure others into a net, and employed for this purpose.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *The devil's tattoo*?
questions.answer: Tapping on the table with one's finger a wearisome number of times
wrong: To doubt the truth of a statement
It is inherited or exists in the family race
Worn out, tired out, utterly fatigued, or exhausted
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Tapping on the table with one's finger a wearisome number of times; tapping on the floor with one's foot in a similar manner; repeating any sound with wearisome pertinacity, giving those who hear the “blue devils” or the “fidgets.”

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *A rough diamond*?
wrong: To become less popular or less successful
To escape accidents in a marvellous manner
A written document of no value
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: An uncultivated genius; a person of excellent parts, but without society manners.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Dirt cheap*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Very low-priced. Dirt is so cheap that persons pay others to take it away.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Done for, or Regularly done for*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Utterly ruined. This “for” is the adverb = thoroughly, very common as a prefix.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Done up*?
wrong: To divide something too small to be worth dividing
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Thoroughly tired and wearied out. Up means ended, completed, as the “game is up” (over, finished), and adverbially it means “completely,” hence to be “done up” is to be exhausted completely.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To draw the long bow*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To exaggerate. Some wonderful tales are told of Robin Hood and other foresters practised in the long bow.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To drive a roaring trade*?
questions.answer: To be doing a brisk business
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To be doing a brisk business. The allusion is to a coachman who drives so fast that his horses pant and roar for breath.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To drop in*?
questions.answer: To make a casual call, not invited
wrong: To look askant with shyness or diffidence
I am very busy, and cannot attend to anything else
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To make a casual call, not invited; to pay an informal visit. The allusion is to fruit and other things falling down suddenly, unexpectedly, or accidentally. It is the intransitive verb, not the transitive, which means to “let fall.”

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To drown the miller*?
questions.answer: To put too much water into grog or tea
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To put too much water into grog or tea. The idea is that the supply of water is so great that even the miller, who uses a water wheel, is drowned with it.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To draw Dun out of the mire*?
questions.answer: To lend a helping hand to one in distress
wrong: To run with the hare and hold with the hounds
He exposed himself to needless danger
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To lend a helping hand to one in distress. The allusion is to an English game, explained by Mr. Gifford in his edition of Ben Jonson, vii. 283. A log of wood is brought into a room. The log, called Dun, is supposed to have fallen into the mire, and the players are to pull him out. Every player does all he can to obstruct the others, and as often as possible the log is made to fall on someone’s toes. Constant allusion is made to this game.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To raise a dust, or To kick up a dust*?
questions.answer: To make a commotion or disturbance
wrong: An actor who appears, speaks, or acts only once
To regard actions in a wrong light
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To make a commotion or disturbance.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *In at one ear, and out at the other*?
wrong: Worn out, tired out, utterly fatigued, or exhausted
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Forgotten as soon as heard.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To eat one’s heart out*?
wrong: A scheme which has been already carried out with success
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To fret or worry unreasonably; to allow one grief or one vexation to predominate over the mind, tincture all one’s ideas, and absorb all other emotions.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *I have eggs on the spit*?
questions.answer: I am very busy, and cannot attend to anything else
wrong: To get or keep the upper hand
A glass of grog before going to bed
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: I am very busy, and cannot attend to anything else. The reference is to roasting eggs on a spit. Eggs were first boiled, then the yolk was taken out, braided up with spices, and put back again; the eggs were then drawn on a “spit,” and roasted.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Elbow grease*?
questions.answer: Perspiration excited by hard manual labour
wrong: A piece of information generally known, but not yet formally announced
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Perspiration excited by hard manual labour. They say “Elbow grease is the best furniture oil.”

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To come to the end of one’s tether*?
questions.answer: To do all that one has ability or liberty to do
wrong: I am quite familiar with it and can do it readily
The inner disc of a target
Said of a fresh and spirited horse
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To do all that one has ability or liberty to do. The allusion is to an animal tied to a rope; he can graze only so far as his tether can be carried out.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Esprit de corps*?
questions.answer: Fellow-feeling for the society with which you are associated
wrong: A jocose and rather depreciating term applied to the leader of a party
I am quite familiar with it and can do it readily
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Fellow-feeling for the society with which you are associated. A military term—every soldier will stand up for his own corps.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *The estates of the realm*?
questions.answer: The powers that have the administration of affairs in their hands
wrong: First-rate, thumping, as a thumping legacy
To make a casual call, not invited
To attack or encounter a threatened danger fearlessly
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
The powers that have the administration of affairs in their hands. The three estates of our own realm are the Lords Spiritual, the Lords Temporal, and the Commons; popularly speaking, the public press is termed the fourth estate. It is a great mistake to call the three estates of England the Sovereign, the Lords, and the Commons, as many do. The word means that on which the realm stands. (Latin, sto, to stand.)

“Herod ... made a supper to his ... chief estates.”—Mark vi. 21.

“The king and the three estates of the realm assembled in parliament.”—Collect for Nov. 5.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Ex pede Herculem*?
questions.answer: From this sample you can judge of the whole
wrong: He exposed himself to needless danger
To acknowledge oneself in the wrong
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: From this sample you can judge of the whole. Plutarch says that Pythagoras ingeniously calculated the height of Hercules by comparing the length of various stadia in Greece. A stadium was 600 feet in length, but Hercules’ stadium at Olympia was much longer. Now, says the philosopher, as the stadium of Olympia is longer than an ordinary stadium, so the foot of Hercules was longer than an ordinary foot; and as the foot bears a certain ratio to the height, so the height of Hercules can be easily ascertained. (Varia Scripta.)

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *In my mind’s eye*?
wrong: To assume the guidance or direction
To look askant with shyness or diffidence
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: In my perceptive thought. The eye sees in two ways: (1) from without; and (2) from within. When we look at anything without, the object is reflected on the retina as on a mirror; but in deep contemplation the inward thought “informs the eye.” It was thus Macbeth saw the dagger; and Hamlet tells Horatio that he saw his deceased father “in his mind’s eye.”

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To have an eye on*?
questions.answer: To keep strict watch on the person or thing referred to
wrong: To conceal oneself or one’s intentions
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To keep strict watch on the person or thing referred to.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To cast sheep’s eyes at one*?
questions.answer: To look askant with shyness or diffidence
wrong: To be disagreeable or quarrelsome about anything
To doubt the truth of a statement
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To look askant with shyness or diffidence.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To face down*?
questions.answer: To withstand with boldness and effrontery
wrong: In a sorry plight, or state of disorder
Good manners, or manners accredited by good society
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To withstand with boldness and effrontery.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *In a fair way*?
wrong: A written document of no value
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: On the right tack. The “fair way” is the proper track through a channel.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Fait accompli*?
questions.answer: A scheme which has been already carried out with success
wrong: To be buried in one’s native place
When Fortune's wheel is lowest, it must turn up again
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
A scheme which has been already carried out with success.

“The subjection of the South is as much a fait accompli as the declaration of independence itself.”—The Times.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To fall away*?
wrong: He is a soft, a noodle
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To lose flesh; to degenerate; to quit a party, as “his adherents fell away gradually [one by one], or rapidly.”

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To fall to*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
To begin [eating, fighting, etc.].

“They sat down .... and without waiting .... fell to like commoners after grace.”—Kane: Arctic Explorations, vol. i. chap. xxx. p. 419.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To fall short of*?
questions.answer: To be deficient of a supply
wrong: A situation of ease and pleasure
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To be deficient of a supply. This is the Latin excido, to fail. To fall short of the mark is a figure taken from archery, quoits, etc., where the missile falls to the ground before reaching the mark.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To fall upon one’s feet*?
wrong: One in which the batsman has made several runs
First-rate, thumping, as a thumping legacy
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To escape a threatened injury; to light upon one’s feet.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Far-fetched*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
Not closely connected; a remote conceit; as, “a far-fetched simile,” a “far-fetched allusion.” Also, obtained from a foreign or distant country, “quod rarum est, carum est.”

“The passion for long, involved sentences ... and far-fetched conceits ... passed away, and a clearer and less ornate style became popular.”—Lecky: England in the Eighteenth Century, vol. i. chap. i. p. 91.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Far gone*?
wrong: To give up as a bad job
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Deeply affected: as, “far gone in love.”

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To play fast and loose*?
questions.answer: To run with the hare and hold with the hounds
wrong: To be "not at home" to visitors
Worn out, tired out, utterly fatigued, or exhausted
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
To run with the hare and hold with the hounds; to blow both hot and cold; to say one thing and do another. The allusion is to a cheating game practised at fairs. A belt is folded, and the player is asked to prick it with a skewer, so as to pin it fast to the table; having so done, the adversary takes the two ends, and looses it or draws it away.

“He forced his neck into a noose, To show his play at fast and loose; And when he chanced t’escape, mistook, For art and subtlety, his luck.” Butler: Hudibras, iii. 2.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To kill the fatted calf*?
questions.answer: To welcome with the best of everything
wrong: To smoke a cigar or pipe
He is a soft, a noodle
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To welcome with the best of everything. The phrase is taken from the parable in the third gospel of the prodigal son. (Luke xv. 30.)

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *An oiled feather*?
wrong: A mighty to-do about a trifle
Intoxication or illness from intemperance in drink
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Kindness of manner and speech. An oiled feather will do more to ease a stubborn lock than great force.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *In full feather*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Flush of money. In allusion to birds not on the moult.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *In high feather*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: In exuberant spirits, joyous. When birds are moulting they mope about, but as soon as they regain their feathers their spirits revive.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Tickled with a feather*?
wrong: You disparage it because it is beyond your reach
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Easily moved to laughter. “Pleased with a feather, tickled with a straw,” is more usual; Rire de la moindre bagatelle. Also annoyed by trifles, worried by little annoyances.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To play second fiddle*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To take a subordinate part. The allusion is to the leader of concerts, who leads with a fiddle.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Fiddler’s Green*?
questions.answer: The land of the leal or “Dixie Land” of sailors
wrong: To be worthy of better things
To make a casual call, not invited
Not to follow the dicta of a party leader, but to act independently
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: The land of the leal or “Dixie Land” of sailors; where there is perpetual mirth, a fiddle that never ceases to untiring dancers, plenty of grog, and unlimited tobacco.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To fight shy*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To avoid. A shy person is unwilling to come forward, and to fight is to resist, to struggle in a contest. To “fight shy,” therefore, is to resist being brought into contest or conflict.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *I have it at my fingers’ ends*?
questions.answer: I am quite familiar with it and can do it readily
wrong: To fret about some loss which can never be repaired
A person of awkward manners dressed so fine that he cannot move easily
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
I am quite familiar with it and can do it readily. It is a Latin proverb (Scire tanquam ungues digitosque), where the allusion is to the statuary, who knows every item of his subject by the touch.

“Costard: Go to; thou hast it ad dunghill, at the fingers’ ends, as they say. Holofernes: O, I smell false Latin; dunghill for unguem.”—Shakespeare: Love’s Labour’s Lost, v. 1.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To fire up*?
wrong: To get or keep the upper hand
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To become indignantly angry. The Latin, “ira exardescere,” “S’enflammer de colère.”

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Like a fish out of water*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Out of place; without one’s usual occupation; restless from lack of employment.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *The flag’s down*?
wrong: To rise out of, to appear at the surface
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
Indicative of distress. When the face is pale the “flag is down.” Alluding to the ancient custom of taking down the flag of theatres during Lent, when the theatres were closed.

“’Tis Lent in your cheeks, the flag’s down.”—Dodsley’s Old Plays (vol. v. 314, article, “Mad World”).

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *A flare-up*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: A rumpus or row. Also a banquet or jovial treat. The first meaning is simply the substantive of the verb. The second meaning refers to dazzle and “splendour” displayed.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Sighing for the flesh-pots of Egypt*?
questions.answer: Hankering for good things no longer at your command
wrong: To be the first to commence a project, etc.
Be off as quickly as possible
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Hankering for good things no longer at your command. The children of Israel said they wished they had died “when they sat by the flesh-pots of Egypt” (Exodus xvi. 3)—i.e. when they sat watching the boilers which contained the meat they were to have for dinner. The expression also means abundance of appetising food.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To flutter the dovecotes*?
questions.answer: To disturb the equanimity of a society
wrong: To be deficient of a supply
A written document of no value
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To disturb the equanimity of a society. The phrase occurs in Coriolanus.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Every man hath a fool in his sleeve*?
wrong: To be doing a brisk business
To make a casual call, not invited
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: No one is always wise. The allusion is to the tricks of jugglers.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Best foot foremost*?
wrong: An achievement to be proud of
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
Use all possible dispatch. To “set on foot” is to set agoing. If you have various powers of motion, set your best foremost.

“Nay, but make haste; the better foot before.” Shakespeare: King John, iv. 2.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To come to the fore*?
wrong: To put too much water into grog or tea
From this sample you can judge of the whole
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To stand out prominently; to distinguish oneself; to stand forth.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *The Fourth Estate of the realm*?
wrong: I am out of my element
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: The daily press. The most powerful of all. Burke, referring to the Reporters’ Gallery, said, “Yonder sits the Fourth Estate, more important than them all.”

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *He who laughs on Friday will weep on Sunday*?
questions.answer: Sorrow follows in the wake of joy
wrong: Hankering for good things no longer at your command
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Sorrow follows in the wake of joy. The line is taken from Racine’s comedy of Les Plaideurs.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Like fun*?
wrong: To regard actions in a wrong light
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Thoroughly, energetically, with delight.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Gall and wormwood*?
wrong: A glass of grog before going to bed
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Extremely disagreeable and annoying.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Tell it not in Gath*?
questions.answer: Don’t let your enemies hear it
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
Don’t let your enemies hear it. Gath was famous as being the birthplace of the giant Goliath.

“Tell it not in Gath, publish it not in the streets of Askelon; lest the daughters of the Philistines rejoice, lest the daughters of the uncircumcised triumph.”—2 Sam. i. 20.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To throw down the gauntlet*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To challenge. The custom in the Middle Ages, when one knight challenged another, was for the challenger to throw his gauntlet on the ground, and if the challenge was accepted the person to whom it was thrown picked it up.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *My evil genius*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: My ill-luck. The Romans maintained that two genii attended every man from birth to death—one good and the other evil. Good luck was brought about by the agency of “his good genius,” and ill luck by that of his “evil genius.”

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *The ghost of a chance*?
wrong: To regard actions in a wrong light
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: The least likelihood. “He has not the ghost of a chance of being elected,” not the shadow of a probability.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To take the gilt off the gingerbread*?
wrong: Soft, wheedling speeches to gain some end
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To destroy the illusion. The reference is to gingerbread watches, men, and other gilded toys, sold at fairs. These eatables were common even in the reign of Henry IV., but were then made of honey instead of treacle.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Hand and glove*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
Sworn friends; on most intimate terms; close companions, like glove and hand.

“And prate and preach about what others prove, As if the world and they were hand and glove.” Cowper.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To get into one’s good graces*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
To be in favour with.

“Having continued to get into the good graces of a buxom widow.”—Dickens: Pickwick.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *He killed the goose to get the eggs*?
questions.answer: He grasped at what was more than his due, and lost an excellent customer
wrong: To be in a state of anxiety, fearful that something will go wrong
To be the tool of another, the medium of doing another's dirty work
It is inherited or exists in the family race
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: He grasped at what was more than his due, and lost an excellent customer. The Greek fable says a countryman had a goose that laid golden eggs; thinking to make himself rich, he killed the goose to get the whole stock of eggs at once, but lost everything.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To give grass*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To confess yourself vanquished. To be knocked down in a pugilistic encounter is to “go to grass;” to have the sack is also to go to grass, as a cow which is no longer fit for milking is sent to pasture.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *With one foot in the grave*?
questions.answer: At the very verge of death
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: At the very verge of death. The expression was used by Julian, who said he would “learn something even if he had one foot in the grave.” The parallel Greek phrase is, “With one foot in the ferry-boat,” meaning Charon’s.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Great wits jump*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Think alike. Thus Shakespeare says, “It jumps with my humour.” (1 Henry IV., i. 2.)

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To grind one down*?
wrong: To make a casual call, not invited
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To reduce the price asked; to lower wages. A knife, etc., is gradually reduced by grinding.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To bring grist to the mill*?
questions.answer: To supply customers or furnish supplies
wrong: Not to follow the dicta of a party leader, but to act independently
Soft, wheedling speeches to gain some end
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To supply customers or furnish supplies.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *It would suit me down to the ground*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Wholly and entirely.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To hold one’s ground*?
wrong: A time of happiness and prosperity
The buyer must be responsible for his own free act
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To maintain one’s authority; not to budge from one’s position; to retain one’s popularity.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To lose ground*?
questions.answer: To become less popular or less successful
wrong: "No more" can be said on the subject
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To become less popular or less successful; to be drifting away from the object aimed at.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To a hair, or To the turn of a hair*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To a nicety. A hairbreadth is the forty-eighth part of an inch.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Hair-splitting*?
wrong: The dominant bully or master spirit
To throw a reproof at one
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
Very minute differences.

“Nothing is more fatal to eloquence than attention to fine hair-splitting distinctions.”—Mathews: Oratory and Orators, chap. ii. p. 36.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Halcyon days*?
questions.answer: A time of happiness and prosperity
wrong: To escape accidents in a marvellous manner
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
A time of happiness and prosperity. Halcyon is the Greek for a kingfisher, compounded of hals (the sea) and kuo (to brood on). The ancient Sicilians believed that the kingfisher laid its eggs and incubated for fourteen days, before the winter solstice, on the surface of the sea, during which time the waves of the sea were always unruffled.

“Amidst our arms as quiet you shall be As halcyon brooding on a winter’s sea.” Dryden.

“The peaceful kingfishers are met together About the deck, and prophesie calm weather.” Wild: Iter Boreale.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Gone to the hammer*?
questions.answer: Applied to goods sent to a sale by auction
wrong: To find a person off his guard
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Applied to goods sent to a sale by auction.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *An old hand*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: One experienced.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To get the upper hand*?
wrong: To rise out of, to appear at the surface
An achievement to be proud of
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To obtain the mastery.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *With handkerchief in one hand and sword in the other*?
questions.answer: Pretending to be sorry at a calamity, but prepared to make capital out of it
wrong: To be in a state of anxiety, fearful that something will go wrong
To suffer the disgrace of a vanquished army
A jocose and rather depreciating term applied to the leader of a party
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
Pretending to be sorry at a calamity, but prepared to make capital out of it.

“Abbé George .... mentions in [a letter] that ‘Maria Theresa stands with the handkerchief in one hand, weeping for the woes of Poland, but with the sword in the other hand, ready to cut Poland in sections, and take her share.’”—Carlyle: The Diamond Necklace, chap. iv.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *The handwriting on the wall*?
questions.answer: An announcement of some coming calamity
wrong: To cut oneself off from all means or hope of retreat
A maladroit hand interfering with a delicate business
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: An announcement of some coming calamity. The allusion is to the handwriting on Belshazzar’s palace-wall announcing the loss of his kingdom. (Dan. v. 5–31.)

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Happy-go-lucky*?
wrong: To suffer some disadvantage while off one's guard
To disturb the equanimity of a society
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: One indifferent to his interests; one who looks to good luck to befriend him.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Hard up*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Short of money. “N’avoir pas de quibus.” “Up” often = out, as, “used up,” “worn out,” “done up,” etc. “Hard up” = nearly out [of cash]. In these, and all similar examples, “Up” is the Old English ofer, over; Latin, s-uper; Greek, huper.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Hard as the nether millstone*?
wrong: The contour or expression of his face
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Unfeeling, obdurate. The lower or “nether” of the two millstones is firmly fixed and very hard; the upper stone revolves round it on a shaft, and the corn, running down a tube inserted in the upper stone, is ground by the motion of the upper stone round the lower one. Of course, the upper wheel is made to revolve by some power acting on it, as wind, water, or some other mechanical force.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To kiss the hare’s foot*?
questions.answer: To be late or too late for dinner
wrong: He is a shrewd fellow not to be imposed on
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
To be late or too late for dinner. The hare has run away, and you are only in time to “kiss” the print of his foot. A common proverb.

“You must kiss the hare’s foot; post festum venisti.”—Cole: Dictionary.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To hark back*?
wrong: Not to come near a person
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To return to the subject. “Revenons à nos moutons” (q.v.). A call to the dogs in fox-hunting, when they have overrun the scent, “Hark [dogs] come back”; so “Hark for’ards!” “Hark away!” etc.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *A hash*?
wrong: One living in ease and luxury
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
A mess, a muddle; as, “a pretty hash he made of it.” A hash is a mess, and a mess is a muddle.

I’ll soon settle his hash for him. I will soon smash him up; ruin his schemes; “give him his gruel”; “cook his goose”; “put my finger in his pie”; “make mince-meat of him.”

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Under hatches*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
Dead and buried. The hatches of a ship are the coverings over the hatchways (or openings in the deck of a vessel) to allow of cargo, etc., being easily discharged.

“And though his soul has gone aloft, His body’s under hatches.”

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To throw the hatchet*?
wrong: At the very point of death
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To tell falsehoods. In allusion to an ancient game where hatchets were thrown at a mark, like quoits. It means the same as drawing the long-bow (q.v.).

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To keep one’s head above water*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To avoid bankruptcy. The allusion is to a person immersed in water; so long as his head is above water his life remains, but bad swimmers find it hard to keep their heads above water.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *The labour of a Hercules*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Very great toil. Hercules was appointed by Eurystheus (3 syl.) to perform twelve labours requiring enormous strength or dexterity.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To be on the high ropes*?
questions.answer: To be very grand and mighty in demeanour
wrong: To throw a reproof at one
To divide something too small to be worth dividing
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To be very grand and mighty in demeanour.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *A hog in armour*?
questions.answer: A person of awkward manners dressed so fine that he cannot move easily
wrong: To cease boasting and assume a lower tone
He grasped at what was more than his due, and lost an excellent customer
Projected, and talked about as likely to occur
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: A person of awkward manners dressed so fine that he cannot move easily. A corruption of “Hodge in armour.”

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *He is not fit to hold the candle to him*?
wrong: To be deficient of a supply
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: He is very inferior. The allusion is to link-boys who held candles in theatres and other places of night amusement.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *An affair of honour*?
questions.answer: A dispute to be settled by a duel
wrong: Treating one without the least consideration
The lions or crack men of the day
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: A dispute to be settled by a duel. Duels were generally provoked by offences against the arbitrary rules of etiquette, courtesy, or feeling, called the “laws of honour;” and, as these offences were not recognisable in the law courts, they were settled by private combat.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *In hot water*?
questions.answer: In a state of trouble, or of anxiety
wrong: Most certainly I shall never do what you say
Fellow-feeling for the society with which you are associated
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: In a state of trouble, or of anxiety. The reference is to the ordeal by hot water (q.v.).

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *At the eleventh hour*?
questions.answer: Just in time not to be too late
wrong: To ascertain how far a person will venture
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Just in time not to be too late; only just in time to obtain some benefit. The allusion is to the parable of labourers hired for the vineyard (Matt. xx.).

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Ill-got, ill-spent*?
wrong: Not yet out of nursery government
"No more" can be said on the subject
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Treasures of wickedness profit nothing. (Prov. x. 2.)

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *A good innings*?
questions.answer: One in which the batsman has made several runs
wrong: To be late or too late for dinner
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: One in which the batsman has made several runs. Figuratively, a run of luck or business. He has had a long innings. A good long run of luck. A term in cricket for the time that the eleven are in, or not out as scouts.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Like an owl in an ivy-bush*?
questions.answer: Having a sapient, vacant look, as some persons have when in their cups
wrong: Abounding in all good things, or of extraordinary fertility
To do all that one has ability or liberty to do
To withstand with boldness and effrontery
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
Having a sapient, vacant look, as some persons have when in their cups; having a stupid vacant stare. Owls are proverbial for their judge-like solemnity, and ivy is the favourite plant of Bacchus. Gray, in his Elegy, refers to the Owl and the Ivy.

“From yonder ivy-mantled tower The moping owl doth to the moon complain Of such as, wandering near her secret bower, Molest her ancient solitary reign.”—Stanza 3.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *A Jack-a-lantern*?
wrong: To assume the guidance or direction
To barter by the rule of thumb
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: A Will-o’-the-wisp, an ignis fatuus.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *A Joe Miller*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: A stale joke; so called from the compilation of jokes under that nom de plume.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *A jolly dog*?
wrong: I am out of my element
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: A bon vivant. Here “jolly” means jovial.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *A Judas kiss*?
wrong: A time of happiness and prosperity
It is in hand, but not yet finished
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
A deceitful act of courtesy. Judas betrayed his Master with a kiss.

“So Judas kissed his Master, And cried, ‘All hail!’ whenas he meant all harm.”—Shakespeare: 3 Henry VI., v. 7.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To keep at arm’s length*?
questions.answer: To prevent another from being too familiar
wrong: To throw a reproof at one
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To prevent another from being too familiar.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To keep one’s countenance*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To refrain from laughing; to preserve one’s gravity.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To kick over the traces*?
questions.answer: Not to follow the dicta of a party leader, but to act independently
wrong: Lay the blame on those who deserve it
To regard actions in a wrong light
Worn out, tired out, utterly fatigued, or exhausted
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
Not to follow the dicta of a party leader, but to act independently; as a horse refusing to run in harness kicks over the traces.

“If the new member shows any inclination to kick over the traces, he will not be their member long.”—Newspaper paragraph, Feb., 1893.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *A killing pace*?
questions.answer: Too hot or strong to last
wrong: To be very grand and mighty in demeanour
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Too hot or strong to last; exceptionally great; exhausting.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To knuckle under*?
wrong: A very severe and undeniable one
To take food after long abstinence
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To kneel for pardon. Knuckle here means the knee, and we still say a “knuckle of veal or mutton,” meaning the thin end of the leg near the joint. Dr. Ogilvie tells us there was an old custom of striking the under side of a table with the knuckles when defeated in an argument; and Dr. Johnson, following Bailey, says the same thing.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *A free-lance*?
questions.answer: One who acts on his own judgment, and not from party motives
wrong: A glass of grog before going to bed
To suffer the disgrace of a vanquished army
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: One who acts on his own judgment, and not from party motives. The reference is to the Free Companies of the Middle Ages, called in Italy condottieri, and in France Compagnies Grandes, which were free to act as they liked, and were not servants of the Crown or of any other potentate. It must be confessed, however, that they were willing to sell themselves to any master and any cause, good or bad.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To lay about one*?
wrong: To throw a reproof at one
To exert oneself to the utmost
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
To strike on all sides.

“He’ll lay about him to-day.”—Shakespeare: Troilus and Cressida, i. 2.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *A lazy man’s load*?
questions.answer: One too heavy to be carried
wrong: He is a soft, a noodle
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: One too heavy to be carried; so called because lazy people, to save themselves the trouble of coming a second time, are apt to overload themselves.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To do one’s level best*?
questions.answer: To exert oneself to the utmost
wrong: To be the first to commence a project, etc.
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To exert oneself to the utmost. Au gré de nos pouvoirs. In 1877 Mr. Hale published a book entitled His Level Best.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To lie low*?
questions.answer: To conceal oneself or one’s intentions
wrong: To be the first to commence a project, etc.
To smoke a cigar or pipe
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
To conceal oneself or one’s intentions.

“All this while Brer Rabbit lay low.”—Uncle Remus.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To lie with one’s fathers*?
questions.answer: To be buried in one’s native place
wrong: A time of happiness and prosperity
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
To be buried in one’s native place. “Reposer avec ses pères.”

“I will lie with my fathers, and thou shalt carry me out of Egypt.”—Genesis xlvii. 30.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *For the life of me*?
wrong: Sin has set his mark on all
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
True as I am alive. Even if my life depended on it; a strong asseveration.

“Nor could I, for the life of me, see how the creation of the world had anything to do with what I was talking about.”—Goldsmith: Vicar of Wakefield.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Large as life*?
questions.answer: Of the same size as the object represented
wrong: Fellow-feeling for the society with which you are associated
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Of the same size as the object represented.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To bear a charmed life*?
questions.answer: To escape accidents in a marvellous manner
wrong: To act in a very disorderly way
In a sorry plight, or state of disorder
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To escape accidents in a marvellous manner.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To the life*?
wrong: Said of a braggart or pretender
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: In exact imitation. “Done to the life.” “Faire le portrait de quelqu’un au naturel” (or) “d’après nature.”

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *The light-fingered gentry*?
wrong: A glass of grog before going to bed
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Pickpockets and shop-lifters.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To curl the lip*?
wrong: I have spent all my money
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To express contempt or disgust.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *The little gentleman in velvet*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: The mole. “To the little gentleman in velvet” was a favourite Jacobite toast in the reign of Queen Anne. The reference was to the mole that raised the mole-hill against which the horse of William III. stumbled at Hampton Court. By this accident the king broke his collar-bone, a severe illness ensued, and he died early in 1702.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Lombard Street to a China orange*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
Long odds. Lombard Street, London, is the centre of great banking and mercantile transactions. To stake the Bank of England against a common orange is to stake what is of untold value against a mere trifle.

“‘It is Lombard Street to a China orange,’ quoth Uncle Jack.”—Bulwer Lytton: The Caxtons.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To look through blue glasses or coloured spectacles*?
questions.answer: To regard actions in a wrong light
wrong: A glass of grog before going to bed
To be doing a brisk business
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To regard actions in a wrong light; to view things distorted by prejudice.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Out on the loose*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Out on the spree; out of moral bounds.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To lose heart*?
wrong: It is inherited or exists in the family race
A coward who hectors, a fool that apes the wise man
To pass without notice, to leave in the lurch
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To be discouraged or despondent. Heart = courage.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Lose the horse or win the saddle*?
wrong: The dominant bully or master spirit
My prime of life is over
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Everything or nothing. “Aut Cæsar, aut nullus.” A man made the bet of a horse that another could not say the Lord’s Prayer without a wandering thought. The bet was accepted, but before half-way through the person who accepted the bet looked up and said, “By-the-bye, do you mean the saddle also?”

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To be at a loss*?
wrong: To gain the rank of knighthood
He has a very good opinion of number one
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To be unable to decide. To be puzzled or embarrassed. As: “I am at a loss for the proper word.” “Je m’y perds,” or “Je suis bien embarrassé de dire.”

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *A lotus-eater*?
questions.answer: One living in ease and luxury
wrong: To conceal oneself or one’s intentions
To withstand with boldness and effrontery
In a sorry plight, or state of disorder
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: One living in ease and luxury. Lord Tennyson has a poem called The Lotus Eaters. The drink is made from the Zizyphus Lotus, which grows in Jerbah, an island near Tunis.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Lubber’s hole*?
questions.answer: A lazy cowardly way of doing what is appointed, or of evading duty
wrong: Cold boiled meat and greens fried
The hour of dusk, when it is too dark to work, and too soon to light candles
Soft, wheedling speeches to gain some end
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: A lazy cowardly way of doing what is appointed, or of evading duty. A seaman’s expression. Sailors call the vacant space between the head of a lower-mast and the edge of the top, the lubber’s hole, because timid boys get through this space to the top, to avoid the danger and difficulties of the “futtock shrouds.”

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *The lungs of London*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: The parks. In a debate, June 30th, 1808, respecting encroachments upon Hyde Park, Mr. Windham said it was the “lungs of London.”

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Magnum opus*?
questions.answer: Chief or most important of a person’s works
wrong: To doubt the truth of a statement
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Chief or most important of a person’s works. A literary man says of his most renowned book it is his magnum opus.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *A margarine substitute*?
wrong: To be worthy of better things
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
A mere imitation. Just as margarine is an imitation and substitute of butter.

“Between a real etching and that margarine substitute a pen-and-ink drawing ... the difference is this: the margarine substitute is essentially flat ... but true etching is in sensible relief.”—Nineteenth Century, May 1891, p. 780.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *The matter’s afoot*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Is in train, is stirring. Il marche bien, it goes well; ça ira.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *In meal or in malt*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
Directly or indirectly; some sort of subsidy. If much money passes through the hand, some profit will be sure to accrue either “in meal or in malt.”

“When other interests in the country (as the cotton trade, the iron trade, and the coal trade) had been depressed, the Government had not been called upon for assistance in meal and malt.”—Sir William Harcourt: On Agricultural Depression, 5th April, 1894.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To take the measure of one’s foot*?
questions.answer: To ascertain how far a person will venture
wrong: Out of work, out of place
Never attempt to controvert the statement of any one in his own special subject
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To ascertain how far a person will venture; to guess of another’s character. The allusion is to “Ex pede Herculem.”

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *A memento mori*?
questions.answer: Something to put us in mind of the shortness and uncertainty of life
wrong: The contour or expression of his face
A good-tempered, jovial, and generous person
Some selfish motive in the background
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
Something to put us in mind of the shortness and uncertainty of life.

“I make as good use of it [Bardolph’s face] as many a man doth of a death’s head or a memento mori.”—Shakespeare: Henry IV., iii. 3.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Meum and Tuum*?
questions.answer: That which belongs to me and that which is another's
wrong: Perspiration excited by hard manual labour
First-rate, thumping, as a thumping legacy
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: That which belongs to me and that which is another's. Meum is Latin for "what is mine," and tuum is Latin for "what is thine." If a man is said not to know the difference between meum and tuum, it is a polite way of saying he is a thief.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *A land of milk and honey*?
questions.answer: Abounding in all good things, or of extraordinary fertility
wrong: Just in time not to be too late
To act in a very disorderly way
A mighty effort made for a small effect
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
That is, abounding in all good things, or of extraordinary fertility. Joel iii. 18 speaks of "the mountains flowing with milk and honey." Figuratively used to denote all the blessings of heaven.

"Jerusalem the golden, With milk and honey blest."

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Milk and Water*?
wrong: Out of work, out of place
He has a very good opinion of number one
To take food after long abstinence
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Insipid, without energy or character; baby-pap (literature, etc.).

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Mind your Eye*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Be careful or vigilant; keep a sharp look out; keep your eyes open to guard against mischief. School-boy wit, Mens tuus ego.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *A Month's Mind*?
wrong: To conceal oneself or one’s intentions
At the very point of death
Lay the blame on those who deserve it
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
An irresistible longing (for something); a great desire.

"I see you have a month's mind for them."—Shakespeare: Two Gentlemen of Verona, i. 2.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Mother Carey is plucking her goose*?
wrong: At the very verge of death
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: It is snowing.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *The mountain in labour*?
questions.answer: A mighty effort made for a small effect
wrong: Too hot or strong to last
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: A mighty effort made for a small effect. The allusion is to the celebrated line of Horace, "Parturiunt montes, nascetur ridiculus mus," which Creech translates, "The travailing mountain yields a silly mouse;" and Boileau, "La montagne en travail enfante une souris."

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To nail one's colours to the mast*?
wrong: A situation of ease and pleasure
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To refuse to surrender. When the colours are nailed to the mast they cannot be lowered in proof of submission.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Neck and Neck*?
wrong: To make a commotion or disturbance
To prevent another from being too familiar
It is in hand, but not yet finished
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Very near together in merit; very close competitors. A phrase used in horse races, when two or more horses run each other very closely.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *The Needful*?
wrong: An achievement to be proud of
To regard actions in a wrong light
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Ready money, cash. The one thing needful for this life.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *A Nest-egg*?
wrong: Don’t let your enemies hear it
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Some money laid by. The allusion is to the custom of placing an egg in a hen's nest to induce her to lay her eggs there. If a person has saved a little money, it serves as an inducement to him to increase his store.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Next Door to*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Very nearly; as "next door to a fool."

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *In the nick of time*?
wrong: The dominant bully or master spirit
Of the same size as the object represented
"No more" can be said on the subject
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Just at the right moment. The allusion is to tallies marked with nicks or notches. Shakespeare has, "'Tis now the prick of noon" (Romeo and Juliet, ii. 4), in allusion to the custom of pricking tallies with a pin, as they do at Cambridge University still. If a man enters chapel just before the doors close, he would be just in time to get nicked or pricked, and would be at the nick or prick of time.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *A Nightcap*?
questions.answer: A glass of grog before going to bed
wrong: To be "not at home" to visitors
Of the same size as the object represented
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
A glass of grog before going to bed. Supposed to promote sleep.

"The nightcap is generally a little whisky left in the decanter. To do it honour it is taken neat. Then all get up and wish 'good-night.'"—Max O'Rell: Friend MacDonald, iii.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Nil Desperandum*?
wrong: A fine day for a fête
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Never say die; never give up in despair.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *No More Poles*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
Give over work. The cry in hop-gardens when the pickers are to cease working.

"When the sun set, the cry of 'No more poles' resounded, and the work of the day was done."—The Ludgate Monthly: Hops and Hop-pickers, November, 1891.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *A Nob of the First Water*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: A mighty boss; a grand panjandrum. First water refers to diamonds.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Non Plus*?
questions.answer: "No more" can be said on the subject
wrong: It is in hand, but not yet finished
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: "No more" can be said on the subject. When a man is come to a non-plus in an argument, it means that he is unable to deny or controvert what is advanced against him. "To non-plus" a person is to put him into such a fix.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To turn up one's nose*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To express contempt. When a person sneers he turns up the nose by curling the upper lip.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To sport one's oak*?
questions.answer: To be "not at home" to visitors
wrong: To prevent another from being too familiar
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To be "not at home" to visitors. At the Universities the "chambers" have two doors, the usual room-door and another made of oak, outside it; when the oak is shut or "sported" it indicates either that the occupant of the room is out, or that he does not wish to be disturbed by visitors.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *That makes no odds*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: No difference; never mind; that is no excuse. An application of the betting phrase.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To play old gooseberry*?
wrong: "No more" can be said on the subject
Not yet out of nursery government
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To be a third person; to be de trop. Old Gooseberry is the name given to a person accompanying an engaged couple.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Went for an old song*?
questions.answer: Was sold for a mere trifle, for a nominal sum or price
wrong: To be worthy of better things
Made the subject of a scandal
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Was sold for a mere trifle, for a nominal sum or price.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To hold out the olive branch*?
wrong: From this sample you can judge of the whole
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To make overtures of peace.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *On dit*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: A rumour, a report; as, "There is an on dit on Exchange that Spain will pay up its back dividends."

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *An Open Secret*?
questions.answer: A piece of information generally known, but not yet formally announced
wrong: Has become a ruined man, or a depraved character
To keep strict watch on the person or thing referred to
To moot it, to throw it out for discussion that it may be winnowed or sifted
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
A piece of information generally known, but not yet formally announced.

"It was an open secret that almost every one [of Lord Palmerston's ecclesiastical appointments] was virtually made by Lord Shaftesbury."—Leisure Hour, 1887.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *An Oyster Part*?
questions.answer: An actor who appears, speaks, or acts only once
wrong: A person of awkward manners dressed so fine that he cannot move easily
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: An actor who appears, speaks, or acts only once. Like an oyster, he opens but once.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To bear the palm*?
wrong: At the very point of death
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To be the best. The allusion is to the Roman custom of giving the victorious gladiator a branch of the palm-tree.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To turn an honest penny*?
questions.answer: To earn a little money by working for it
wrong: To look askant with shyness or diffidence
In for a penny, in for a pound
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To earn a little money by working for it.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *I'm in a pretty pickle*?
questions.answer: In a sorry plight, or state of disorder
wrong: A dispute to be settled by a duel
To withstand with boldness and effrontery
To be the first to commence a project, etc.
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
In a sorry plight, or state of disorder.

"How cam'st thou in this pickle?" Shakespeare: Tempest, v. 1.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Plates or Plates of Meat*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Slang for feet. One of the chief sources of slang is rhyme. Thus meat rhymes with feet, and "warming my plates" is slang for warming my feet.
