Similarly, "Rory O'More" is slang for door, and "there came a knock at the Rory O'More" means there was a knock at the door. A prescott is slang for waistcoat.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Pleased as Punch*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Greatly delighted. Our old friend Punch is always singing with self-satisfaction in all his naughty ways, and his evident "pleasure" is contagious to the beholders.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To plume oneself*?
wrong: To regard actions in a wrong light
Sorrow follows in the wake of joy
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
To be conceited of . . .; to boast of . . . Plume is a feather, and to plume oneself is to feather one's own conceit.

"Mrs. Bute Crawley . . . plumed herself upon her resolute manner of performing (what she thought right)."—Thackeray: Vanity Fair.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *A Plymouth Cloak*?
wrong: He is a soft, a noodle
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: A good stout cudgel. In the time of the Crusades many men of good family used to land at Plymouth utterly destitute. They went to a neighbouring wood, cut themselves a good stout club, and, stopping the first passenger that passed by, provided themselves with money and clothing. (Fuller: Worthies.)

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To stand on points*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
On punctilios; delicacy of behaviour.

"This fellow doth not stand upon points."—Shakespeare: Midsummer Night's Dream, v. 1.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To put up the shutters*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To announce oneself a bankrupt. Do you think I am going to put up the shutters if we can manage to keep going?

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Putting on Frills*?
wrong: To be doing a brisk business
In for a penny, in for a pound
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Giving oneself airs.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Mauvais Quart d'Heure*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: A time of annoyance. The time between the arrival of the guests and the announcement of dinner is emphatically called the mauvais quart d'heure; but the phrase has a much larger application: thus we say the Cabinet Ministers must have had a mauvais quart d'heure when opening a number of telegrams of a troublesome character.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Queen Anne is Dead*?
questions.answer: The reply made to the teller of stale news
wrong: Intoxication or illness from intemperance in drink
To be the first to commence a project, etc.
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: The reply made to the teller of stale news.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Queen's Weather*?
questions.answer: A fine day for a fête
wrong: To be worthy of better things
To welcome with the best of everything
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: A fine day for a fête; so called because Queen Victoria is, for the most part, fortunate in having fine weather when she appears in public.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To be on the qui vive*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: On the alert; to be quick and sharp; to be on the tiptoe of expectation, like a sentinel.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *In Quick Sticks*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Without more ado; quickly. To cut one's stick is to start off, and to cut one's stick quickly is to start off immediately.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Rack and Ruin*?
wrong: Said of a braggart or pretender
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
Utter destitution. Here "rack" is a variety of wrack and wreck.

"The worst of all University snobs are those unfortunates who go to rack and ruin from their desire to ape their betters."—Thackeray: Book of Snobs, chap. xv. p. 87.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *A Rainy Day*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Evil times. Lay by something for a rainy day. Save something against evil times.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To Rat*?
questions.answer: To forsake a losing side for the stronger party
wrong: An announcement of some coming calamity
To exert oneself to the utmost
My nerves are shaken, my equilibrium of mind is disturbed
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
To forsake a losing side for the stronger party. It is said that rats forsake ships not weatherproof. A rat is one who rats or deserts his party. Hence workmen who work during a strike are called "rats."

"Averting . . . The cup of sorrow from their lips, And fly like rats from sinking ships." Swift: Epistle to Mr. Nugent.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Drawing a red herring across the path*?
questions.answer: Trying to divert attention from the main question by some side-issue
wrong: To look askant with shyness or diffidence
The dominant bully or master spirit
A jocose and rather depreciating term applied to the leader of a party
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Trying to divert attention from the main question by some side-issue. A red herring drawn across a fox's path destroys the scent and sets the dogs at fault.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To take the reins*?
questions.answer: To assume the guidance or direction
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To assume the guidance or direction.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *A Rift in the Lute*?
questions.answer: A small defect which mars the general result
wrong: A species of sale by auction
To look askant with shyness or diffidence
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
A small defect which mars the general result.

"Unfaith in aught is want of faith in all. It is the little rift within the lute That by-and-by will make the music mute, And ever widening, slowly silence all." Tennyson: Merlin and Vivien; Vivien's Song.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Ring Down*?
wrong: Soft, wheedling speeches to gain some end
Too hot or strong to last
He exposed himself to needless danger
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Conclude, end at once. A theatrical phrase, alluding to the custom of ringing a bell to give notice for the fall of the curtain. Charles Dickens says, "It is time to ring down on these remarks." (Speech at the Dramatic Fête.)

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *He drives a roaring trade*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: He does a great business; his employees are driven till all their wind is gone. Hence fast, quick.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *A Roland for an Oliver*?
questions.answer: A blow for a blow, tit for tat
wrong: To assume the guidance or direction
I am quite familiar with it and can do it readily
Not yet out of nursery government
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
A blow for a blow, tit for tat. Roland and Oliver were two of the paladins of Charlemagne, whose exploits are so similar that it is very difficult to keep them distinct. What Roland did Oliver did, and what Oliver did Roland did. At length the two met in single combat, and fought for five consecutive days on an island in the Rhine, but neither gained the least advantage.

The etymologies connecting the proverb with Charles II., General Monk, and Oliver Cromwell, are wholly unworthy of credit, for even Shakespeare alludes to it: "England all Olivers and Rolands bred" (1 Henry VI., i. 2).

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To run a man down*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To abuse, depreciate. A hunting term.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *A screw loose*?
wrong: A species of sale by auction
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Something amiss. The allusion is to joinery kept together by screws.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Quite at sea*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Wide of the mark; quite wrong; like a person in the open ocean without compass or chart.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Over shoes, over boots*?
questions.answer: In for a penny, in for a pound
wrong: To be deficient of a supply
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
In for a penny, in for a pound.

“Where true courage roots, The proverb says, ‘once over shoes, o’er boots.’”—Taylor’s Workes, ii. 145 (1630).

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To shake in one’s shoes*?
questions.answer: To be in a state of nervous terror
wrong: One who listens stealthily to conversation
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To be in a state of nervous terror.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *He shot wide of the mark*?
wrong: Lay the blame on those who deserve it
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: He was altogether in error. The allusion is to shooting at the mark or bull’s-eye in archery, but will now apply to our modern rifle practice.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Shut up*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Hold your tongue. Shut up your mouth.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Sine Die*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: No time being fixed; indefinitely in regard to time. When a proposal is deferred sine die, it is deferred without fixing a day for its reconsideration, which is virtually “for ever.”

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Sine qua Non*?
wrong: To doubt the truth of a statement
Not to be involved in wrong-doing
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: An indispensable condition. Latin, Sine qua non potest esse or fieri (that without which [the thing] cannot be, or be done).

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To sing small*?
questions.answer: To cease boasting and assume a lower tone
wrong: He just touched me as he went past
To suffer some disadvantage while off one's guard
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To cease boasting and assume a lower tone.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To sit on thorns or on tenterhooks*?
questions.answer: To be in a state of anxiety, fearful that something will go wrong
wrong: To look askant with shyness or diffidence
Worn out, tired out, utterly fatigued, or exhausted
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To be in a state of anxiety, fearful that something will go wrong.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To slate one*?
questions.answer: To criticise, expose in print, show up, reprove
wrong: Of the same size as the object represented
The buyer must be responsible for his own free act
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To criticise, expose in print, show up, reprove. A scholastic term. Rebellious and idle boys are slated, that is, their names are set down on a slate to expose their offence, and some punishment is generally awarded.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To laugh in one’s sleeve*?
questions.answer: To ridicule a person not openly but in secret
wrong: To exert oneself to the utmost
A mighty effort made for a small effect
Good manners, or manners accredited by good society
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To ridicule a person not openly but in secret; to conceal a laugh by hiding your face in the large sleeves at one time worn by men.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *He does not think small beer of himself*?
questions.answer: He has a very good opinion of number one
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
He has a very good opinion of number one.

“To express her self-esteem [it might be said] that she did not think small beer of herself.”—De Quincey: Historical Essays.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To smell a rat*?
questions.answer: To suspect something about to happen
wrong: Has become a ruined man, or a depraved character
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To suspect something about to happen. The allusion is to a cat or dog smelling out vermin.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *It smells of the lamp*?
wrong: Soft, wheedling speeches to gain some end
The signal for the final judgment
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: A literary production manifestly laboured. Plutarch attributes the phrase to Pytheas the orator, who said, “The orations of Demosthenes smell of the lamp,” alluding to the current tale that the great orator lived in an underground cave lighted by a lamp, that he might have no distraction to his severe study.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *No smoke without fire*?
wrong: One who acts on his own judgment, and not from party motives
Lay the blame on those who deserve it
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Every slander has some foundation. The reverse proverb, “No fire without smoke,” means no good without some drawback.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To go snacks*?
wrong: Don’t throw good money after bad
I am out of my element
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To share and share alike.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Soft Soap*?
wrong: To regard actions in a wrong light
Worn out, tired out, utterly fatigued, or exhausted
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Flattery, complimentary words.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To come the old soldier over one*?
questions.answer: To dictate peremptorily and profess superiority of knowledge and experience
wrong: The powers that have the administration of affairs in their hands
Fellow-feeling for the society with which you are associated
Has become a ruined man, or a depraved character
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To dictate peremptorily and profess superiority of knowledge and experience.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To win his spurs*?
questions.answer: To gain the rank of knighthood
wrong: To put too much water into grog or tea
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To gain the rank of knighthood. When a man was knighted the person who dubbed him presented him with a pair of gilt spurs.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To put down one’s staff in a place*?
wrong: Saying “Be thou fed,” will not feed a hungry man
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To take up one’s residence. The allusion is to the tent-staff: where the staff is placed, there the tent is stretched, and the nomad resides.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *My stars and garters*?
questions.answer: An expletive, or mild kind of oath
wrong: To welcome with the best of everything
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: An expletive, or mild kind of oath. The stars and garters of knighthood. Shakespeare makes Richard III. swear “By my George, my garter, and my crown!” (Richard III., iv. 4.)

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *It is on the stocks*?
questions.answer: It is in hand, but not yet finished
wrong: It is inherited or exists in the family race
To act in a very disorderly way
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: It is in hand, but not yet finished. The stocks is the frame in which a ship is placed while building, and so long as it is in hand it is said to be or to lie on the stocks.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *A storm in a teapot*?
questions.answer: A mighty to-do about a trifle
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: A mighty to-do about a trifle. “A storm in a puddle.”

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *He stuck his spoon in the wall*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Took up his residence. Sometimes it means took up his long home, or died. In primitive times a leather strap was very often nailed to the wall, somewhere near the fireplace, and in this strap were stuck such things as scissors, spoons for daily use, pen-case, and so on. In Barclay’s Ship of Fools is a picture of a man stirring a pot on the fire, and on the wall is a strap with two spoons stuck into it.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *In the swim*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
In society. An angler’s phrase. A lot of fish gathered together is called a swim, and when an angler can pitch his hook in such a place he is said to be “in a good swim.” To know persons in the swim is to know society folk, who always congregate together.

“Cottontree, who knows nearly everybody in the swim of European society ... informs him that Lucy Annerley is the daughter of Sir Jonas Stevens.”—A. C. Gunter: Mr. Potter of Texas, book iii. chap. xiv.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Turning the tables*?
questions.answer: Rebutting a charge by bringing forth a counter-charge
wrong: To be buried in one’s native place
Pretending to be sorry at a calamity, but prepared to make capital out of it
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Rebutting a charge by bringing forth a counter-charge.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Up a tree*?
questions.answer: In a difficulty, in a mess
wrong: To find a person off his guard
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: In a difficulty, in a mess. It is said that Spurgeon used to practise his students in extempore preaching, and that one of his young men, on reaching the desk and opening the note containing his text, read the single word “Zacchæus” as his text. He thought a minute or two, and then delivered himself thus:—“Zacchæus was a little man, so am I; Zacchæus was up a tree, so am I; Zacchæus made haste and came down, and so do I.”

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *A tyrant’s vein*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: A ranting, bullying manner. In the old moralities the tyrants were made to rant, and the loudness of their rant was proportionate to the villainy of their dispositions. Hence to out-Herod Herod is to rant more loudly than Herod; to o’erdo Termagant is to rant more loudly than Termagant.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Upper Crust*?
questions.answer: The lions or crack men of the day
wrong: To suffer some disadvantage while off one's guard
Projected, and talked about as likely to occur
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
The lions or crack men of the day. The phrase was first used in Sam Slick. The upper crust was at one time the part of the loaf placed before the most honoured guests. Thus, in Wynkyn de Worde’s Boke of Keruinge (carving) we have these directions: “Then take a lofe in your lyfte hande, and pare ye lofe rounde about; then cut the ouer-cruste to your souerayne ...” Furnivall, in Manners and Meales, etc., says the same thing—“Kutt the vpper cruste for your souerayne.”

“I want you to see Peel, Stanley, Graham, Shiel, Russell, Macaulay, old Joe, and so on. They are all upper crust here.”

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Upper Storey*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: The head. “Ill-furnished in the upper storey;” a head without brains.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *The Upper Ten Thousand*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: The aristocracy. The term was first used by N. P. Willis, in speaking of the fashionables of New York, who at that time were not more than ten thousand in number.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Used up*?
questions.answer: Worn out, tired out, utterly fatigued, or exhausted
wrong: Prepare for action by removing everything not required
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
Worn out, tired out, utterly fatigued, or exhausted. Used up alludes to articles used up. Worn out alludes to dresses and articles worn out by use. Exhausted alludes to wells, water, etc., dried up. Tired out means tired utterly.

“Being out night after night, she got kinder used up.”—Sam Slick: Human Nature, p. 192.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To ventilate a subject*?
questions.answer: To moot it, to throw it out for discussion that it may be winnowed or sifted
wrong: Rebutting a charge by bringing forth a counter-charge
To criticise, expose in print, show up, reprove
To escape accidents in a marvellous manner
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To moot it, to throw it out for discussion that it may be winnowed or sifted. To ventilate a room is to let air and light into it, to drive away bad gases, etc. So in ventilating a subject, light is thrown on it, and all that is false, extraneous, or doubtful is blown away.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *The viper and the file*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: The biter bit. Æsop says a viper found a file, and tried to bite it, under the supposition that it was good food; but the file said that its province was to bite others, and not to be bitten. The viper of real life does not bite or masticate its food, but swallows it whole.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *A warm reception*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
A hot opposition. Also, a hearty welcome.

“The Home Rule members are prepared to give the Coercion Bill a warm reception; Mr. Parnell’s followers will oppose it tooth and nail.”—Newspaper paragraph, May 19th, 1885.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To throw cold water on a scheme*?
wrong: To be buried in one’s native place
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To discourage the proposal; to speak of it slightingly.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *The waterworks*?
wrong: To exert oneself to the utmost
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
The shedding of tears. Many other meanings also.

“‘Oh, miss, I never thought to have seen this day,’ and the waterworks began to play.”—Thackeray.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *We left our country for our country’s good*?
wrong: I am very busy, and cannot attend to anything else
To give up as a bad job
To doubt the truth of a statement
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: We are transported convicts. The line occurs in a prologue written by George Barrington (a notorious pickpocket) for the opening of the first playhouse at Sydney, in Australia, 16th January, 1796.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *He knows what’s what*?
questions.answer: He is a shrewd fellow not to be imposed on
wrong: To make a commotion or disturbance
To be very grand and mighty in demeanour
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
He is a shrewd fellow not to be imposed on. One of the senseless questions of logic was “Quid est quid?”

“He knew what’s what, and that’s as high As metaphysic wit can fly.”—Butler: Hudibras, part i. canto 1.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To whistle down the wind*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To defame a person. The cognate phrase “blown upon” is more familiar. The idea is to whistle down the wind that the reputation of the person may be blown upon.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To take or have the wind*?
questions.answer: To get or keep the upper hand
wrong: One in which the batsman has made several runs
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To get or keep the upper hand. Lord Bacon uses the phrase. “To have the wind of a ship” is to be to the windward of it.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To take one under your wing*?
wrong: Of the same size as the object represented
To assume the guidance or direction
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To patronise and protect. The allusion is to a hen gathering her chicks under her wing.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *He put his head into the wolf’s mouth*?
questions.answer: He exposed himself to needless danger
wrong: To stint him, to give him scanty meals
To become less popular or less successful
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: He exposed himself to needless danger. The allusion is to the fable of the crane that put its head into a wolf’s mouth in order to extract a bone. The fable is usually related of a fox instead of a wolf.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *The wooden walls of Old England*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: The ships of war. We must now say, “The iron walls of Old England.”

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Yeoman’s Service*?
wrong: To get or keep the upper hand
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
Regular hard work; effectual service; excellent service whether in a good or bad cause. The reference is to the yeomen of the Free Companies.

“The whole training of Port Royal did him yeoman’s service.”—Shorthouse: Sir Percival, p. 56.

“We found a long knife, and a knotted handkerchief stained with blood, with which Claude had no doubt recently done yeoman’s service.”—Miss Robinson: Whitefriars, chap. viii.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To pass under the yoke*?
questions.answer: To suffer the disgrace of a vanquished army
wrong: The hour of dusk, when it is too dark to work, and too soon to light candles
A blow for a blow, tit for tat
To rise out of, to appear at the surface
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To suffer the disgrace of a vanquished army. The Romans made a yoke of three spears—two upright and one resting on them. When an army was vanquished, the soldiers had to lay down their arms and pass under this archway of spears.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Above-board*?
wrong: Cold boiled meat and greens fried
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: In a straightforward manner. Conjurers place their hands under the table when they are preparing their tricks, but above when they show them. “Let all be above-board” means “let there be no under-hand work, but let us see everything.”

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *A perfect Babel*?
wrong: To assume the guidance or direction
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: A thorough confusion. “A Babel of sounds.” A confused uproar, in which nothing can be heard but hubbub. The allusion is to the confusion of tongues at Babel. (Genesis xi.)

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Into the bargain*?
wrong: I am out of my element
To acknowledge oneself in the wrong
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: In addition thereto; besides what was bargained for.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Thrown on one’s beam-ends*?
wrong: To leave, forsake, or neglect him
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Driven to my last shift. A ship is said to be on her beam-ends when she is laid by a heavy gale completely on her beams or sides. Not unfrequently the only means of righting her in such a case is to cut away her masts.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To hit below the belt*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
To strike unfairly. It is prohibited in prize-fighting to hit below the waist-belt. To call men knaves and fools, to charge a man with nepotism, to make a slanderous report which is not actionable, indeed to take away a man’s character in any way where self-defence is impossible, is “hitting him below the belt.”

“Lord Salisbury hits hard, but never hits below the belt.”—Daily Telegraph, November, 1886.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *A wet blanket*?
wrong: Treating one without the least consideration
To go beyond the prescribed limits
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: A discouragement, a marplot. A person is a wet blanket who discourages a proposed scheme. “Treated with a wet blanket,” discouraged. “A wet blanket influence,” etc. A wet blanket is used to smother fire, or to prevent one escaping from a fire from being burnt.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *None of your blarney*?
questions.answer: Soft, wheedling speeches to gain some end
wrong: To be "not at home" to visitors
The powers that have the administration of affairs in their hands
To be worthy of better things
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Soft, wheedling speeches to gain some end; sugar-words. Cormack Macarthy held the castle of Blarney in 1602, and concluded an armistice with Carew, the Lord President, on condition of surrendering the fort to the English garrison. Day after day his lordship looked for the fulfilment of the terms, but received nothing except protocols and soft speeches, till he became the laughing-stock of Elizabeth’s ministers, and the dupe of the Lord of Blarney.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *I’ve got into the wrong box*?
questions.answer: I am out of my element
wrong: Two means of accomplishing his object
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: I am out of my element. Lord Lyttelton used to say he ought to have been brought up to some business; that whenever he went to Vauxhall and heard the mirth of his neighbours, he used to fancy pleasure was in every box but his own. Wherever he went for happiness, he somehow always got into the wrong box.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *That’s a chestnut*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: A stale joke. In The Broken Sword, an old melodrama by William Dillon, Captain Xavier is for ever telling the same jokes with variations. He was telling about one of his exploits connected with a cork-tree, when Pablo corrects him, “A chestnut-tree you mean, captain.” “Bah! (replied the captain) I say a cork-tree.” “A chestnut-tree,” insists Pablo. “I must know better than you (said the captain); it was a cork-tree, I say.” “A chestnut (persisted Pablo). I have heard you tell the joke twenty-seven times, and I am sure it was a chestnut.”

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To put one on short commons*?
questions.answer: To stint him, to give him scanty meals
wrong: To make a casual call, not invited
In a difficulty, in a mess
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To stint him, to give him scanty meals. In the University of Cambridge the food provided for each student at breakfast is called his commons; hence food in general or meals.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *He came a cropper*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: He fell head over heels. To get a cropper. To get a bad fall. “Neck and crop” means altogether, and to “come a cropper” is to come to the ground neck and crop.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *A crucial test*?
questions.answer: A very severe and undeniable one
wrong: "No more" can be said on the subject
To ascertain how far a person will venture
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: A very severe and undeniable one. The allusion is to a fancy of Lord Bacon’s, who said that two different diseases or sciences might run parallel for a time, but would ultimately cross each other: thus, the plague might for a time resemble other diseases, but when the bubo or boil appeared, the plague would assume its specific character.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *The crack of doom*?
questions.answer: The signal for the final judgment
wrong: To be very grand and mighty in demeanour
Of the same size as the object represented
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: The signal for the final judgment.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Down in the mouth*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Out of spirits; disheartened. When persons are very sad and low-spirited, the corners of the mouth are drawn down. “Down in the jib” is a nautical phrase of the same meaning.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Eaves-dropper*?
questions.answer: One who listens stealthily to conversation
wrong: The buyer must be responsible for his own free act
To put too much water into grog or tea
A maladroit hand interfering with a delicate business
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
One who listens stealthily to conversation. The derivation of the term is not usually understood. The owners of private estates in Saxon times were not allowed to cultivate to the extremity of their possessions, but were obliged to leave a space for eaves. This space was called the yfes-drype (eaves-drip). An eaves-dropper is one who places himself in the eaves-drip to overhear what is said in the adjacent house or field.

“Under our tents I’ll play the eaves-dropper, To hear if any mean to shrink from me.” Shakespeare: Richard III., v. 3.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Bare-faced*?
wrong: Too hot or strong to last
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Impudence unconcealed. A “bare-faced lie” is a lie told shamelessly and without prevarication.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To put one through his facings*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
To examine; to ascertain if what appears on the surface is superficial only.

“The Greek books were again had out, and Grace .... was put through her facings.”—A. Trollope.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Fagged out*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Wearied with hard work. Fatigued contracted into fa’g’ed.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Fishing for compliments*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Laying a bait for praise.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *I’m in a fix*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: A predicament. The allusion is to machinery which will not move. The Northumberland was in a terrible fix at the launch, when it refused to leave the dock. (1866.)

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To play with one eye on the gallery*?
wrong: To disturb the equanimity of a society
To regard actions in a wrong light
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
To work for popularity. As an actor who sacrifices his author for popular applause, or a stump political orator “orates” to catch votes.

“The instant we begin to think about success and the effect of our work—to play with one eye on the gallery—we lose power, and touch, and everything else.”—Rudyard Kipling: The Light that Failed.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To give one the go-by*?
questions.answer: To pass without notice, to leave in the lurch
wrong: Fair speeches, which look like promises of favour, but end in nothing
To rise out of, to appear at the surface
An actor who appears, speaks, or acts only once
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To pass without notice, to leave in the lurch.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *The grapes are sour*?
questions.answer: You disparage it because it is beyond your reach
wrong: Just in time not to be too late
A “tuck-in,” or feast which swells out the paunch
At the very verge of death
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: You disparage it because it is beyond your reach. The allusion is to the well-known fable of the fox, which tried in vain to get at some grapes, but when he found they were beyond his reach went away saying, “I see they are sour.”

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *He is only half-baked*?
questions.answer: He is a soft, a noodle
wrong: To supply customers or furnish supplies
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: He is a soft, a noodle. The allusion is to bread, piecrust, etc., only half-cooked.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To draw the longbow*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To exaggerate. The force of an arrow in the longbow depends on the strength of the arm that draws it, so the force of a statement depends on the force of the speaker’s imagination. The longbow was the favourite weapon of the English from the reign of Edward II. till it was superseded by fire-arms. The “longbow” was the hand-bow, as distinguished from the crossbow or bow fitted on a stock.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *He has joined the majority*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: He is dead. Blair says, in his Grave, “’Tis long since Death had the majority.” “Abiit ad plures;” “Quin prius me ad plures penetravi” (Plautus: Trinummus, line 14). “Beatos eos fore, quando cum pluribus habitarint.” (Polybius, viii. xxx. 7.)

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To make mincemeat of*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Utterly to demolish; to shatter to pieces. Mincemeat is meat cut up very fine.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To be no more*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
To exist no longer; to be dead.

“Cassius is no more.”—Shakespeare: Julius Cæsar.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To go nap*?
questions.answer: To stake all the winnings on the cards in hand
wrong: Out of work, out of place
The powers that have the administration of affairs in their hands
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To stake all the winnings on the cards in hand; hence, to risk all on one venture. Nap is a game of cards; so called from Napoleon III.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To catch one napping*?
questions.answer: To find a person off his guard
wrong: To get or keep the upper hand
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To find a person off his guard. (Anglo-Saxon, hnappung, slumbering.)

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Ex nihilo nihil fit*?
questions.answer: From nothing comes nothing—i.e. every effect must have a cause
wrong: A coward who hectors, a fool that apes the wise man
To acknowledge oneself in the wrong
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: From nothing comes nothing—i.e. every effect must have a cause. It was the dictum of Xenophanes, founder of the Eleatic school (sixth century), to prove the eternity of matter. We now apply the phrase as equivalent to “You cannot get blood from a stone.” You cannot expect clever work from one who has no brains.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *A hard nut to crack*?
wrong: Cold boiled meat and greens fried
An actor who appears, speaks, or acts only once
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: A difficult question to answer; a hard problem to solve. (Anglo-Saxon, hnut, a nut.)

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Heaping Pelion upon Ossa*?
wrong: It is in hand, but not yet finished
Soft, wheedling speeches to gain some end
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
Adding difficulty to difficulty; fruitless efforts. The allusion is to the attempt of the giants to scale heaven by piling Mount Ossa upon Mount Pelion.

“Ter sunt conati imponere Pelio Ossam.” Virgil: Georgics, i. 281.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *None but himself can be his parallel*?
wrong: To give up as a bad job
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
Wholly without a peer; “Quæris Alcidæ parem;” “nemo proximus nec secundus.” There are many similar sentences; for example:—

“Nemo est, nisi ipse.”—Seneca: Hercules Furens, i. 81.

“And but herself admits no parallel.” Massinger: Duke of Millaine, iii. 4.

“None but himself himself can parallel.” Anagram on John Lilburn. (1658.)

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To cry peccavi*?
questions.answer: To acknowledge oneself in the wrong
wrong: To cease boasting and assume a lower tone
To pass without notice, to leave in the lurch
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To acknowledge oneself in the wrong. It is said that Sir Charles Napier, after the battle of Hyderabad, in 1843, used this word as a pun upon his victory—“Peccavi” (I have sinned, i.e. Sinde).

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *In a Pickwickian sense*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note:
An insult whitewashed. Mr. Pickwick accused Mr. Blotton of acting in “a vile and calumnious manner,” whereupon Mr. Blotton retorted by calling Mr. Pickwick “a humbug.” It finally was made to appear that both had used the offensive words only in a Pickwickian sense, and that each had, in fact, the highest regard and esteem for the other. So the affront was adjusted, and both were satisfied.

“Lawyers and politicians daily abuse each other in a Pickwickian sense.”—Bowditch.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *In borrowed plumes*?
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Assumed merit; airs and graces not merited. The allusion is to the fable of the jackdaw who dressed up in peacock’s feathers.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Well posted up in the subject*?
wrong: Not to come near a person
To take food after long abstinence
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Thoroughly informed. The metaphor is from posting up accounts, where one can see everything at a glance.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Riding rough-shod over one*?
questions.answer: Treating one without the least consideration
wrong: A dull, unprogressive person, somewhat fossilised
A species of sale by auction
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Treating one without the least consideration. The allusion is to riding a horse rough-shod.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Set the saddle on the right horse*?
questions.answer: Lay the blame on those who deserve it
wrong: In for a penny, in for a pound
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Lay the blame on those who deserve it.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To save appearances*?
questions.answer: To do something to obviate or prevent exposure or embarrassment
wrong: To supply customers or furnish supplies
Projected, and talked about as likely to occur
He has a very good opinion of number one
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To do something to obviate or prevent exposure or embarrassment.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Look out for squalls*?
wrong: To give up as a bad job
To cut oneself off from all means or hope of retreat
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Expect to meet with difficulties. A nautical term.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Tied to your mother’s apron-strings*?
questions.answer: Not yet out of nursery government
wrong: To throw a reproof at one
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Not yet out of nursery government; not free to act on your own responsibility. The allusion is to tying naughty young children to the mother’s or nurse’s apron.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *The trail of the serpent is over them all*?
questions.answer: Sin has set his mark on all
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: Sin has set his mark on all. (Thomas Moore: Paradise and the Peri.)

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *To trump up*?
questions.answer: To devise or make up falsely
wrong: He has a very good opinion of number one
To leave, forsake, or neglect him
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: To devise or make up falsely; to concoct.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *I am quite unhinged*?
questions.answer: My nerves are shaken, my equilibrium of mind is disturbed
wrong: To be "not at home" to visitors
To put too much water into grog or tea
Fair speeches, which look like promises of favour, but end in nothing
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: My nerves are shaken, my equilibrium of mind is disturbed; I am like a door which has lost one of its hinges.

questions.question: What did the Victorians mean by *Dyed in the wool*?
wrong: Not to come near a person
questions.source: Brewer, Dictionary of Phrase and Fable (1898)
questions.note: A hearty good fellow. Cloth which is wool-dyed (not piece-dyed) is true throughout “and will wash.”

questions.question: It's 1870. At a friend's house you chatted with someone, but you were never introduced. You pass them in the street the next day. What do you do?
questions.answer: Don't bow: without an introduction you aren't acquainted
wrong: Bow, and stop to chat about the party
Raise your hat, but don't stop to speak
questions.source: Routledge's Manual of Etiquette (c. 1875)
questions.note: Persons who have met at the house of a mutual friend, without being introduced, should not bow if they afterwards meet elsewhere. A bow implies acquaintance; and persons who have not been introduced are not acquainted.

questions.question: You've been given a letter of introduction to a distinguished family. Do you deliver it in person?
questions.answer: Never: it puts you in a most undignified position
wrong: Always: anything else would seem cold
Yes, and wait politely while it's read
Only if the family is expecting you
questions.source: Routledge's Manual of Etiquette (c. 1875)
questions.note: Never deliver a letter of introduction in person. It places you in the most undignified position imaginable, and compels you to wait while it is being read, like a servant who has been told to wait for an answer.

questions.question: It's winter and you're paying a morning visit. When do you call?
questions.answer: Between two and four in the afternoon
wrong: Between nine and eleven in the morning
questions.source: Routledge's Manual of Etiquette (c. 1875)
questions.note: A morning visit should be paid between the hours of two and four p.m., in winter, and two and five in summer.

questions.question: You're paying a ceremonious call. How long do you stay?
questions.answer: No less than ten minutes and no more than fifteen
wrong: About an hour, and not a minute less
At least half an hour, or you'll seem cold
Until the tea things have been cleared
questions.source: Hartley, The Gentlemen's Book of Etiquette (1860)
questions.note: A ceremonious call should never extend over more than fifteen minutes, and it should not be less than ten minutes.

questions.question: You've stood up to leave a call, and your hostess warmly urges you to stay a little longer. What's correct?
questions.answer: Go anyway: once you've risen, it's best to leave
wrong: Sit down again: refusing would be ungracious
Stay exactly five minutes more, then go
Stay until the next visitor arrives
questions.source: Routledge's Manual of Etiquette (c. 1875)
questions.note: You will, perhaps, be urged to remain, but, having once risen, it is best to go. There is always a certain air of gaucherie in resuming your seat and repeating the ceremony of leave-taking.

questions.question: You're paying a call and need to check the time on your pocket watch. What do you do?
questions.answer: Ask permission, and apologise, pleading other appointments
wrong: Glance at it discreetly, below the table
Check it openly: callers keep to time
Ask your hostess the time instead
questions.source: Routledge's Manual of Etiquette (c. 1875)
questions.note: If you have occasion to look at your watch during a call, ask permission to do so, and apologise for it on the plea of other appointments.

questions.question: You're off to a Victorian luncheon party. Do you wear your diamonds and pearls?
questions.answer: No: they belong to evening dress, never before dinner
wrong: Yes, but only a single string of pearls
Yes: luncheon is the place to show them off
Only if the hostess is wearing hers
questions.source: Routledge's Manual of Etiquette (c. 1875)
questions.note: Diamonds, pearls, rubies, and all transparent precious stones belong to evening dress, and should on no account be worn before dinner.

questions.question: You want one gemstone that marks you out as a person of taste. Which does the manual single out?
questions.source: Routledge's Manual of Etiquette (c. 1875)
questions.note: Of all precious stones, the opal is one of the most lovely and the least common-place. No vulgar man purchases an opal.

questions.question: You're choosing a scent for an evening party. Which two does the manual call the most objectionable of all?
questions.source: Routledge's Manual of Etiquette (c. 1875)
questions.note: Perfumes should be used only in the evening, and then in moderation. Nothing is more vulgar than a coarse ordinary scent; and of all coarse, ordinary scents, the most objectionable are musk and patchouli.

questions.question: You're stepping out into the street. What must your gloves be made of?
questions.answer: Kid or calf, and nothing else
questions.source: Routledge's Manual of Etiquette (c. 1875)
questions.note: Never be seen in the street without gloves; and never let your gloves be of any material that is not kid or calf. Worsted or cotton gloves are unutterably vulgar.

questions.question: You're a guest at a Victorian dinner and the bread comes round. How do you deal with your piece?
questions.answer: Break it: no one cuts bread
wrong: Cut it neatly with your own knife
Slice it with the bread knife provided
Butter the whole piece, then bite
questions.source: Routledge's Manual of Etiquette (c. 1875)
questions.note: Then let me tell you that no one cuts bread. You should always break it.

questions.question: A roast bird is going round the dinner table. How do you ask for some?
questions.answer: Ask for chicken or capon, never 'fowl'
wrong: Ask for 'a little of the fowl'
Point to it and say nothing
questions.source: Routledge's Manual of Etiquette (c. 1875)
questions.note: You should have asked for chicken or capon. The word "fowl" is never heard out of the kitchen.

questions.question: Your tea is far too hot to drink. What's correct?
questions.answer: Wait for it to cool, then drink from the cup
wrong: Pour a little into the saucer to cool
Blow on it gently across the cup
Stir it briskly until it's cool enough
questions.source: Routledge's Manual of Etiquette (c. 1875)
questions.note: Nothing can be more vulgar than to pour tea or coffee into a saucer. You should have waited till it cooled, and then have drunk it from the cup.

questions.question: You arrive at a dinner party to find dinner already being served. What does one authority advise?
questions.answer: Retreat to a restaurant and send an apology
wrong: Slip in quietly and take your seat
Apologise warmly to the hostess and join in
Wait in the hall until the next course
questions.source: Routledge's Manual of Etiquette (c. 1875)
questions.note: if you do not reach the house till dinner is served, you had better retire to a restaurateur's, and thence send an apology, and not interrupt the harmony of the courses by awkward excuses and cold acceptance.

questions.question: You're laying the table for a Victorian dinner party. How much room does each guest get?
questions.source: Routledge's Manual of Etiquette (c. 1875)
questions.note: A space of two feet should be allowed to each person.

questions.question: Two of your dinner guests are celebrated wits. Where do you seat them?
questions.answer: Well apart: side by side, they extinguish each other
wrong: Side by side, so they spark off each other
Together at the centre of the table
Both at the head, either side of the host
questions.source: Routledge's Manual of Etiquette (c. 1875)
questions.note: It is obviously a bad plan to place two such persons in close proximity. They extinguish each other.

questions.question: You're a guest at a Victorian dinner and your host asks whether you'll take "soup or fish". What would an experienced diner do?
wrong: Choose the soup, as the lighter course
Choose the fish, as the grander course
Leave the choice to your host
questions.source: Routledge's Manual of Etiquette (c. 1875)
questions.note: They are as much separate courses as the fish and the meat; and all experienced diners take both.

questions.question: The soup has arrived. How do you take it?
questions.answer: From the side of the spoon, without a sound
wrong: From the tip of the spoon, in small sips
From the bowl, tipped up to your lips
A whole spoonful at once, tipped in neatly
questions.source: Routledge's Manual of Etiquette (c. 1875)
questions.note: In eating soup, remember always to take it from the side of the spoon, and to make no sound in doing so.

questions.question: You'd like to offer your neighbour at dinner some mutton. Which word must you never use?
questions.answer: "Assist", as in "May I assist you to some?"
wrong: "Send", as in "Shall I send you some?"
"Help", as in "May I help you to some?"
"Offer", as in "May I offer you some?"
questions.source: Routledge's Manual of Etiquette (c. 1875)
questions.note: Never offer to "assist" your neighbours to this or that dish. The word is inexpressibly vulgar--all the more vulgar for its affectation of elegance. "Shall I send you some mutton?" or "may I help you to grouse?" is better chosen and better bred.

questions.question: Asparagus is served at a Victorian dinner. How do you eat it?
questions.answer: Watch what the others do, and follow suit
wrong: Always with a knife and fork, never fingers
Always with your fingers, never cutlery
questions.source: Routledge's Manual of Etiquette (c. 1875)
questions.note: In eating asparagus, it is well to observe what others do, and act accordingly.

questions.question: You're eating cherries at dessert. What does the manual prefer you do with the stones?
questions.answer: Drop them unseen into your hand, then onto the plate
wrong: Drop them from your lips straight onto the plate
Tuck them into your napkin as you go
Line them up neatly round your plate's rim
questions.source: Routledge's Manual of Etiquette (c. 1875)
questions.note: Others cover the lips with the hand, drop them unseen into the palm, and so deposit them on the side of the plate. In our own opinion, the last is the better way

questions.question: Someone across the dinner table invites you to take wine with them. What do you do?
questions.answer: Pour a little fresh wine, look at them, bow slightly, sip
wrong: Stand and propose a toast to them
Rise and clink glasses across the table
Call out their name and raise your glass high
questions.source: Routledge's Manual of Etiquette (c. 1875)
questions.note: In accepting, you have only to pour a little fresh wine into your glass, look at the person who invited you, bow slightly, and take a sip from the glass.

questions.question: Your host has lumps of clear ice put into the guests' wine glasses. What does the manual make of it?
questions.answer: A new fashion that should be abolished as soon as possible
wrong: A refreshing innovation for the summer
Quite correct, but only with red wines
Acceptable, provided the ice is very clear
questions.source: Routledge's Manual of Etiquette (c. 1875)
questions.note: This is an innovation that cannot be too strictly reprehended or too soon abolished.

questions.question: You knock over a glass and break it at a dinner party. What's correct?
questions.answer: Don't apologise: let your face show your regret
wrong: Apologise at once to the hostess
Offer to pay for a replacement
Send a note of apology the next morning
questions.source: Routledge's Manual of Etiquette (c. 1875)
questions.note: If you should unfortunately overturn or break anything, do not apologize for it. You can show your regret in your face, but it is not well-bred to put it into words.

questions.question: One slice is left on the dish, and it's offered to you. What do you do?
questions.answer: Take it: refusing because it's the last is ill-bred
wrong: Decline it, so as not to seem greedy
Offer to halve it with your neighbour
questions.source: Routledge's Manual of Etiquette (c. 1875)
questions.note: To abstain from taking the last piece on the dish, or the last glass of wine in the decanter, only because it is the last, is highly ill-bred.

questions.question: You're giving a private ball. What should you arrange on the pavement outside?
questions.answer: A policeman with a lantern, for the whole evening
wrong: A footman with a torch at each corner
A small band playing on the doorstep
Straw laid in the road to muffle the carriages
questions.source: Routledge's Manual of Etiquette (c. 1875)
questions.note: The best thing that the giver of a private ball can do under these circumstances, is to engage a policeman with a lanthorn to attend on the pavement during the evening

questions.question: You're hosting a ball. Should you introduce a poor dancer to an excellent one?
questions.answer: Never: you'd be punishing one friend to oblige another
wrong: Yes: the good dancer will help them improve
Yes, but only for a quadrille
Only if the good dancer agrees first
questions.source: Routledge's Manual of Etiquette (c. 1875)
questions.note: A thoughtful hostess will never introduce a bad dancer to a good one, because she has no right to punish one friend in order to oblige another.

questions.question: You and your spouse are at a ball together. Do you dance with each other?
questions.answer: No: married people don't dance together in society
wrong: Yes: the first dance is always yours
Yes, but only the last waltz
Yes, but never more than twice
questions.source: Routledge's Manual of Etiquette (c. 1875)
questions.note: It is not customary for married persons to dance together in society.

questions.question: You're staying at a country house and spot a book in the library you'd like to read in your room. What's correct?
questions.answer: Ask to borrow it, and cover it if necessary
wrong: Take it up: a guest has the run of the library
Read it only in the library itself
Take it, and mention it at breakfast
questions.source: Routledge's Manual of Etiquette (c. 1875)
questions.note: You should never take a book from the library to your own room without requesting permission to borrow it. When it is lent, you should take every care that it sustains no injury while in your possession, and should cover it, if necessary.

questions.question: You're a guest at a country house where they dine late and take no supper. How do you know it's time for bed?
questions.answer: A servant appears with wine, water and biscuits
wrong: The host winds the hall clock
The drawing-room lamps are turned down
The hostess rings a little bell
questions.source: Routledge's Manual of Etiquette (c. 1875)
questions.note: The signal for retiring to rest is generally given by the appearance of the servant with wine, water, and biscuits, where a late dinner-hour is observed and suppers are not the custom.

questions.question: You're talking about an acquaintance who isn't there. What does the manual call the most flagrant offence against taste?
questions.answer: Calling them by the first letter of their name
wrong: Giving their full title every time
questions.source: Routledge's Manual of Etiquette (c. 1875)
questions.note: Above all, never name anybody by the first letter of his name. Married people are sometimes guilty of this flagrant offence against taste.

questions.question: You're a Victorian gentleman on a call, and you've brought your hat into the drawing-room. You simply must put it down. Where?
wrong: On the lid of the piano
questions.source: Routledge's Manual of Etiquette (c. 1875)
questions.note: The hat, however, must never be laid on a table, piano, or any article of furniture; it should be held gracefully in the hand. If you are compelled to lay it aside, put it on the floor.

questions.question: You're a Victorian gentleman sealing a letter. What colour wax do you use?
wrong: Dark blue, as the most refined
Any colour, to suit your taste
questions.source: Routledge's Manual of Etiquette (c. 1875)
questions.note: A gentleman should never use sealing-wax of any colour but red, nor paper of any hue but white.

questions.question: You're out riding and meet a lady you know who is on foot. You'd like to talk. What's correct?
questions.answer: Dismount and lead your horse while you talk
wrong: Stay in the saddle but bring your horse to a walk
Raise your hat and talk from the saddle
Ask her to wait while you stable your horse
questions.source: Routledge's Manual of Etiquette (c. 1875)
questions.note: If you are on horseback and wish to converse with a lady who is on foot, you must dismount and lead your horse, so as not to give her the fatigue of looking up to your level.

questions.question: You're at an evening party and feeling the cold. Where must you never stand?
questions.answer: On the hearth-rug with your back to the fire
wrong: By the window, in the draught
questions.source: Routledge's Manual of Etiquette (c. 1875)
questions.note: Never stand upon the hearth-rug with your back to the fire, either in a friend's house or your own.

questions.question: You're leaving a crowded party. What about saying goodnight to the hostess?
questions.answer: Don't seek her out: you might break up the party
wrong: Find her and thank her before you go
Send a servant to give her your thanks
Wait for a lull, then bid her a formal goodnight
questions.source: Routledge's Manual of Etiquette (c. 1875)
questions.note: In retiring from a crowded party it is unnecessary that you should seek out the hostess for the purpose of bidding her a formal good night. By doing this you would, perhaps, remind others that it was getting late, and cause the party to break up.

questions.question: You've been served at dinner, but the food is far too hot to eat. What's correct?
questions.answer: Take up your knife and fork and appear to begin
wrong: Wait until everyone else has been served
Send it back to be cooled a little
questions.source: Routledge's Manual of Etiquette (c. 1875)
questions.note: As soon as you are helped, begin to eat; or, if the viands are too hot for your palate, take up your knife and fork and appear to begin.

questions.question: You're a cavalry officer going to a ball. What must you leave off?
questions.source: Routledge's Manual of Etiquette (c. 1875)
questions.note: Cavalry officers should never wear spurs in a ball-room.

questions.question: You're a Victorian gentleman dancing a long half-hour with your partner. How much conversation should you manage?
questions.answer: At least three or four observations
wrong: One remark at the start, then silence
Only a word of thanks at the end
questions.source: Routledge's Manual of Etiquette (c. 1875)
questions.note: If it be only upon the news of the day, a gentleman should be able to offer at least three or four observations to his partner in the course of a long half-hour.

questions.question: A fellow guest tells an obviously absurd anecdote. What do you do?
questions.answer: Listen politely, with every appearance of belief
questions.source: Hartley, The Gentlemen's Book of Etiquette (1860)
questions.note: No matter how absurd are the anecdotes that may be told in your presence, you must never give any sign of incredulity.

questions.question: You're a person of science, and a technical term slips out in polite conversation. What now?
questions.answer: Leave it: explaining it would be the greater error
wrong: Explain it at once, in plain words
Ask whether anyone would like it explained
questions.source: Hartley, The Gentlemen's Book of Etiquette (1860)
questions.note: If, however, you unconsciously use such a term or phrase, do not then commit the still greater error of explaining its meaning.

questions.question: You find an insect in your salad at a dinner party. What do you do?
questions.answer: Pass your plate to the waiter without a word
wrong: Quietly mention it to the hostess
Remove it discreetly and carry on
Push the salad aside and leave it
questions.source: Hartley, The Gentlemen's Book of Etiquette (1860)
questions.note: If in the leaves of your salad, or in a plate of fruit you find a worm or insect, pass your plate to the waiter, without any comment, and he will bring you another.

questions.question: At a private dinner you need something from the side table. How do you ask for it?
questions.answer: Call a servant by name, or make a sign without speaking
wrong: Call "Waiter!" in a low, pleasant voice
Ask the hostess to have it brought
Fetch it from the side table yourself
questions.source: Hartley, The Gentlemen's Book of Etiquette (1860)
questions.note: never address those in attendance as "Waiter!" as you would at a hotel or restaurant, but call one of them by name; if you cannot do this, make him a sign without speaking.

questions.question: You're cutting fruit at dessert. Which knife do you use?
wrong: A small steel blade with a pearl handle
questions.source: Hartley, The Gentlemen's Book of Etiquette (1860)
questions.note: Do not cut fruit with a steel knife. Use a silver one.

questions.question: Dinner is over and you'd love to slip off home. How long must you stay in the drawing-room?
wrong: Half an hour at the very most
No time at all: leave after the dessert
questions.source: Hartley, The Gentlemen's Book of Etiquette (1860)
questions.note: It is excessively rude to leave the house as soon as dinner is over. Respect to your hostess obliges you to stay in the drawing-room at least an hour.

questions.question: You're a guest at a Victorian dinner and the cheese arrives. What do you eat it with?
wrong: Your fingers, on a piece of bread
questions.source: Hartley, The Gentlemen's Book of Etiquette (1860)
questions.note: Never put a knife into your mouth, not even with cheese, which should be eaten with a fork.

questions.question: You're offered an orange at dessert. What should you peel it with?
questions.source: Hartley, The Gentlemen's Book of Etiquette (1860)
questions.note: Apropos of which, I may hint that no epicure ever yet put a knife to an apple, and that an orange should be peeled with a spoon.

questions.question: You're a Victorian gentleman at an upstairs window, and a lady you know passes in the street below. Do you bow?
questions.answer: No: you may bow up to a window, never down from one
wrong: Yes, a slight bow is quite correct
Only if she looks up and sees you first
Yes, but only after she has bowed to you
questions.source: Hartley, The Gentlemen's Book of Etiquette (1860)
questions.note: You may bow to a lady who is seated at a window, if you are in the street; but you must not bow from a window to a lady in the street.

questions.question: You arrive on a call and see at once that you've come at a bad time, but you've already been seen. What do you do?
questions.answer: Don't leave at once: your retreat is cut off
wrong: Slip out quietly while they're distracted
questions.source: Hartley, The Gentlemen's Book of Etiquette (1860)
questions.note: do not instantly retire unless you have entered unperceived and can so leave, in which case leave immediately; if, however, you have been seen, your instant retreat is cut off.

questions.question: You're having visiting cards printed. What goes on them?
questions.answer: Your name and address, and nothing else
questions.source: Hartley, The Gentlemen's Book of Etiquette (1860)
questions.note: A card should have nothing written upon it, but your name and address. To leave a card with your business address, or the nature of your profession written upon it, shows a shocking ignorance of polite society.

questions.question: You're a fashionable Englishman taking a promenade in Hyde Park later in the day. Which gloves?
questions.source: Hartley, The Gentlemen's Book of Etiquette (1860)
questions.note: To enter London in his tilbury, beaver skin gloves. Later in the day, to promenade in Hyde Park, colored kid gloves, dark.

questions.question: You're a Victorian gentleman who shaves, and money is no object. How many razors should you keep?
questions.answer: Seven, one for each day of the week
wrong: Two, used turn and turn about
Three: one each for morning, noon and night
questions.source: Hartley, The Gentlemen's Book of Etiquette (1860)
questions.note: If you can afford it, you should have a case of seven razors, one for each day of the week, so that no one shall be too much used.

questions.question: Lavender gloves have become the new fashion for the evening. Should you wear them?
questions.answer: No: they're economical, and all economy is an abomination
wrong: Yes, with a black coat they're perfect
Only at a small, quiet dinner
Yes, if they're fresh each evening
questions.source: Hartley, The Gentlemen's Book of Etiquette (1860)
questions.note: Recently, indeed, a fashion has sprung up of wearing lavender gloves in the evening. They are economical, and as all economy is an abomination, must be avoided.

questions.question: A stranger bows to you in the street, plainly mistaking you for someone else. What do you do?
questions.answer: Bow back, to spare them embarrassment
wrong: Stop and explain they've mistaken you
Pretend not to have noticed it
Ask them kindly where you've met
questions.source: Hartley, The Gentlemen's Book of Etiquette (1860)
questions.note: If any one bows to you in the street, return the bow. It may be an acquaintance whose face you do not immediately recognize, and if it is a stranger who mistakes you for another, your courteous bow will relieve him from the embarrassment arising from his mistake.

questions.question: You've sat down to play the piano at a party, but the room is still chattering. What do you do?
questions.answer: Begin anyway: don't wait for silence
wrong: Wait on the stool until all is quiet
Strike a firm chord to gain attention
Ask the hostess to call for quiet
questions.source: Hartley, The Gentlemen's Book of Etiquette (1860)
questions.note: If you play yourself, do not wait for silence in the room before you begin.

questions.question: You've been asked to sing at an evening party. How much do you give them?
wrong: One verse, and a curtsey or bow
questions.source: Routledge's Manual of Etiquette (c. 1875)
questions.note: Two verses of a song, or four pages of a piece, are at all times enough to give pleasure. If your audience desire more they will ask for more

questions.question: You're writing to the daughters of Mr Smith. How do you address the eldest?
wrong: As "Miss A. Smith", with her initial
questions.source: Hartley, The Gentlemen's Book of Etiquette (1860)
questions.note: Remember, in directing letters to young ladies, the eldest one in a family is addressed by the surname alone, while the others have also the proper name

questions.question: You fancy a cigar on your walk. When may you smoke in the street?
wrong: At any hour, if no one is near
Only once you reach the park
questions.source: Hartley, The Gentlemen's Book of Etiquette (1860)
questions.note: One must never smoke, again, in the streets; that is, in daylight. The deadly crime may be committed, like burglary, after dark, but not before.

questions.question: You're paying a call and notice a pile of other people's visiting cards on the table. What's correct?
questions.answer: Leave them alone: don't turn them over
wrong: Look through them for mutual friends
Glance at the top few, discreetly
Ask your host about the most notable one
questions.source: Hartley, The Gentlemen's Book of Etiquette (1860)
questions.note: It is in bad taste, though often done, to turn over the cards on a table, when you are calling.

questions.question: You're leaving town and paying your farewell calls. What do you write in the corner of your card?
questions.source: Routledge's Manual of Etiquette (c. 1875)
questions.note: Leave-taking cards have P.P.C. (pour prendre congé) written in the corner. Some use P.D.A. (pour dire adieu).

questions.question: You'd like to give a present to someone well above you in rank. What's always safe?
wrong: Something costly, to show your respect
A fine book, inscribed with their name
Nothing: gifts should only go downwards
questions.source: Routledge's Manual of Etiquette (c. 1875)
questions.note: Offerings of flowers and game are unexceptionable, and may be made even to those whose position is superior to that of the giver.

questions.question: It's New Year's Day in an old English household. What gift would the ladies be glad of?
questions.answer: Pins, or money in their place: hence 'pin-money'
wrong: A china teacup from the master of the house
A silver thimble from each of the servants
A new pair of pattens for the muddy lanes
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: Pins were acceptable new year’s gifts to the ladies, instead of the wooden skewers which they used till the end of the fifteenth century. Sometimes they received a composition in money: and hence allowances for their separate use is still denominated “pin-money.”

questions.question: It's the eve of Twelfth-day at Pauntley, Gloucestershire, and the farm servants are heading out into a wheat field. What for?
questions.answer: To light twelve straw fires and toast the master in cyder
wrong: To bury a cake at the field's edge for the fairies
To walk the furrows ringing handbells at the crows
To sprinkle the young wheat with Christmas ale
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: On the eve of Twelfth-day all the servants of every farmer assemble together in one of the fields that has been sown with wheat. At the end of twelve lands, they make twelve fires in a row with straw

questions.question: It's Twelfth-night and the plum cake is being sliced. What's hidden inside?
questions.answer: A bean for the king and a pea for the queen
wrong: A sprig of holly for the youngest at the table
An acorn for the master and a hazelnut for the mistress
A clove for the cook and a button for the butler
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: the cake was full of plums, with a bean in it for the king, and a pea for the queen, so as to determine them by the slices.

questions.question: It's Twelfth-day on the Isle of Man, and they're 'cutting off the fiddler's head'. What's going on?
questions.answer: He says whom each girl will marry, and it's taken as an oracle
wrong: He plays one last tune and every dancer must freeze
The girls crown him with holly as king of the barn
He must guess which girl is holding the hidden ring
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: On Twelfth-day, the fiddler lays his head in some one of the girls’ laps, and a third person asks, who such a maid, or such a maid shall marry, naming the girls then present one after another

questions.question: It's the day after Twelfth-day, the first day back at work after Christmas. What do the men get up to in the evening?
questions.answer: Setting the women's flax alight, and getting a soaking for it
wrong: Racing their ploughs round the green for a ham
Carrying the yule log's ashes out to the fields
Ringing the church bells backwards to end Christmas
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: the burning of the flax and tow belonging to the women, was the men’s diversion in the evening of the first day of labour after the twelve days of Christmas, and that the women repaid the interruption to their industry by sluicing the mischief-makers.

questions.question: It's St Agnes' night and you'd like to dream of the one you'll marry. What does old Aubrey say to do?
questions.answer: Pull out a row of pins one by one, sticking one in your sleeve
wrong: Walk backwards round the house three times at midnight
Put a slice of wedding cake in your left shoe
Comb your hair before the glass by a single candle
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: Upon St. Agnes’ night you take a row of pins, and pull out every one, one after another, saying a Pater Noster, sticking a pin in your sleeve, and you will dream of him or her you shall marry.

questions.question: It's Christmas in the West Country and St George and the mummers are at the door. What are they wearing?
questions.answer: Shirt-sleeves, beribboned white trousers and tall pasteboard caps
