wrong: Masks of straw and coats turned inside out
Sheepskin cloaks and crowns of holly and ivy
Their Sunday best with oak leaves in their hats
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: St. George and the other tragic performers are dressed out somewhat in the style of morris-dancers, in their shirt-sleeves, and white trowsers much decorated with ribands and handkerchiefs

questions.question: It's 1826 at Hatherleigh in Devon, and you've just come from a funeral. What do the church bells do?
questions.answer: Ring a lively peal, as they would elsewhere after a wedding
wrong: Ring the curfew an hour early that night
Stay silent for a month of mourning
Ring muffled at dawn and dusk for a week
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: after a funeral the church bells ring a lively peal, as in other places after a wedding

questions.question: Our ancestors have moved a church bell to a new steeple. What might it do, unless it's rung in the evening and tied up?
questions.answer: Take a nightly trip back to its old church
wrong: Crack at the first christening it rings for
Ring by itself whenever someone in the parish dies
Refuse to sound for the new parson
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: When a bell was removed from its original and favourite situation, it was sometimes supposed to take a nightly trip to its old place of residence, unless exercised in the evening, and secured with a chain or rope.

questions.question: On St Bartholomew's eve, the boys of St Paul's school run into the scholars of St Anthony's. What do they call them?
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: they would call them St. Anthony’s pigs, and they again would call the others pigeons of Paul’s; because many pigeons were bred in Paul’s church, and St. Anthony was always figured with a pig following him.

questions.question: It's a great frost, and thousands are flocking onto the frozen Thames. What do they find there?
questions.answer: Swings, bookstalls, skittles and dancing in a barge
wrong: A ploughing match on the ice for a silver cup
A tented chapel holding services on the ice
An ice palace built by order of the lord mayor
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: Swings, bookstalls, dancing in a barge, suttling-booths, playing at skittles, and almost every appendage of a fair on land, appeared now on the Thames.

questions.question: It's Candlemas eve in the Western Isles. The mistress and servants dress up a sheaf of oats and lay it in a basket. What next?
questions.answer: Lay a club by it, cry 'Brüd is come!' and read the ashes at dawn
wrong: Carry it three times sunwise round the hearth
Set it on the roof to watch for the first lambs
Burn it at dawn and scatter the ashes on the fields
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: lay a wooden club by it, and this they call Brüd’s Bed; and the mistress and servants cry three times, ‘Brüd is come, Brüd is welcome!’ This they do just before going to bed. In the morning they look among the ashes, and if they see the impression of Brüd’s club there, they reckon it a presage of a good crop, and prosperous year

questions.question: It's Candlemas at Lyme Regis, and the man who buys the family's wood-ashes has sent his yearly present: a large candle. What's done with it?
questions.answer: It's lit at nightfall, and all sit up together till it burns out
wrong: It's set in the window to guide travellers on the road
It's cut in twelve, and one piece burned each month
It's burned on the ash-heap to bless next year's ashes
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: The coming of the Candlemas candle was looked forward to by the young ones as an event of some consequence; for, of usage, they had a sort of right to sit up that night, and partake of the refreshment, till all retired to rest, the signal for which was the self-extinction of the Candlemas candle.

questions.question: It's St Valentine's eve at Swaffham in Norfolk. Your door flies open and something comes rolling in. What is it?
questions.answer: A valentine tied to an apple or orange, then a loud knock
wrong: A wreath of ivy with a sweetheart's initials
A ball of red wool to follow to your valentine
A gingerbread heart with a name iced on it
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: Watching for a convenient opportunity, the door is slyly opened, and the valentine, attached to an apple or an orange, is thrown in; a loud rap at the door immediately follows

questions.question: It's the night before St Valentine's day and you want to dream of your sweetheart. What goes on your pillow?
questions.answer: Five bay leaves: one at each corner and one in the middle
wrong: A sprig of rosemary tied with red thread
A slice of plum cake wrapped in a stocking
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: I got five bay-leaves, and pinned four of them to the four corners of my pillow, and the fifth to the middle; and then, if I dreamt of my sweetheart, Betty said we should be married before the year was out.

questions.question: It's St Valentine's day, 1779, in a little Kent village. The girls are crowded round a bonfire, cheering. What's burning?
questions.answer: A 'holly boy' figure they've stolen from the boys
wrong: Last year's valentines, for luck in love
A straw figure of Old Winter
The last of the Christmas evergreens
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: The girls from five or six to eighteen years old were assembled in a crowd, burning an uncouth effigy which they called a “holly boy,” and which they had stolen from the boys

questions.question: It's four in the morning on Shrove Tuesday at Hoddesdon, Hertfordshire, and the old curfew bell rings. What does it mean?
questions.answer: Pancakes may be made and eaten until it rings again at eight
wrong: The market may open early for eggs and flour
Every house must sweep its chimney before noon
All fires must be put out until Ash Wednesday
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: rang on the morning of Shrove Tuesday at four o’clock, after which hour the inhabitants are at liberty to make and eat _pancakes_, until the bell rings again at eight o’clock at night.

questions.question: It's Shrove Tuesday, 1676, and the sun is shining. What do some say that means?
questions.answer: The sun will shine as much every day in Lent
wrong: A cold, late spring and a poor hay crop
A wet Easter and plenty of mushrooms
The cuckoo will come early this year
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: Others affirm that so much as the sun shineth on that day, the like will shine every day in Lent.

questions.question: It's St Piran's day in Cornwall. What are the tinners up to?
questions.answer: Taking the day off: the saint told their forebears tin's secrets
wrong: Carrying a block of tin to the church to be blessed
Racing barrows of ore from the pit to the smelting-house
Leaving candles down the mine for the knockers
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: having a tradition that some secrets regarding the manufacture of tin was communicated to their ancestors by that saint, they leave the manufacture to shift for itself for that day and keep it as a holiday.

questions.question: It's 11 March at Newark-upon-Trent, and the town-hall is giving penny loaves to anyone who asks. Why?
questions.answer: For Hercules Clay, who dreamt three times his house would burn
wrong: For the end of a famine the year the Trent froze
For a baker who fed the town through the plague
For a mayor who found the town's charter in a ditch
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: Clay (then a tradesman residing in Newark market-place) dreamed three nights successively, that his house was set fire to by the besiegers. Impressed by the repetition of this warning, as he considered it, he quitted his house

questions.question: It's mid-Lent in olden times, and boys come into the village carrying a figure made of straw. What happens?
questions.answer: It's Death: folk drive them off, or pay to have it taken away
wrong: It's the patron saint: folk bow and give it bread
It's a scarecrow: they set it to guard the sown peas
It's the harvest lord: they ride it round the parish
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: On this day boys went about, in ancient times, into the villages with a figure of death made of straw; from whence they were generally driven by the country people; who disliked it as an ominous appearance, while some gave them money to get the mawkin carried off.

questions.question: It's Easter Day at Queen's College, Oxford. What's the first dish brought to the table?
questions.answer: A red herring set like a man on horseback, on a corn salad
wrong: A pike set like a soldier on guard, on watercress
A great pie baked in the shape of the college gate
A gammon carved like a swan, on a bed of parsley
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: the first dish brought to the table on Easter-day, is a red herring, riding away on horseback, that is to say, a herring placed by the cook, something after the likeness of a man on horseback, set on a corn sallad.

questions.question: It's Easter eve in Cumberland, and the boys have been begging eggs. What do they do with them?
questions.answer: Boil and dye them, then roll and toss them about the fields
wrong: Hide them in the hedges for the girls to find
Leave them on the church step for the poor
Blow them out and hang them on a thorn bush
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: These eggs are hardened by boiling, and tinged with the juice of herbs, broom-flowers, &c. The eggs being thus prepared, the boys go out and play with them in the fields; rolling them up and down, like bowls, upon the ground

questions.question: It's 1 April 1826, and the youngsters want to make an April fool of you. Which errand might they send you on?
questions.answer: To a shop for half a pint of 'pigeon's milk'
wrong: To the grocer's for an ounce of 'sunbeam salt'
To the draper's for a yard of 'thunder ribbon'
To the baker's for a dozen 'yesterday's buns'
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: The like knowledge is also gained by an errand to some shop for half a pint of “pigeon’s milk,” or an inquiry at a bookseller’s for the “Life and Adventures of Eve’s Mother.”

questions.question: It's 1 April 1825. A boy stops you: 'Sir, there's something out of your pocket.' 'What?' What does he say next?
questions.answer: 'Your hand, sir. Ah! you April fool!'
wrong: 'A hole, sir, and your money with it!'
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: the waggery of the day is--“Sir, there’s something _out_ of your pocket.” “Where?” “There!” “What?” “Your _hand_, sir--Ah! you April fool!”

questions.question: It's Easter Monday at Bury St Edmund's, and there's a spirited game of trap-and-ball going on until sunset. Who's playing?
questions.answer: Twelve old women, led by a celebrated 'mistress of the sport'
wrong: The town's twelve aldermen in their gowns
The grammar-school boys against the choir
The bell-ringers against the town's bakers
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: On Shrove Tuesday, Easter Monday, and the Whitsuntide festivals, twelve old women side off for a game at trap-and-ball, which is kept up with the greatest spirit and vigour until sunset.

questions.question: It's May-day in the London suburbs, about 1805, and a Jack-o'-the-Green is dancing. What's he carrying?
questions.answer: A long walking stick with floral wreaths, whisked about
wrong: A tin trumpet to blow at every corner
A brass bell to ring at every door
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: A Jack-o’-the-Green always carried a long walking stick with floral wreaths; he whisked it about in the dance, and afterwards walked with it in high estate like a lord mayor’s footman.

questions.question: It's May-day on the green at Temple Sowerby, Westmorland, and there's a grindstone for first prize. What's the contest?
questions.answer: Lying: the best liar takes the grindstone
wrong: Carrying a sack of meal up the fell
Whistling longest on a single breath
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: which consist of a grindstone as the head prize; a hone or whetstone, for a razor, as the second; and whetstones of an inferior description, for those who can only reach a state of mediocrity in “the noble art of lying.”

questions.question: It's dawn on 1 May 1791, and a crowd heads into the fields. What are they up to?
questions.answer: Washing their faces in the dew, to make themselves beautiful
wrong: Hunting four-leaved clover to wear all May
Listening for the first cuckoo, for luck
Racing to be first to touch the maypole
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: a number of persons went into the fields and bathed their faces with the dew on the grass, under the idea that it would render them beautiful.

questions.question: It's 8 May, Flora day, and the whole town is given over to mirth, music and feasting. Someone has been caught working. What happens to them?
questions.answer: Carried off astride a pole and made to leap the river, or pay
wrong: Set in the stocks with a garland round their neck
Made to dance alone in the market-place
Their tools hung on the maypole till evening
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: Should any persons be found at work, they are instantly seized, set astride on a pole, and jolted away on men’s shoulders, amidst thousands of huzzas, &c., and at last sentenced to leap _over_ the river

questions.question: It's Holy Thursday, and the parish schoolboys follow the minister round to the parish boundaries. What are they doing?
questions.answer: Striking the boundaries with peeled willow wands
wrong: Lighting lanterns at each boundary stone
Planting an acorn by each boundary stone
Tying a ribbon to each boundary tree
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: followed by the boys of the parish school, headed by their master, to go in procession to the different parish boundaries; which boundaries the boys strike with peeled willow wands that they bear in their hands, and this is called “beating the bounds.”

questions.question: It's 1751, and a woolcomber and his wife from Weathersfield appear at the manor court of Little Dunmow. What do they claim?
questions.answer: The flitch of bacon, by the custom of the manor
wrong: A cheese, for the best-kept cottage garden
A new spinning wheel, from the lord of the manor
The right to graze a cow on the common
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: “John Shakeshanks, woolcomber, and Anne his wife, of the parish of Weathersfield, in Essex, appeared at the customary court at Dunmow-parva, and claim’d the bacon according to the custom of that manor.”

questions.question: It's Midsummer eve in Ripon, and you moved to a new neighbourhood this year. What does custom expect of you?
questions.answer: Spread a table in the street with bread, cheese and ale for all
wrong: Sweep the street from your door to the market cross
Give a loaf to each of the four nearest houses
Ring the minster bell once at midnight
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: every housekeeper, who, in the course of the year, has changed his residence into a new neighbourhood, spreads a table before his door in the street, with bread, cheese, and ale, for those who choose to resort to it.

questions.question: It's St John's eve in Chester, 1564, and the watch is being set with a pageant 'according to ancient custom'. What's in it?
questions.answer: Four giants, a unicorn, a camel, a dragon and hobby-horses
wrong: A whale, a mermaid, a ship and a pair of lions
A castle on wheels, a phoenix and twelve bears
Three kings, a star, an ark and a griffin
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: a pageant which is expressly said to be “according to ancient custom,” is ordained to consist of four giants, one unicorn, one dromedary, one camel, one luce, one dragon, and six hobby-horses with other figures.

questions.question: It's Midsummer day in a Northumberland village, and there are stools out by the doors. What's on them?
questions.answer: Cushions of flowers set in clay, shown to beg for a feast
wrong: Bowls of milk for the passing fairies
Midsummer cakes, one for each traveller
Garlands of St John's wort for the vicar to bless
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: it is customary on this day to dress out stools with a cushion of flowers. A layer of clay is placed on the stool, and therein is stuck, with great regularity, an arrangement of all kinds of flowers, so close as to form a beautiful cushion.

questions.question: It's the month before Lammas, and the herdsmen's bands are slowly building something. What?
questions.answer: Towers of sods with a flagstaff, to meet at on Lammas day
wrong: Bonfires of furze on every hilltop
Stone cairns to mark the summer grazing
A great wicker hut for the Lammas feast
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: Each of these communities agreed to build a _tower_ in some conspicuous place, near the centre of their district, which was to serve as the place of their rendezvous on Lammas day. This tower was usually built of sods

questions.question: It's 1 August on the Thames, and six young watermen just out of their apprenticeships race from London Bridge to Chelsea. For what?
questions.answer: A waterman's coat and silver badge, Dogget's bequest
wrong: A purse of guineas and a new wherry
A gilt cup from the lord mayor
The right to row the king's barge for a year
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: to the purchase of a like coat and badge, to be rowed for in honour of the day by six young watermen whose apprenticeships had expired the year before.

questions.question: It's Bartholomew-tide in an old printing-house, and the journeymen are making new paper windows. What does the master give them?
questions.answer: A feast called a way-goose, before candle-light work begins
wrong: A day's holiday to see Bartholomew Fair
A new leather apron for every journeyman
A shilling each for the ink-maker's ale
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: at which time the master printer makes them a feast called a _way-goose_, to which is invited the corrector, founder, smith, ink-maker, &c.

questions.question: It's the end of harvest in Hertfordshire, and the reapers tie together the tops of the last blades of corn. What next?
questions.answer: Throw their sickles at it; whoever cuts the knot wins
wrong: Race round the field: the first back cuts the knot
Draw straws: the shortest straw cuts the knot
Pelt it with clods: whoever topples it wins
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: The reapers tie together the tops of the last blades of corn, which they call “mare,” and standing at some distance, throw their sickles at it, and he who cuts the knot, has the prize, with acclamations and good cheer.

questions.question: It's harvest at Hitchin, and a farmer drives furiously home with his last load of corn. What are the people chasing him with?
questions.answer: Bowls full of water, to throw on it
wrong: Lanterns, to light him home through the lanes
Handbells, rung till the cart's unloaded
Sheaves of their own, to toss on the load
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: it was formerly the custom at Hitchin, in Hertfordshire, for each farmer to drive furiously home with the last load of his corn, while the people ran after him with bowls full of water in order to throw on it

questions.question: It's a September play-day at old Eton, and the scholars are off to gather nuts. What must they do first?
questions.answer: Write verses on autumn's plenty and the coming winter's cold
wrong: Construe a page of Virgil to the head master
Sing a Latin grace in the chapel
Pay a penny each towards the masters' supper
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: but before leave was granted for their excursion, they were required to write verses on the fruitfulness of autumn, and the deadly cold of the coming winter.

questions.question: It's autumn in cider country, and the farmers have left plenty of small apples, 'griggles', on the trees. Who are they for?
questions.answer: The village boys, who climb up and clear the trees
wrong: The pigs, turned into the orchard after picking
The parson, as part of his tithe
The wassailers, to hang up as offerings at Christmas
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: The small apples are called _griggles_. These, the farmers leave pretty abundantly on the trees, with an understanding that the urchins will have mercy on the boughs

questions.question: It's bailiff-election day at Kidderminster, and the town-house bell rings. What starts?
questions.answer: 'Lawless hour': everyone pelts each other with cabbage stalks
wrong: A race to the church to be first to vote
The town crier reads the old charter aloud
Every shop must put up its shutters for an hour
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: On the election of a bailiff the inhabitants assemble in the principal streets to throw cabbage stalks at each other. The town-house bell gives signal for the affray. This is called lawless hour.

questions.question: It's Michaelmas day. What's the popular saying about eating goose today?
questions.answer: You'll never want money all the year round
wrong: Your own geese will thrive all year
The frost will hold off till Martinmas
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: If you eat goose on Michaelmas-day you will never want money all the year round.

questions.question: It's the first week of October at St Magnus, London Bridge. By Sir John Salter's will, what must the Salters' beadles say there?
questions.answer: 'How do you do brother Salter? I hope you are well!'
wrong: 'God rest Sir John, who gave us bread and salt!'
'Brother Salter, the salt is sweet this year!'
'Here's to Sir John, the Salters' good friend!'
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: ordered that the beadles and servants should go to the said church the first week in October, three times each person, and say, “How do you do brother Salter? I hope you are well!”

questions.question: It's St Simon and St Jude's day. What weather does everyone expect?
questions.answer: Rain: the day is held as rainy as St Swithin's
wrong: The first hard frost of the winter
A gale to strip the last leaves
A fine day, the last of the summer
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: This anniversary was deemed as rainy as St. Swithin’s.

questions.question: It's Hallowe'en in Ireland. A young woman lays three nuts on the bars of the grate, each named for a lover. One cracks and jumps. What does it mean?
wrong: That lover will propose before Christmas
That lover is thinking of her that very moment
That lover will travel far before they meet
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: If a nut cracks or jumps, the lover will prove unfaithful; if it begins to blaze or burn, he has a regard for the person making the trial.

questions.question: It's the eve of 1 November in North Wales, and the autumn fire is lit. Everyone runs through the smoke and throws in a stone. Why do they all run off at the end?
questions.answer: To escape the black short-tailed sow
wrong: To chase the last sparks down the hill
To be home before the church bell tolls
To beat the fairies to the crossroads
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: such as running through the fire and smoke, each casting a stone into the fire, and all running off at the conclusion to escape from the black short-tailed sow

questions.question: At the country sports, ten or eleven candidates are tied in something up to their necks for a race of about five hundred yards. What's the sport?
questions.answer: Jumping in sacks, for a cheese
wrong: Rolling in barrels, for a ham
Hopping in hampers, for a goose
Shuffling in blankets, for a pudding
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: Ten or eleven candidates are chosen; they are tied in sacks up to their necks, and have to jump about five hundred yards.

questions.question: Martins have built a nest in the corner of your bedroom window. What does it mean?
questions.answer: Good luck, the more so if the same birds come back
wrong: A wedding in the house within the year
A hard winter is on its way
Someone in the house will soon go overseas
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: It is considered a presage of good, for this bird to build its nest in the corner of the bedroom-window; and particularly so, should the first inhabitants return in the season.

questions.question: It's St Clement's day and the boys have been round the houses. What have they collected, and what happens to it?
questions.answer: Apples, roasted together, some dropped hot into ale or cider
wrong: Candle-ends, to light a bonfire on the green
Flour and lard, for a great pancake on the hill
Nuts, cracked by the fire to tell fortunes
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: Having collected a good store of apples, which they seldom failed to do, the boys repaired to some one of their houses, where they roasted and ate the apples

questions.question: It's early December in the north of England, and there's a Penny Lottery on. What might your penny win you?
questions.answer: A whole garden, sold while it lies dormant
wrong: A year's free shaving at the barber's
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: About this time, when gardens look in a dormant state, there are frequently Penny Lotteries in the north of England; and very often a whole garden is purchased for one penny.

questions.question: It's St Nicholas's day, long ago, and the choir boys of a cathedral choose one of their number. To be what?
questions.answer: A bishop, in robes and mitre, until Innocents' day
wrong: The saint's page, carrying gifts to the poor
Keeper of the keys, to lock the masters out
Captain of the bell-ringers until New Year
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: the choir boys in cathedral churches, chose one of their number to maintain the state and authority of a bishop, for which purpose the boy was habited in rich episcopal robes, wore a mitre on his head, and bore a crosier in his hand

questions.question: It's the St Nicholas visit. Each of the family leaves a shoe on a table in a room that's then carefully locked. What's found in the morning?
questions.answer: The table covered with bonbons, toys and trinkets
wrong: Every shoe newly blacked and mended
A letter from the saint tucked in each shoe
Each shoe turned round to point at the door
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: the board is found covered with _bons bons_, toys, and trinkets.

questions.question: It's St Thomas's day in Kent, and women are going 'a gooding' for money. What do they give in return?
questions.answer: Sprigs of palm and branches of primroses
wrong: Candles dipped for the long nights
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: Going a _gooding_ on St. Thomas’s day formerly prevailed in England. Women begged money, and in return presented the donors with sprigs of palm and branches of primroses.

questions.question: It's Christmas eve, 1790, in Devon, and the country people sing a wassail. What do they do with the toast from the wassail-bowl?
questions.answer: Throw it to the apple-trees, for a fruitful year
wrong: Float it on the mill-pond for the fish
Lay it on the hearth for the Christmas spirits
Share it with the first stranger at the door
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: it was then customary for the country people to sing a wassail or drinking-song, and throw the toast from the wassail-bowl to the apple-trees in order to have a fruitful year.

questions.question: Christmas eve at Quainton, Bucks: two thousand people go by lantern-light to watch a blackthorn bud. It doesn't. What do they decide?
questions.answer: That 25 December can't be the right Christmas-day
wrong: That the parish must plant a new thorn
That a poor harvest is coming next year
That the vicar must bless the tree at Twelfth-night
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: The people finding no appearance of a bud, it was agreed by all, that December 25 (new style) could not be the right Christmas-day, and accordingly refused going to church

questions.question: It's Christmas morning, and the old folk tell the children to go down to the valley and stoop to the ground. What will they hear?
questions.answer: The bells of a church beneath them, ringing merrily
wrong: The fairies' Christmas feast under the hill
The old mill turning beneath the water
The river singing under the ice
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: Even now, it is usual on Christmas morning for old men and women to tell their children and young friends to go to the valley, stoop down, and hear the bells ring merrily.

questions.question: It's St Stephen's day in the North Riding of Yorkshire. Large goose pies go to needy neighbours, all but one. What becomes of that one?
questions.answer: It's put by and not tasted till Candlemas
wrong: It's given to the vicar for Twelfth-night
It's sent to the lord of the manor with the rent
It's eaten by the bell-ringers on New Year's eve
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: except one which is carefully laid up, and not tasted till the purification of the virgin, called Candlemas.

questions.question: It's Childermas, 1517, among the sages of the law, and Henry VIII has ordered that a mock king should sit and have due service. Which king?
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: “that the _king of cockneys_, on _Childermas-day_, should sit and have due service; and that he and all his officers should use honest manner and good order

questions.question: It's St Patrick's day: the bells are ringing and the piper's playing. What have the children got pinned to their sleeves?
questions.answer: 'Patrick's crosses': little prints of a cross or the saint
wrong: Tiny paper stars cut out by their mothers
Little bells to ring in the procession
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: children have “Patrick’s crosses” pinned to their sleeves. These are small prints of various kinds; some of them merely represent a cross, others are representations of Saint Patrick

questions.question: It's the king's birthday, 1819, at Bexhill in Sussex, and twenty-five old men dine together at the Bell Inn. What's special about them?
questions.answer: Their ages averaged eighty-one, the king's own age
wrong: Each had served at sea under Nelson
They were all born the same week as the king
They had rung the bells at his coronation
questions.source: Hone's Every-Day Book (1826-27)
questions.note: Twenty-five old men, inhabitants of the parish, whose united ages amounted to 2025, averaging eighty-one each (the age of the king) dined together at the Bell Inn

questions.question: You're hanging a horseshoe over the door as a luck token. Which way up should it go, by the popular notion?
questions.answer: Points upward, or else the luck may be spilled out
wrong: Points towards the street, to call the luck in
On its side, with the points towards the hinges
Points to the left, towards the rising sun
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: From a scientific standpoint, therefore, the horse-shoe, when used as a protective symbol, should be placed with its convex arch uppermost; but as a luck token, the reverse position is the proper one, else, according to a popular notion, the luck may be spilled out.

questions.question: You're nailing up a horseshoe in eastern Pennsylvania. Which way do the prongs point, and why?
questions.answer: Inward, so the luck may be spilled into the house
wrong: Outward, to catch the luck of passers-by
Downward, so the luck runs onto the doorstep
Towards the chimney, where luck comes in
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: In eastern Pennsylvania, however, even in recent times, the horse-shoe is often placed with the prongs pointing inward, so that the luck may be spilled into the house.

questions.question: You find a horseshoe in Northumberland and carefully count the holes with no nails in. What do they tell you?
questions.answer: How soon you may expect to be married
wrong: How many children you will one day have
How many pounds you will come into this year
How many visitors will call before Sunday
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: In Northumberland the holes free of nails are carefully counted, as these indicate, presumably in years, how soon the finder of the shoe may expect to be married.

questions.question: You live among the Wends of the Spreewald and have just found a horseshoe. What mustn't you do?
questions.answer: Tell any neighbour about your good fortune
wrong: Pick it up with your bare right hand
Carry it home after the sun has set
Let it touch the ground a second time
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: the lucky finder of a horse-shoe is careful not to tell any neighbor of his good fortune, but proceeds at once to fasten the shoe over the door of his house, or on the threshold, with three nails, and by three blows of a hammer, so that evil spirits may not enter.

questions.question: You find a horseshoe in Tuscany. Where do you keep it?
questions.answer: In a little red bag with some hay, in your bed
wrong: In a blue bag hung over the kitchen fire
Under the doorstep, wrapped in a vine leaf
In your left boot until the next full moon
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: In Tuscany a horse-shoe when found is placed in a small red bag with some hay, which the Tuscans consider also a luck-bringing article, and the twofold charm is kept in its owner’s bed.

questions.question: In the Thuringian Forest, an old shoe off the road won't do for your bedroom threshold. Who must have forged it?
questions.answer: A bachelor of good character, on Saint John's Eve
wrong: A seventh son, on Midsummer morning
A widowed smith, at the dark of the moon
A smith's apprentice, on his very first day
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: in order to serve its purpose as a talisman, a Thuringian horse-shoe must have been forged by a bachelor of wholesome life and good character, on Saint John’s Eve.

questions.question: It's about 1850 in Perthshire, and your minister preaches against the horseshoes on the farm doors. What does the parish do?
questions.answer: Move them from the outsides of the doors to the insides
wrong: Paint them black so he can't spot them
Nail them up on the church door instead
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: his superstitious parishioners removed the guardian horse-shoes from the outsides of the doors, and nailed them up on the insides.

questions.question: In the far north of Scotland, you and your neighbour have fallen out. Where does a horseshoe keep you both safe?
wrong: Over your door, points towards their house
Buried at midnight under their gate
On your roof, facing their chimney
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: if a horse-shoe be placed between the houses of quarrelsome neighbors, neither incurs any risk of evil as a result of the other’s ill-wishes.

questions.question: You're out with the Scottish fishing fleet and a shipmate swears. What does everyone do?
questions.answer: Cry "Cauld airn!" and each grab a piece of iron
wrong: Spit over the side and touch the mast
Throw a pinch of salt into the sea
Turn round three times and whistle
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: if, when plying their vocation, one of their number chance to indulge in profanity, the others at once call out, “Cauld airn!” and each grasps a handy piece of the metal as a counter influence to the misfortune which would else pursue them throughout the day.

questions.question: You walk into a house in north-west Scotland while the butter is being churned. What's expected of you?
questions.answer: Lay your hand on the churn, to show you mean no harm
wrong: Leave at once and come back when it's done
Drop a pinch of salt in for luck
Say "God speed the butter" from the doorway
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: In northwestern Scotland whoever enters a house where butter is being made is expected to lay his hand upon the churn, thereby signifying that he has no evil designs against the butter-maker

questions.question: It's 1627, and the salt falls towards a superstitious guest at dinner. What finally comforts him?
questions.answer: A waiter pouring wine in his lap
wrong: Throwing a pinch over his left shoulder
Being served a second helping of bread
The whole table drinking his health
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: Bishop Hall wrote, in 1627, that when salt fell towards a superstitious guest at dinner, he was wont to exhibit signs of mental agitation, and refused to be comforted until one of the waiters had poured wine in his lap.

questions.question: You spill the salt in Norway. What will it cost you, by popular belief?
questions.answer: As many tears as it takes to dissolve the salt
wrong: A year of bad luck for every grain
A lost coin for every grain
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: According to a popular Norwegian belief, one will shed as many tears as may suffice to dissolve the quantity of salt which he has spilled

questions.question: You spill salt in Bucks County, Pennsylvania. Besides tossing a pinch over your left shoulder, what must you do?
questions.answer: Crawl under the table and come out the other side
wrong: Walk three times round the table
Sweep it up with your left hand only
Move your chair to the other side
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: In Bucks County, Pennsylvania, in order to avert ill-luck after salt has been spilled, one should not only toss a pinch of the spilled salt over the left shoulder, but should also crawl under a table and come out on the opposite side.

questions.question: You've spilt salt in New England, and a toss over the left shoulder isn't enough. Where must the grains go?
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: for in order thoroughly to break the spell, these particles must be thrown on the stove.

questions.question: By one remarkable superstition, what awaits you in the hereafter for spilling salt?
questions.answer: A year outside the gate of Paradise for every grain
wrong: Counting every grain again before you go in
No salt at all at the heavenly feast
A year sweeping heaven's steps for every grain
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: as a penalty for spilling salt, one must wait outside the gate of Paradise for as many years as there are grains of salt spilled.

questions.question: A 1586 book of symbols says spilling salt on the table is ominous. What is lucky to spill?
questions.answer: Wine, especially if unmixed with water
wrong: Milk, especially fresh from the cow
Water, especially from a holy well
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: Wherefore many consider it ominous to spill salt on the table, and, on the other hand, propitious to spill wine, especially if unmixed with water.

questions.question: In the north of England, someone helps you to salt at table. What does the old couplet say?
questions.answer: "Help me to salt, help me to sorrow"
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: it is reckoned unlucky to be helped to salt at table, and this idea has found expression in the popular couplet, “Help me to salt, help me to sorrow.”

questions.question: In Russia, you have to pass your neighbour the salt. How do you stop it causing a quarrel?
questions.answer: Smile amicably as you offer it
wrong: Pass it with your left hand
Set it down rather than hand it over
Say a blessing over it first
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: But if in proffering the salt one smiles amicably, all danger of a quarrel is happily averted, and the act is wholly relieved of its ominous character.

questions.question: You run a Japanese household. When won't you buy salt?
wrong: On the first day of the month
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: The mistress of a household will not buy it at night, and when purchased in the daytime a small quantity is thrown into the fire in order to prevent discord in the family, and to avert misfortune generally.

questions.question: It's 1789 and Robert Burns's family escort him to his new house at Ellisland. What's carried in their midst?
questions.answer: A bowl of salt resting on the family Bible
wrong: A horseshoe on a velvet cushion
A loaf of bread and a lump of coal
Embers from the old hearth in an iron pot
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: he was escorted on his route thither along the banks of the river Nith by a procession of relatives, and in their midst was borne a bowl of salt resting on the family Bible.

questions.question: Why might a Scottish fisherman throw a little salt into the sea?
wrong: To pay the sea for its fish
To keep the nets from rotting
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: Scotch fishermen have a traditional custom of salting their nets “for luck,” and they also sometimes throw a little salt into the sea “to blind the fairies.”

questions.question: You're an Andalusian peasant. What's the most endearing thing you can call your sweetheart?
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: no more endearing or flattering language can be used in addressing a woman, whether wife or sweetheart, than to call her “the salt-box of my love.”

questions.question: It's St Augustine's time, and you sneeze while putting on your shoes in the morning. What do you do?
wrong: Take them off and start with the other foot
Put the shoes on the wrong feet
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: St. Augustine wrote that, in his time, so prevalent was faith in the omens of sneezing that a man would return to bed if he happened to sneeze while putting on his shoes in the morning.

questions.question: In Elizabethan England, you sneeze twice while talking business with someone. What should you do?
questions.answer: Get up and go straight about your business: you'll prosper
wrong: Let the matter drop, for it will come to nought
Wait for a third sneeze before deciding
Shake hands at once and seal the bargain
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: If that any man talk with another about any matter and snese twise or iiij tymes, let him by and by arise, yf he sett, or yf he be stand, let him move hymself and go straightway without any stays about his business, for he shall prosper.

questions.question: In Selkirkshire, you sneeze as you first step out of bed. What does it tell you?
questions.answer: Strangers will come today, one for each sneeze
wrong: Letters will come today, one for each sneeze
Rain will fall today, an hour for each sneeze
You'll quarrel today, once for each sneeze
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: “When they sneeze in first stepping out of bed in the morning, they are thence certified that strangers will be there in the course of the day, in numbers corresponding to the times they sneeze.”

questions.question: In old Flanders, someone sneezes while you're in the middle of a story. What does it prove?
questions.answer: That what you're saying is the truth
wrong: That you'd better change the subject
That a stranger is at the door
That you'll be proved wrong by nightfall
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: It was a Flemish belief that a sneeze during a conversation proved that what one said was the truth, a doctrine which must have commended itself to snuff-takers.

questions.question: You sneeze twice in old Japan. What does it mean?
questions.answer: Someone is finding fault with you
wrong: An old friend is about to visit
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: Thus, one sneeze indicates that some one is praising him, while two betoken censure or disparagement; a triple sneeze is commonplace, and means simply that a person has taken cold.

questions.question: You sneeze on New Year's Eve in China, an ill omen for the year. How do you put it right?
questions.answer: Beg a tortoise cake from each of three families, eaten by midnight
wrong: Light three red candles before midnight
Sweep the doorstep three times before midnight
Eat a bowl of noodles without speaking
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: According to a Chinese superstition a sneeze on New Year’s Eve is ominous for the coming year; and, to offset this, the sneezer must visit three families of different surnames, and beg from each a small tortoise-shaped cake, which must be eaten before midnight.

questions.question: You're a gentleman in old France and you sneeze in company. What does etiquette require?
questions.answer: Take off your hat, then return everyone's salutes
wrong: Turn your back and cover your face
Bow to the host and beg his pardon
Leave the room until it has passed
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: In France the rules of etiquette formerly required that a gentleman who sneezed in the presence of another should take off his hat, and on the subsidence of the paroxysm he was expected formally to return the salutes of all present.

questions.question: Someone sneezes on Rarotonga. What do you say, and why?
questions.answer: "Ha! you have come back!", to welcome their wandering spirit
wrong: "Go away!", to chase a spirit out of them
"Stay a while!", to keep their luck from leaving
"Bless the wind!", for the breath that left them
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: They therefore deem it proper to welcome back the wandering spirit, the form of greeting varying in the different islands. The phrase employed by the natives of Raratonga, for example, means “Ha! you have come back!”

questions.question: You sneeze in Siam. By the Siamese account, what has just happened?
questions.answer: The Supreme Judge has turned to your page in his book
wrong: Someone in the house is about to quarrel
Your luck has turned for the coming week
A traveller has set out on the road to you
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: They believe that the Supreme Judge of the spiritual world is continually turning over the pages of a book containing an account of the life and doings of every human being; and when he comes to the page relating to any individual, the latter never fails to sneeze.

questions.question: A poor soul under a Wurmlingen bridge sneezes three times as you cross. What would have freed him?
questions.answer: Saying "God help thee!" for the third sneeze too
wrong: Dropping a coin into the stream below
Calling his name out loud three times
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: Thereupon a voice from under the bridge exclaimed pitifully, “If you had only said, ‘God help thee!’ a third time, I should have been freed from the spell which binds me.”

questions.question: Someone hiccups in Turkistan. What's the polite, luck-bringing thing to say?
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: When, also, any one hiccoughs, it is etiquette to say, “You stole something from me,” and this phrase at such times is supposed to produce good luck.

questions.question: It's 1455 in Germany and you sneeze three times. What did popular belief say that meant?
questions.answer: Four thieves are about the house
wrong: Three guests are on the road
A letter is coming from far away
Rain before the next church bell
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: we learn that in Germany there was a popular belief that three sneezes indicated the presence of four thieves around the house.

questions.question: Your cat sneezes in Shetland. What's it telling you?
questions.answer: Cold north winds in summer, snow in winter
wrong: A visitor before the week is out
A good catch for the boats tomorrow
A letter from someone over the sea
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: In Shetlandic and Welsh folk-lore the sneeze of a cat indicates cold north winds in summer and snow in winter

questions.question: You farm by Hesiod's "Works and Days". Which day of the month is excellent for reaping corn?
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: Thus he recommends the eleventh of the month as excellent for reaping corn, and the twelfth for shearing sheep.

questions.question: Why won't West Sussex folk let the children go blackberrying on 10 October?
questions.answer: The Devil goes afield that day
wrong: The fairies claim the hedges that day
The first frost spoils the fruit that day
The berries belong to the birds from then
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: The peasantry of West Sussex in England will not permit their children to go blackberrying on the tenth day of October, on account of a belief that the Devil goes afield on that day

questions.question: You're getting married in 1890s Glasgow, like a large share of couples there. Which day do you pick?
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: This opinion finds favor in Glasgow, where a large proportion of marriages take place on this day; whereas, in the midland counties of England, less than two per cent. of the weddings occur on the sixth day of the week.

questions.question: In Shropshire, you hear something new on a Friday. What does it do to you?
questions.answer: Gives you another wrinkle and adds a year to your age
wrong: Brings a week of rain after it
Turns out to be false by Sunday
Means worse news before the month is out
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: according to a Shropshire saying, “if you hear anything new on a Friday, it gives you another wrinkle on your face, and adds another year to your age.”

questions.question: It's a Friday in Ireland and a stranger knocks. What should you take especial care to do?
questions.answer: Not open the door to them
wrong: Offer them a cup of milk
Ask their name before they cross the threshold
Give them a pinch of salt as they leave
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: In Ireland Friday is _facile princeps_ among unlucky days, and especial care should be taken not to open the door of one’s dwelling to any stranger on that day.

questions.question: Paris theatres put on nearly two hundred new pieces a year. For many years, how many opened on a Friday?
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: This is shown by statistics of the Parisian theatres, where there are produced on an average nearly two hundred new pieces annually, and for many years not one of these has had its first performance on a Friday.

questions.question: You're giving a Paris dinner party and find you're thirteen. Who do you send for?
questions.answer: A quatorzième, to occupy the fourteenth seat
wrong: A priest, to bless the table
A footman, to lay one place fewer
The concierge's cat, for the fourteenth chair
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: The Parisian _pique-assiette_, a person whose title corresponds to the English “trencher friend” or “sponger,” is also known as a _quatorzième_, his chief mission being to occupy the fourteenth seat at a banquet.

questions.question: You've rashly dined thirteen at table. How is all the evil averted?
questions.answer: The whole company rises to its feet together
wrong: The youngest guest sits apart for the pudding
A fourteenth place is laid for the pudding
Everyone touches the table leg at once
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: All evil, however, was supposed to be averted by the entire company rising to their feet together.

questions.question: You've booked the thirteenth box at an Italian theatre. What number is on its door?
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: In Italy shrewd theatrical managers have found it expedient to change the number of Box 13 to 12A

questions.question: You're in Persia and need to mention the number thirteen. What do you say instead?
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: When they wish to allude to this number, instead of mentioning the proper term, they use words meaning “much more” or “nothing.”

questions.question: Your baker gives you thirteen loaves for twelve. Why did the custom begin?
questions.answer: Heavy fines for short weight: the extra loaf was a precaution
wrong: The oven held twelve loaves and one for the baker
The thirteenth was a tithe loaf for the church
Bakers kept one back to test the batch
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: it was formerly a common practice to give thirteen loaves for twelve, the extra piece being called the _in-bread_ or _to-bread_. This custom is supposed to have originated at a time when heavy fines were imposed for short weights, the additional bread being given by bakers as a precautionary measure.

questions.question: A courtier tells Edward VI that Christ's College, a Master and twelve Fellows, is a superstitious number, and to cut a Fellowship or two. What does the king do?
questions.answer: Adds a thirteenth Fellowship, to spoil the conceit
wrong: Takes away two Fellowships, as advised
Adds a second Master to make it even
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: “Oh, no!” said the King, “I have a better way than that to mar their conceit; I will add a thirteenth Fellowship unto them;” which he did accordingly, and so it remaineth unto this day.

questions.question: You're building a house in Siam. What must every staircase have?
wrong: Twelve steps, one for each month
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: every house must have an uneven number of rooms, windows, and doors; each staircase must have an uneven number of steps.

questions.question: A Bavarian peasant passing a haunted place carries a new knife marked with three crosses, a loaf baked on Epiphany Eve, and what?
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: considers himself amply fortified against evil if he takes the precaution to carry three things; namely, (1) a new knife which has never cut anything, marked on the blade with three crosses; (2) a loaf of bread baked on Epiphany Eve; (3) a black cat.

questions.question: You're Cato the Censor, told gravely that rats have gnawed your boots. What's your reply?
questions.answer: It would portend evil only if the boots had gnawed the rats
wrong: Then the gods want me to stay at home today
Then I shall go to the Senate barefoot
Then send for the soothsayer at once
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: “If the boots had gnawed the rats,” he said, “it might have portended evil.”

questions.question: You're an ancient Greek farmer with mice in the field. How do you drive them away?
questions.answer: Write them a message and stick it on a stone in the field
wrong: Bury a bronze cat at the field's edge
Leave them a share of grain at the gate
Ring a bell at each corner at dawn
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: The Grecian husbandmen were accustomed to drive away mice by writing them a message on a piece of paper and sticking it on a stone in the infested field.

questions.question: On Christmas Eve, a Bohemian peasant throws the dinner leftovers on the barn floor. What does he say?
questions.answer: "O mice, eat these remnants and leave the grain in peace!"
wrong: "Little mice, go to the neighbour's barn!"
"Feast tonight, mice, and fast all year!"
"Christ's Mass for man and mouse alike!"
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: whatever food remains from the midday meal is thrown upon the barn floor, and the following sentence is repeated: “O mice, eat these remnants and leave the grain in peace!”

questions.question: You're defending some rats summoned to court at Autun. Why can't your clients appear?
questions.answer: The road is full of cats, all alert to the case
wrong: The summons wasn't read in their own tongue
It's harvest time and they're busy
Their homes are under the courthouse floor
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: He represented to the judge that his clients found it extremely difficult to obey the summons issued to them by the court, owing to their being obliged to traverse a region abounding in cats

questions.question: How did people in Britain once believe they could be rid of rats?
questions.answer: By cursing them in rhyming verse
wrong: By whistling a tune backwards in the barn
By writing their names on the granary door
By ringing the church bell at midnight
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: In Great Britain there formerly prevailed a belief that rats could be rhymed to death by anathematizing them in metrical verse

questions.question: Among the Kirghis, you hear a magpie cry from the east. What's coming?
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: If from the north, it portends evil; from the south, a remarkable occurrence; from the east, it denotes the coming of guests; and from the west, a journey.

questions.question: Why, say the Bohemians, does a great horse let a little child lead it?
questions.answer: It sees everything ten times bigger than it is
wrong: It knows children can see spirits
It remembers being a foal itself
Children smell of milk, which calms it
questions.source: Robert Means Lawrence, The Magic of the Horse-shoe (1898)
questions.note: It is a Bohemian superstition that a horse sees everything magnified tenfold, and that this is the reason why the noble animal submits to being led by a little child.
